name: Bed Frames
summary: A frame just has to support the mattress properly. The one feature with health evidence is raising the head of the bed, which helps night-time reflux.
what:
Frames range from simple slatted platforms to box-spring foundations and powered adjustable bases. For sleep, the job is even support: slats close enough together, plus a centre rail and legs on larger sizes. Many mattress warranties specify the base, so check before you buy.

**Adjustable bases** raise the head and/or the feet. Raising the upper body helps night-time heartburn and can reduce snoring that's worse on your back; massage, 'zero-gravity' and app features are comfort extras.

evidence.summary: There's no evidence that frame style affects health. Raising the head of the bed has small trials behind it: a systematic review of five trials found it improved reflux symptoms and acid exposure, though all were at risk of bias. In one study of people with sleep apnea, raising the head and trunk 30° cut breathing events from about 24 to 18 an hour, which is an improvement but not a treatment on its own.

claims.claim: Raising the head of the bed reduces night-time reflux
claims.note: Small trials consistently show less acid exposure and fewer symptoms, and guidelines recommend it for night-time symptoms.

claims.claim: An adjustable base treats sleep apnea
claims.note: Elevation reduced apnea events modestly in one study. It doesn't replace diagnosis and proper treatment.

claims.claim: 'Zero-gravity' positions improve circulation and recovery
claims.note: No trials behind the claim.

claims.claim: Built-in massage improves sleep
claims.note: No evidence; it's a comfort feature.

look_for: Support that meets your mattress warranty: close-set slats (check the maker's maximum gap) or a solid platform.
A centre rail and support legs for queen and king sizes, and a weight limit that covers mattress plus sleepers.
A height that lets you sit on the edge with your feet flat, so getting in and out is easier and safer.
For reflux: something that raises your whole upper body, such as blocks under the head-end legs or an adjustable base, not just your head.
For powered bases: quiet motors, a way to lower it in a power cut, and a split base if partners want different positions.
skip: Massage modes, 'zero-gravity' presets and under-bed lights sold as health features.
Paying for sleep tracking built into a base. It can't diagnose anything either.
safety: Powered bases have moving parts that can trap fingers, limbs or pets. Keep children and animals clear.
Needing to sit up to breathe at night, or waking breathless, can signal heart or lung disease. See a clinician rather than just raising the bed.
Heartburn more than twice a week, trouble swallowing, vomiting or weight loss need medical assessment.
how_to_use: For reflux: raise the head end about 15-20 cm (6-8 in), stop eating 2-3 hours before bed, and try lying on your left side.

studies.title: Head of bed elevation to relieve gastroesophageal reflux symptoms: a systematic review
studies.authors: Albarqouni L, Moynihan R, Clark J, Scott AM, Duggan A, Del Mar C
studies.finding_summary: Five trials (228 people): two raised the bed on blocks, one used a wedge, two used both. All four trials reporting symptoms found improvement with elevation, backed by better oesophageal pH, but all were at high risk of bias.

studies.title: Effect of bed head elevation during sleep in symptomatic patients of nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux
studies.authors: Khan BA, Sodhi JS, Zargar SA, Javid G, Yattoo GN, Shah A, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 20 people with night-time reflux slept a week with the head of the bed raised on 20-cm blocks. Supine acid exposure, acid clearance time and symptom scores fell, and sleep disturbance improved in 65%.

studies.title: Head-Of-Bed Elevation (HOBE) for Improving Positional Obstructive Sleep Apnea (POSA): An Experimental Study
studies.authors: Iannella G, Cammaroto G, Meccariello G, Cannavicci A, Gobbi R, Lechien JR, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 45 people with obstructive sleep apnea slept with the head and trunk raised 30°. The apnea-hypopnea index fell from 23.8 to 17.7 events per hour, with less collapse at the soft palate and throat walls.

name: Bed Wedge Pillows
summary: An inclined foam wedge. Raising your upper body is one of the few reflux measures with trial support; it can't tell you whether your snoring is harmless.
what:
Wedges are firm foam inclines, usually about 18-30 cm (7-12 in) high. A **long, gentle wedge** that starts at your waist raises your whole upper body, which is the version that helps night-time reflux. Short, steep wedges mostly lift your head and can bend you at the waist. Knee and leg wedges are sold for back comfort and swollen legs.

The alternative is raising the head end of the bed itself on blocks or an adjustable base, which several reflux trials used.

evidence.summary: A 2021 systematic review of five trials (228 people; two used bed blocks, one a wedge, two both) found head-of-bed elevation improved reflux symptoms and acid exposure, though all trials were at high risk of bias. In a small 2026 trial of 24 people still having night-time reflux on a morning acid-suppressing drug, adding a wedge worked as well as an extra evening dose and improved sleep quality more. For snoring, elevation reduces breathing events modestly in some people; it doesn't treat sleep apnea.

claims.claim: A wedge relieves night-time acid reflux
claims.note: Small trials consistently show less acid exposure and fewer symptoms when the upper body is raised.

claims.claim: A wedge stops snoring
claims.note: It can help snoring that's worst on your back, but it can't tell you whether that snoring is a sign of sleep apnea.

claims.claim: Stacking pillows works just as well
claims.note: Stacked pillows mostly bend your neck and waist, which can press on your stomach and make reflux worse.

claims.claim: Leg wedges improve circulation
claims.note: Raising swollen legs can ease swelling; broader circulation claims haven't been tested.

look_for: Length: a wedge long enough to start at your waist or lower back, not just under your head.
Height: about 15-20 cm (6-8 in) of lift at the head end is the usual target for reflux.
Firm, high-density foam that doesn't sink overnight, and a non-slip base.
A width that suits how much you move, and a removable, washable cover.
skip: Short, steep 'reflux pillows' that only lift your head.
Cooling gel tops sold as a health feature.
safety: Heartburn more than twice a week, trouble or pain swallowing, vomiting, black stools or weight loss need medical assessment.
Needing to prop yourself up to breathe, or waking breathless, can signal heart failure or lung disease. See a doctor.
Loud snoring with daytime sleepiness or pauses in breathing: get checked for sleep apnea before relying on a wedge.
Never use wedges or sleep positioners for babies. They are a suffocation risk.
how_to_use: Combine it with not eating in the 2-3 hours before bed, and try lying on your left side.
Give it a couple of weeks; sleeping on an incline takes getting used to.

studies.title: Head of bed elevation to relieve gastroesophageal reflux symptoms: a systematic review
studies.authors: Albarqouni L, Moynihan R, Clark J, Scott AM, Duggan A, Del Mar C
studies.finding_summary: Five trials (228 people): two raised the bed on blocks, one used a wedge, two used both. All four trials reporting symptoms found improvement with elevation, backed by better oesophageal pH, but all were at high risk of bias.

studies.title: Effect of bed head elevation during sleep in symptomatic patients of nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux
studies.authors: Khan BA, Sodhi JS, Zargar SA, Javid G, Yattoo GN, Shah A, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 20 people with night-time reflux slept a week with the head of the bed raised on 20-cm blocks. Supine acid exposure, acid clearance time and symptom scores fell, and sleep disturbance improved in 65%.

studies.title: Wedge Pillow Versus Evening Proton Pump Inhibitor for Nocturnal Reflux Symptoms: A Noninferiority Randomized Trial
studies.authors: Hirunrattanaporn K, Prueksapanich P, Gonlachanvit S, Patcharatrakul T
studies.finding_summary: 24 people with night-time reflux despite a morning acid-suppressing drug added either a wedge pillow or an evening dose for 4 weeks. The wedge was not inferior for night-time symptoms and gave better sleep quality.

studies.title: Systematic review: Clinical effectiveness of interventions for the treatment of nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux
studies.authors: Schuitenmaker JM, Kuipers T, Smout AJPM, Fockens P, Bredenoord AJ
studies.finding_summary: 31 studies of night-time reflux treatments. The authors recommend a stepwise approach: head-of-bed elevation, a longer gap between dinner and bed, sleeping on the left side, then acid-suppressing medicine.

name: Blackout Curtains
summary: The simplest route to a dark bedroom. Lab work shows light during sleep affects heart rate and insulin; judge curtains by how well they seal, not the fabric claim.
what:
Blackout curtains, liners and shades use a dense weave or a coated backing to block light. How dark the room gets depends as much on fitting as on fabric: light leaks round the sides, top and bottom, so wide panels, rods mounted above and beyond the frame, and shades fitted inside the recess with side channels make the difference.

Many also cut draughts, and 'thermal' versions reduce heat gain and loss at the window.

evidence.summary: No trials test curtains themselves, but the case for darkness is supported in the lab: one night of sleep with moderate room light (100 lux) raised night-time heart rate and next-morning insulin resistance in healthy adults compared with dim light (under 3 lux). In 552 older adults, any light during the darkest hours was linked with more obesity, diabetes and hypertension, an observational finding that can't prove cause.

claims.claim: Blocking outside light helps you sleep
claims.note: Light at night suppresses melatonin and can wake you, especially at a summer dawn. The evidence is mechanistic and lab-based rather than trials of blinds.

claims.claim: Sleeping in the dark protects metabolic health
claims.note: A one-night lab study and observational data point the same way; long-term benefit hasn't been tested.

claims.claim: '100% blackout' means a pitch-dark room
claims.note: The fabric may block all light, but gaps round the frame usually don't.

claims.claim: Blackout curtains block noise
claims.note: Heavy fabric softens some higher-pitched sound; it won't silence traffic.

look_for: Coverage: panels wider and longer than the window, mounted above and beyond the frame, or a shade fitted inside the recess with side channels.
A blackout lining or coated backing. Hold the fabric up to a bright light to check.
Cordless designs if children live in or visit the home.
Washable, or at least easy to clean. Heavy curtains collect dust.
skip: 'Noise-cancelling' claims. Expect a small reduction, not silence.
Paying extra for a '100% blackout' fabric when the fit will leak light anyway.
safety: Looped cords on blinds and shades can strangle young children. Choose cordless or keep cords out of reach with tension devices.
A fully dark room makes night-time trips riskier, especially for older adults. Use a dim, warm night-light low down.
how_to_use: Open them, or get outside, soon after waking. Darkness at night works best alongside bright light in the morning.
Cover standby lights and chargers too.

studies.title: Light exposure during sleep impairs cardiometabolic function
studies.authors: Mason IC, Grimaldi D, Reid KJ, Warlick CD, Malkani RG, Abbott SM, Zee PC
studies.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
studies.finding_summary: In healthy adults, one night of sleep with moderate room light (100 lux) raised night-time heart rate, lowered heart rate variability and increased next-morning insulin resistance compared with sleep in dim light (under 3 lux).

studies.title: Light at night in older age is associated with obesity, diabetes, and hypertension
studies.authors: Kim M, Vu TH, Maas MB, Braun RI, Wolf MS, Roenneberg T, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 552 adults aged 63-84 wore light sensors for a week. Any light during the darkest 5 hours was linked with higher odds of obesity (1.82), diabetes (2.00) and hypertension (1.74); the design cannot show cause.

name: Blankets
summary: A layer you add or remove to fine-tune warmth. Comfort and washability are the point; no blanket has health benefits.
what:
Blankets let you adjust warmth night to night, which is easier than switching duvets. Cotton (woven, waffle or knit) is breathable and washable; wool is warm for its weight and handles moisture well; fleece and plush polyester are warm and cheap but trap heat and sweat; 'cooling' blankets use smooth synthetic or lyocell fibres that feel cool to the touch.

Layering is the useful idea for sleep: two light layers you can shed beat one heavy layer you kick off at 3am.

evidence.summary: There are no trials of blankets and health. Sleep-temperature research shows humid heat under the covers disturbs sleep, which supports breathable layers you can adjust. Beyond that, choose by feel.

claims.claim: Cooling blankets lower your body temperature
claims.note: They feel cool to the touch (sometimes quoted as a 'Q-max' value), but the sensation fades as the fabric warms. There's little sleep data.

claims.claim: Wool regulates temperature for better sleep
claims.note: Wool handles moisture well, and small wool-industry-funded studies found wool sleepwear helped slightly, but wool versus polyester bedding made no difference in a lab study.

look_for: Weight and weave for your climate. Open weaves (waffle, cellular) breathe best.
Machine-washable at the temperature you need.
A size that covers the bed without dragging on the floor.
Pilling resistance if you choose fleece or plush.
skip: 'Temperature-regulating' claims without data.
Treating organic or fair-trade labels as health features. They're ethical choices, which is a fine reason on its own.
safety: No loose blankets for babies under 12 months. Use a baby sleeping bag instead.

name: Blue Light Glasses
summary: Clear 'computer' lenses do nothing proven for eye strain or sleep. Amber lenses worn before bed have small trials behind them, but dimming the lights does much the same.
what:
Two different products share the name. **Clear or lightly tinted 'blue-light' lenses**, sold for screen use, filter a slice of blue light. **Amber or orange blue-blocking glasses**, worn in the last hours before bed, block most short-wavelength light, the kind that most strongly suppresses melatonin and pushes your body clock later.

Screens are only one source of evening light; overhead lighting and overall brightness matter too. Dimming lights and screens in the evening does much of what the glasses promise.

evidence.summary: A 2023 Cochrane review of 17 small trials found blue-filtering lenses may not reduce eye strain from screens, and their effect on sleep is uncertain (six trials split evenly, very low certainty). Small trials of amber lenses worn for 2 hours before bed are more encouraging: in 14 people with insomnia symptoms, a week of amber lenses improved sleep ratings compared with clear placebo lenses. No trial has shown any benefit for macular or retinal health.

claims.claim: Blue-light glasses reduce digital eye strain
claims.note: The Cochrane review found little or no difference from ordinary lenses (low-certainty evidence). Screen breaks and correcting your prescription do more.

claims.claim: Blue-light glasses improve sleep
claims.note: Amber lenses worn before bed helped in small trials; clear screen lenses have little evidence behind them.

claims.claim: They protect your eyes from damage by screen light
claims.note: No trial has shown a benefit to retinal or macular health, and screen light levels aren't known to damage the retina.

look_for: For sleep: amber or orange lenses with a published transmission chart showing they block most blue light (roughly 400-500 nm).
Wraparound frames so light doesn't reach your eyes from the sides.
Comfort if you'll wear them nightly, and a plan for the bright bathroom light that undoes them.
If you just want less glare, an anti-reflective coating on your normal glasses is enough.
skip: Clear 'computer' lenses sold to prevent eye strain or protect the retina.
'Clinically proven' or 'evidence-based' on the packaging without a cited trial.
Blocking blue light during the day. Daytime light keeps you alert and anchors your body clock.
safety: Don't drive in amber or orange lenses at night. They cut light and distort colours, including traffic signals.
Eye strain, headaches or blurred vision deserve a proper eye test; an uncorrected prescription is a common cause.
Trials occasionally reported headaches, discomfort and low mood with blue-blocking lenses. Stop if they don't suit you.
how_to_use: Put amber lenses on about 2 hours before bed and keep them on until lights out.
Dimming room lights and screens gets you most of the way without glasses.

studies.title: Blue-light filtering spectacle lenses for visual performance, sleep, and macular health in adults
studies.authors: Singh S, Keller PR, Busija L, McMillan P, Makrai E, Lawrenson JG, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 17 small RCTs. Blue-filtering lenses may not reduce eye strain from computer use, probably don't change visual acuity, and have uncertain effects on sleep (six trials split evenly, very low certainty); no trial assessed macular health.

studies.title: Blocking nocturnal blue light for insomnia: A randomized controlled trial
studies.authors: Shechter A, Kim EW, St-Onge MP, Westwood AJ
studies.finding_summary: 14 adults with insomnia symptoms wore amber blue-blocking or clear placebo lenses for 2 hours before bed for a week each. Amber lenses improved insomnia ratings, subjective sleep quality and total sleep time.

studies.title: Evening wear of blue-blocking glasses for sleep and mood disorders: a systematic review
studies.authors: Hester L, Dang D, Barker CJ, Heath M, Mesiya S, Tienabeso T, Watson K
studies.finding_summary: 29 publications including 16 RCTs (453 patients) of evening amber glasses. The authors found good support for shorter sleep onset in sleep disorders, jet lag and shift work, preliminary signals in mania, and conflicting results in depression.

name: Body Pillows
summary: Long pillows for side sleepers and pregnancy. No trials test the pillow itself, but going to sleep on your side in late pregnancy is linked with fewer stillbirths.
what:
Body pillows come as a straight bolster, a C, J or U shape that wraps front and back, or a small wedge for the bump. Side sleepers use them to rest the upper arm and knee, which stops the top hip and shoulder rolling forward. In pregnancy they support the bump and back and make side sleeping easier to keep up.

The trade-off is size: U-shaped pillows take up a lot of bed, and a partner may feel crowded.

evidence.summary: There are no trials of body pillows for sleep or pain. The strongest related evidence is about position, not pillows: a meta-analysis of individual data from case-control studies found that going to sleep on your back from 28 weeks of pregnancy was linked with about 2.6 times the odds of late stillbirth compared with the left side, while the right side was as safe as the left. Whether a pillow helps you stay on your side hasn't been tested.

claims.claim: A body pillow helps you sleep on your side in pregnancy
claims.note: Plausible and widely recommended for comfort, but not studied.

claims.claim: In pregnancy you must sleep on your left side
claims.note: Going to sleep on either side carried similar risk. The back was the risky position.

claims.claim: Body pillows improve spinal alignment and relieve back or hip pain
claims.note: No trials.

claims.claim: They stop snoring by keeping you off your back
claims.note: Keeping off your back can help positional snoring, but body pillows haven't been tested for it.

look_for: A shape for your need: a straight or J shape for side-sleeping support, a U or C shape for front and back support in pregnancy.
A removable, washable cover.
Adjustable fill (shredded foam or fibre) so it isn't too thick between your knees.
A size that fits your bed and your partner.
skip: 'OB-GYN designed' or 'orthopedic' labels as proof of benefit.
A large U-shape before trying a simple bolster or a regular pillow between your knees.
safety: From about 28 weeks of pregnancy, settle to sleep on your side (either side). If you wake on your back, just turn over.
Reduced baby movements, or new severe pain in pregnancy, need your midwife or doctor the same day.
Never let a baby sleep on or against a body, pregnancy or nursing pillow, and keep them out of a baby's sleep space.

studies.title: An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis of Maternal Going-to-Sleep Position, Interactions with Fetal Vulnerability, and the Risk of Late Stillbirth
studies.authors: Cronin RS, Li M, Thompson JMD, Gordon A, Raynes-Greenow CH, Heazell AEP, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Data from case-control studies of pregnancies from 28 weeks. Going to sleep on the back was linked with 2.6 times the odds of late stillbirth compared with the left side; the right side was as safe as the left.

name: Cooling Pads
summary: Gel and fabric pads feel cool only briefly; water or air systems keep cooling all night. A cool room does most of the work, and pads fine-tune it.
what:
There are three groups. **Passive** gel mats and 'cool-touch' or phase-change fabrics feel cool until they warm to your skin temperature. **Wicking** pads and sheets move sweat away so you feel less clammy. **Active** systems pump chilled water through a pad or blow air under the covers all night.

Heat and humidity under the covers are what wake hot sleepers, so the aim is to let heat and moisture escape, not to feel cold at bedtime.

evidence.summary: Lab studies show that drawing heat away through the mattress modestly increases deep sleep: first in 15 young men, then in a three-centre study of 72 adults, a high-heat-capacity mattress increased slow-wave sleep and lowered heart rate. Reviews of thermal studies show that heat, and especially humid heat, increases waking. Trials of specific consumer cooling pads are few, small and often funded by the makers.

claims.claim: Cooling the sleep surface gives you deeper sleep
claims.note: Lab studies of conductive cooling found more deep sleep; consumer products are rarely tested independently.

claims.claim: Gel pads keep you cool all night
claims.note: Passive gel absorbs heat until it reaches skin temperature, then stops cooling until it can shed that heat.

claims.claim: Phase-change fabrics regulate your temperature
claims.note: They buffer small amounts of heat for a short time; effects on sleep are barely tested.

claims.claim: Cooling pads help menopausal hot flushes and night sweats
claims.note: A plausible comfort measure with little direct trial evidence.

look_for: Start with the room: around 18°C (65°F), a fan, and lighter bedding.
For heavy sweating: breathable, wicking layers rather than a waterproof or thick foam surface.
For active systems: noise, temperature range, dual-zone control, water upkeep and any subscription cost.
Washability and a fit that suits your mattress depth.
skip: 'Space technology' and 'X degrees cooler' claims. A cool-to-touch reading doesn't tell you how you'll sleep.
A gel topper bought to fix a hot memory-foam mattress. The foam still traps heat.
safety: New night sweats with fever or weight loss, or sweats that repeatedly soak the bed, need a medical check.
Don't use active cooling for babies, and take care if you have poor circulation, Raynaud's or reduced sensation.
For water-based systems, keep the unit on a stable surface and check hoses for leaks.

studies.title: Sleep on a high heat capacity mattress increases conductive body heat loss and slow wave sleep
studies.authors: Kräuchi K, Fattori E, Giordano A, Falbo M, Iadarola A, Aglì F, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 15 healthy young men slept in the lab on a high- or low-heat-capacity mattress. The high-heat-capacity mattress lowered core temperature slightly (up to 0.28°C), increased slow-wave sleep by 16% and improved rated sleep quality.

studies.title: Enhanced conductive body heat loss during sleep increases slow-wave sleep and calms the heart
studies.authors: Herberger S, Penzel T, Fietze I, Glos M, Cicolin A, Fattori E, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 72 adults of varied age and weight slept on a high-heat-capacity mattress that draws heat from the back. Deep sleep (N3) increased and heart rate fell, tied to greater heat transfer from core to back skin.

studies.title: Effects of thermal environment on sleep and circadian rhythm
studies.authors: Okamoto-Mizuno K, Mizuno K
studies.finding_summary: Review of thermal sleep studies: heat exposure increases wakefulness and reduces deep and REM sleep, humid heat makes it worse, and bedding and clothing largely determine how cold affects sleep.

name: CPAP Machines & Accessories
summary: CPAP is first-line treatment for obstructive sleep apnea. It is a prescription medical device: get tested first, then mask fit and nightly use decide whether it works.
what:
CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) blows air through a mask at a set pressure that holds your throat open during sleep. **Auto-adjusting** machines vary the pressure within a prescribed range; **bilevel** machines use separate pressures for breathing in and out, for people who need higher pressures or have other breathing problems. Heated humidifiers and heated tubing reduce dryness and congestion. Masks come as **nasal pillows** (small cushions at the nostrils), **nasal** masks, and **full-face** masks for mouth breathers. This shelf also includes travel machines, CPAP pillows and cleaners.

Obstructive sleep apnea is common and often missed. Warning signs: loud, regular snoring; breathing pauses, choking or gasping that someone notices; daytime sleepiness or dozing while driving; morning headaches; waking to pass urine; and high blood pressure that's hard to control. Diagnosis needs a sleep study, often done at home, and in the US the machine and mask need a prescription.

evidence.summary: PAP removes most breathing events, and randomized trials show it reduces daytime sleepiness and improves quality of life and mood; the American Academy of Sleep Medicine strongly recommends it for adults with obstructive sleep apnea and excessive sleepiness. It lowers blood pressure modestly (about 2-3 mmHg on average, more with more hours of use). In the large SAVE trial it didn't prevent heart attacks or strokes in people with existing heart disease, but average use was only 3.3 hours a night, and pooled data link 4+ hours a night with fewer repeat events.

claims.claim: CPAP reduces daytime sleepiness
claims.note: Consistent in randomized trials; it's the main reason guidelines strongly recommend it.

claims.claim: CPAP lowers blood pressure
claims.note: Pooled trials show about 2.5/2.0 mmHg lower, with more benefit for each extra hour of nightly use.

claims.claim: CPAP prevents heart attacks and strokes
claims.note: The largest trial found no reduction in people with heart disease. People who used it 4+ hours a night did better in pooled analyses, but that can partly reflect healthier habits.

claims.claim: CPAP makes driving safer
claims.note: Observational studies of drivers with apnea show crash risk falls sharply after treatment, and sleepiness improves within days.

claims.claim: You can choose a machine yourself without a sleep test
claims.note: Pressure needs and even the right type of machine depend on the diagnosis. Central sleep apnea and some heart and lung conditions need different settings or devices.

claims.claim: Ozone or UV cleaners are needed to keep CPAP safe
claims.note: Mild soap and water, following the maker's instructions, is enough. The FDA has warned about ozone and UV cleaners that weren't authorised for this use.

look_for: A mask that fits your face and sleep style: nasal pillows for minimal contact, full-face if you breathe through your mouth. Most people try more than one, and fit drives whether you'll keep using it.
A heated humidifier, and heated tubing, if you get a dry mouth, nosebleeds or condensation in the mask.
Comfort settings: a ramp that starts at low pressure, and pressure relief when you breathe out.
Usage data your clinician can see (hours of use, mask leak, remaining events). Insurers often require proof of use.
A travel unit if you fly often, with battery options and approval for in-flight use.

For any second-hand or older machine: have your provider check and set it, and look it up in the FDA recall database. A large 2021 recall covered millions of machines with degrading sound-dampening foam.
skip: Ozone 'sanitisers'. Soap and water does the job, and ozone irritates the lungs.
Buying a machine online without a diagnosis and a prescribed pressure setting.
Upgrading for app features or special algorithms when your current setup works. Ask your clinician whether it would change anything.
safety: Don't self-prescribe. Central sleep apnea, heart failure, lung disease and other conditions change which device and settings are safe.
Tell your prescriber about recent facial, sinus, ear or skull-base surgery, a history of collapsed lung, or severe lung disease.
If you have untreated apnea and daytime sleepiness, don't drive when drowsy.
Tell your care team early about dryness, leaks, pressure discomfort or claustrophobia. Most problems are fixable, and quietly giving up is the commonest way treatment fails.
Clean the mask and tubing, and replace cushions, filters and tubing on the schedule your supplier gives.
If CPAP really doesn't work for you, alternatives include oral appliances, positional therapy, weight loss (including medicines) and, for some people, surgery or nerve stimulation.
how_to_use: Use it all night, every night. At least 4 hours on 70% of nights is the threshold many US insurers use to judge adherence, but more hours bring more benefit.
Get used to the mask while awake, for example wearing it while reading or watching TV.
Use the ramp setting so the pressure starts low as you fall asleep.
Wash the cushion and tubing with mild soap as your supplier advises, and use distilled water in the humidifier.
Bring your usage data to follow-up visits; leak and remaining events show whether settings need changing.

studies.title: Treatment of Adult Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Positive Airway Pressure: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline
studies.authors: Patil SP, Ayappa IA, Caples SM, Kimoff RJ, Patel SR, Harrod CG
studies.finding_summary: Strongly recommends PAP for adults with obstructive sleep apnea and excessive sleepiness, suggests it for impaired quality of life and comorbid hypertension, and requires diagnosis by objective testing plus follow-up of usage data.

studies.title: CPAP for Prevention of Cardiovascular Events in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
studies.authors: McEvoy RD, Antic NA, Heeley E, Luo Y, Ou Q, Zhang X, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 2,717 adults with moderate-to-severe sleep apnea and heart or brain vascular disease. With average use of 3.3 hours a night, CPAP did not reduce cardiovascular events over 3.7 years, but it reduced snoring and sleepiness and improved quality of life and mood.

studies.title: CPAP vs Mandibular Advancement Devices and Blood Pressure in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
studies.authors: Bratton DJ, Gaisl T, Wons AM, Kohler M
studies.finding_summary: 51 trials (4,888 patients). CPAP lowered blood pressure by about 2.5/2.0 mmHg versus inactive control, with about 1.5 mmHg more systolic reduction per extra hour of nightly use; oral appliances gave similar reductions.

studies.title: Adherence to CPAP Treatment and the Risk of Recurrent Cardiovascular Events: A Meta-Analysis
studies.authors: Sánchez-de-la-Torre M, Gracia-Lavedan E, Benitez ID, Sánchez-de-la-Torre A, Moncusí-Moix A, Torres G, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 4,186 people with heart disease and sleep apnea from three RCTs. Overall CPAP did not change recurrent cardiovascular events (HR 1.01), but in an on-treatment analysis good adherence (4+ hours a night) was linked with lower risk (HR 0.69).

name: Duvet Covers
summary: A washable shell for your duvet. Choose by fabric, fit and closure; there are no health claims to weigh.
what: A duvet cover protects the duvet and is the part you actually wash. Fabric choices mirror sheets: crisp percale or linen for hot sleepers, smoother sateen, brushed flannel for cold rooms. The practical details decide whether you'll like it: interior corner ties that stop the duvet bunching, a closure you can live with (buttons, a hidden zip or an envelope), and a size that matches your duvet.

evidence.summary: Nothing to study here: comfort, looks and easy washing are the point. The heat and moisture points that apply to sheets apply here too.

claims.claim: Linen or lyocell covers regulate your temperature
claims.note: Breathable weaves feel cooler, but the duvet inside decides most of the warmth.

claims.claim: Higher thread count means a better cover
claims.note: Weave and fibre quality matter more than the number.

look_for: A size that matches your duvet, so it doesn't bunch or sag.
Interior corner ties or loops.
A closure you like: zips are fastest, buttons are easiest to repair.
A weave for your temperature, washable at the temperature you need.
skip: Thread-count bragging and 'temperature-regulating' labels.

name: Duvets & Comforters
summary: How warm a duvet is depends on the amount and type of fill, not the label. Pick the warmth for your room and a build you can wash, and ignore 'hypoallergenic'.
what:
A duvet (comforter) is an insulating fill inside a fabric shell. **Down** gives the most warmth for its weight and lasts longest. **Fill power** measures loft (higher means more warmth per gram), while the **fill weight** decides how warm the duvet actually is. **Down-alternative** fibre is cheaper, easier to wash and suits people avoiding animal products. **Wool** is less lofty but handles moisture well.

Construction matters: baffle-box stitching stops down from shifting, while sewn-through channels are lighter and cooler. In the UK and Europe a **tog** rating gives a standard warmth number; many US products just say 'lightweight' or 'all-season'.

evidence.summary: No trials link duvet type to health. A small lab study found no sleep difference between wool and polyester bedding, while a cooler room (17°C rather than 22°C) improved sleep, so the right warmth for your room matters more than the fibre. Dust mites live in every fill; a hot wash kills them.

claims.claim: Hypoallergenic duvets prevent allergy symptoms
claims.note: The term isn't regulated and mites colonise any fill. A duvet you can wash hot helps more.

claims.claim: Higher fill power is always warmer
claims.note: Higher fill power means more loft per gram, but total warmth depends on how much fill there is.

claims.claim: Temperature-regulating fills stop night sweats
claims.note: No independent sleep trials. Choosing a lighter duvet does more.

look_for: A warmth rating (tog, or fill weight) that suits your room and season. Hot sleepers go lighter, or buy two light duvets to combine in winter.
Washability: ideally machine-washable at 60°C; many down duvets need a large machine or professional cleaning.
A tightly woven, breathable shell so the fill doesn't leak.
Baffle-box construction for down, and corner loops so it doesn't slide around inside the cover.
Down welfare standards if that matters to you. They say nothing about health.
skip: 'Hypoallergenic' and 'temperature-regulating' claims.
A very warm, high-fill duvet for a warm bedroom. You'll just overheat.
safety: Babies under 12 months shouldn't have duvets, quilts or pillows. Use a baby sleeping bag.

studies.title: The effects of fabric for sleepwear and bedding on sleep at ambient temperatures of 17°C and 22°C
studies.authors: Shin M, Halaki M, Swan P, Ireland AH, Chow CM
studies.finding_summary: 17 healthy young adults slept in the lab under different fabric and temperature conditions. Wool sleepwear shortened time to fall asleep versus cotton, there was no effect of wool versus polyester bedding, and people slept better at 17°C than at 22°C.

studies.title: The role of water temperature and laundry procedures in reducing house dust mite populations and allergen content of bedding
studies.authors: McDonald LG, Tovey E
studies.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
studies.finding_summary: Washing at 55°C or hotter killed all dust mites. A cold wash removed over 90% of mite allergen but left most live mites in the bedding; detergents did not improve killing at lower temperatures.

name: Earplugs
summary: Cheap and effective at cutting noise if you insert them properly. The evidence comes mostly from noisy hospital wards; the trade-off is missing alarms.
what:
**Foam** plugs block the most sound when rolled thin and inserted deep. **Silicone putty** covers the ear opening and suits small or sensitive ear canals. **Flanged** and filtered 'high-fidelity' plugs block less sound but more evenly, which some people find less claustrophobic. Custom-moulded plugs fit best but cost more. Sleep earbuds that play masking sound are a separate, pricier option.

The rating on the box (NRR in the US, SNR in Europe) is a lab figure. Real-world protection is usually much lower, mostly because plugs aren't inserted deeply enough.

evidence.summary: A Cochrane review of intensive-care trials found low-quality evidence that earplugs and/or eye masks improve sleep and may lower delirium risk, and a systematic review of 19 studies found mostly subjective improvements. In healthy volunteers exposed to recorded ICU noise and light, earplugs plus masks restored REM sleep and melatonin. There are few trials at home, where noise is usually lower.

claims.claim: Earplugs improve sleep in noisy settings
claims.note: Consistent but low-quality evidence, mostly from hospitals and lab noise simulations.

claims.claim: The highest noise rating is best for sleep
claims.note: A higher rating helps only if the plug fits and stays in. For sleep, a comfortable plug you'll wear all night beats a high number.

claims.claim: Noise-cancelling sleep earbuds block snoring better than foam
claims.note: Active cancellation works best on steady low tones; irregular snoring is harder. Few independent tests.

look_for: A fit for your ear canal. A variety pack is the cheapest way to find it.
A low profile if you sleep on your side.
Foam for maximum blocking, silicone putty for small or sensitive canals, reusable silicone to cut waste.
Filtered plugs if you want to still hear some sound, for example in a shared room.
skip: Chasing the highest rating if the plug is uncomfortable or falls out.
App-connected earbuds when a plug does the job, unless you want masking sound or an alarm only you can hear.
safety: You may not hear smoke alarms, a baby or someone at the door. Consider a vibrating or bed-shaker alarm if you rely on hearing one.
Nightly use can push wax deeper or irritate the ear canal. See a clinician if you get ear pain, discharge or hearing changes.
Insert plugs with clean hands, replace disposable foam plugs often, and wash reusable ones to reduce infection risk.
Don't use them with a perforated eardrum or an active ear infection without medical advice.
how_to_use: Foam: roll into a thin, crease-free cylinder, pull the top of your ear up and back, insert, and hold for 20-30 seconds while it expands.
If they work loose, try a smaller size or another shape rather than pushing deeper.

studies.title: Non-pharmacological interventions for sleep promotion in the intensive care unit
studies.authors: Hu RF, Jiang XY, Chen J, Zeng Z, Chen XY, Li Y, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 30 trials (1,569 ICU adults). Low-quality evidence that earplugs and/or eye masks increased total sleep time and lowered delirium risk (risk ratio 0.55); most studies using objective sleep measures found no benefit.

studies.title: Effect of the use of earplugs and eye mask on the quality of sleep in intensive care patients: a systematic review
studies.authors: Locihová H, Axmann K, Padyšáková H, Fejfar J
studies.finding_summary: 19 studies (1,379 people). Most found better subjective sleep quality with earplugs and eye masks, and possibly less delirium; objective measures were not clearly improved and study methods varied widely.

studies.title: Effects of earplugs and eye masks on nocturnal sleep, melatonin and cortisol in a simulated intensive care unit environment
studies.authors: Hu RF, Jiang XY, Zeng YM, Chen XY, Zhang YH
studies.finding_summary: 14 healthy volunteers slept with recorded ICU noise and light. The noise and light reduced REM sleep; wearing earplugs and eye masks gave more REM sleep, fewer arousals and higher melatonin.

name: Heated Blankets
summary: Electric blankets and heated mattress pads warm the bed. No sleep benefit is proven; the real questions are about safety: overheating, burns and fire.
what:
**Electric blankets** go over you; **heated mattress pads** go under the sheet and warm you from below, with nothing heavy on top. Modern ones use thin wires, thermostats and auto-off timers, and some run on low voltage through a transformer. Dual controls let partners set different levels.

A sensible way to use one is to warm the bed beforehand and switch it off or right down when you get in. A warm bed helps you settle, but your body needs to cool to stay asleep.

evidence.summary: No trials show heated blankets improve sleep. Two older prospective studies of electric-blanket use in early pregnancy found no consistent link with miscarriage (one saw a small, non-significant increase with use around conception). Burns from heating pads and blankets are well documented in people with reduced sensation, such as diabetic neuropathy.

claims.claim: A heated blanket helps you fall asleep faster
claims.note: Pre-warming the bed is comfortable, but no trials show a sleep benefit.

claims.claim: Low-EMF or DC designs are healthier
claims.note: There's no good evidence that the weak magnetic fields from electric blankets harm health. Low-voltage designs are a reasonable electrical-safety choice, not a proven health one.

claims.claim: Safe to leave on all night
claims.note: Only if the maker says it's designed for overnight use, on a low setting with working overheat protection, and never for people who can't feel heat or turn it off.

look_for: A recognised safety certification, such as UL or ETL in the US or your country's equivalent.
Overheat protection and an auto-off timer.
Dual controls, and a detachable controller so you can wash it.
A heated mattress pad if you want warmth without extra weight on top.
Low settings that are genuinely low for overnight use.
skip: 'Zero-EMF' and other health claims.
'Therapy' marketing for aches and pains beyond ordinary warmth.
safety: Don't use one if you can't feel heat properly or can't switch it off yourself: diabetes with neuropathy, spinal injury, paralysis, some older adults, or after sedating medicines or alcohol.
Never for babies or young children, and never on a baby's bed.
In pregnancy, to be cautious, warm the bed first and switch it off before you get in, to avoid overheating.
Fire safety: don't fold, bunch or tuck it in while it's on; don't use it with a hot-water bottle, or on an adjustable bed unless the maker allows it; unplug it when not in use.
Check it before each winter and replace it if wires show, the fabric is scorched or frayed, or the controller is damaged.
Don't use one where there is bedwetting or incontinence. Water and wiring don't mix.
how_to_use: Switch it on 20-30 minutes before bed, then turn it off or to the lowest setting when you get in.

studies.title: Spontaneous abortion and exposure to electric blankets and heated water beds
studies.authors: Belanger K, Leaderer B, Hellenbrand K, Holford TR, McSharry J, Power ME, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 2,967 pregnant women. Electric blanket use around conception had a slight, non-significant association with miscarriage after adjustment (OR 1.74, 95% CI 0.96-3.15), with no dose-response; heated water beds showed no link.

studies.title: The use of electric bed heaters and the risk of clinically recognized spontaneous abortion
studies.authors: Lee GM, Neutra RR, Hristova L, Yost M, Hiatt RA
studies.finding_summary: Women using electric bed heaters in the first trimester did not have higher miscarriage rates than non-users, and risk did not rise with more intense use; the magnetic fields added less overnight exposure than had been assumed.

studies.title: Electric heating pad burns
studies.authors: Bill TJ, Edlich RF, Himel HN
studies.finding_summary: Two patients with numb skin suffered partial- and full-thickness foot burns from an electric heating pad; the authors stress that people with sensory loss are especially prone to these burns.

name: Mattress Protectors
summary: Worth having to keep sweat and spills out and protect your warranty. They don't treat allergies, and waterproof layers can sleep warmer.
what:
A protector is a thin, usually waterproof layer that fits over the mattress like a fitted sheet, or zips all the way round it as an **encasement**. It keeps sweat, spills, bedwetting and stains out of the mattress, which matters because many warranties are voided by stains, and it's far easier to wash than a mattress.

The waterproof membrane is usually polyurethane (quiet and fairly breathable) or vinyl (cheaper, crinklier and hotter). Zippered encasements are also sold for bed bugs, which needs one tested for that purpose.

evidence.summary: Protectors are hygiene and warranty kit, not health products. Allergen-proof encasements reduce mite allergen in the mattress, but large randomized trials found they didn't improve asthma or allergic rhinitis when used alone.

claims.claim: Protects your mattress and your warranty
claims.note: A waterproof layer keeps stains and fluids out, and many warranties exclude stained mattresses.

claims.claim: An allergen barrier relieves allergies or asthma
claims.note: Two large trials found no clinical benefit from impermeable covers used alone.

claims.claim: Cooling or phase-change protectors keep you cool
claims.note: Phase-change finishes absorb a little heat briefly, and a waterproof membrane tends to add warmth.

look_for: A polyurethane membrane rather than vinyl if you want it quiet and less sweaty.
A deep enough skirt to stay on your mattress plus any topper.
Washing and drying instructions you can follow at home.
For bed bugs: a full zippered encasement tested for bed bugs, left on for at least a year.
For bedwetting or incontinence: an absorbent top layer over the waterproof backing, and a spare for night-time changes.
skip: Allergy-cure claims for encasements.
'Cooling' and mineral-infused 'recovery' fabrics.
safety: Asthma or allergies: covers are at best one part of a plan. See a clinician about treatment.
Cribs: use only a protector made for that crib mattress and fitted tightly, with no loose plastic or extra padding.

studies.title: Control of exposure to mite allergen and allergen-impermeable bed covers for adults with asthma
studies.authors: Woodcock A, Forster L, Matthews E, Martin J, Letley L, Vickers M, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 1,122 adults with asthma got allergen-impermeable or ordinary bed covers. Mite allergen in mattresses fell at 6 months, but peak flow and the ability to stop inhaled steroids did not differ between groups, including in mite-sensitive patients.

studies.title: Evaluation of impermeable covers for bedding in patients with allergic rhinitis
studies.authors: Terreehorst I, Hak E, Oosting AJ, Tempels-Pavlica Z, de Monchy JG, Bruijnzeel-Koomen CA, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 279 people with mite-allergic rhinitis used impermeable or ordinary covers on mattress, pillow and duvet for a year. Mite allergen in mattresses fell, but symptoms and nasal provocation results did not improve.

name: Mattress Toppers
summary: A 2-4 inch layer that changes how a mattress feels. A cheaper way to soften a too-firm bed; it can't fix a sagging one. No health claims hold up.
what:
Toppers sit on the mattress under the fitted sheet. Memory foam softens and contours but can sleep warm; latex is springier and more breathable; fibre and down toppers add plushness but compress fastest.

They're a good way to test whether a softer feel helps before replacing a mattress, or to make a guest bed bearable. They don't add support: on a mattress that already dips, a topper just dips with it.

evidence.summary: No trials test consumer toppers for sleep or pain. The mattress evidence (medium-firm beat firm for chronic low-back pain) makes softening an overly firm bed reasonable, but that is an extrapolation. Pressure-redistributing mattresses and overlays for people at risk of pressure sores are a separate clinical category with their own Cochrane reviews; a comfort topper isn't one of them.

claims.claim: Makes a firm mattress feel softer
claims.note: That's a physical property of the layer, and it's all a topper is designed to do.

claims.claim: Fixes a sagging mattress
claims.note: A topper follows the shape underneath it. A sagging core needs replacing.

claims.claim: Gel or copper infusions keep you cool
claims.note: Gel adds a brief cool touch; the foam around it still traps heat. Copper 'antimicrobial' or 'recovery' claims have no sleep evidence.

claims.claim: Relieves back and joint pain
claims.note: No trials. If softening helps your comfort, that's the benefit.

look_for: Material for heat and feel: latex and perforated foam breathe better than solid memory foam.
Thickness: 2-3 inches is enough to change the feel. Thicker toppers raise the bed and need deeper sheets.
Higher-density foam, which resists body impressions longer.
Corner straps or a non-slip base so it doesn't shift, and a removable, washable cover.
A return policy. Feel is personal.
skip: Copper, charcoal or 'antimicrobial' infusions sold as health features.
A topper bought to rescue a mattress that already dips.
Thin convoluted 'egg-crate' foam as a long-term fix. It compresses quickly.
safety: Never add a topper or any soft layer to a baby's sleep surface.

If you're bed-bound or at risk of pressure sores (limited mobility, poor sensation), ask a nurse or occupational therapist for a clinically specified pressure-redistributing mattress or overlay rather than a comfort topper.
Very soft, thick foam can make turning over and getting up harder for people with weakness or joint problems.

studies.title: Foam surfaces for preventing pressure ulcers
studies.authors: Shi C, Dumville JC, Cullum N, Rhodes S, McInnes E
studies.finding_summary: 29 trials (9,566 people, mostly older adults in acute care). Low-certainty evidence that foam surfaces may carry a higher risk of new pressure ulcers than alternating-pressure or reactive air surfaces; most studies were small.

name: Mattresses
summary: The one bed purchase with a real trial behind it: for back pain, medium-firm beat firm. Beyond that, choose by fit to your body and sleep position, and a fair trial.
what:
A mattress is a support core (coils, dense foam or latex) under comfort layers that let your shoulders and hips sink in. Its job is to keep your spine roughly in line in your usual position without pressure points. Side sleepers and lighter people usually need more give; heavier people and back or stomach sleepers usually need more support.

The main types (all-foam, latex, innerspring and hybrid) differ mostly in feel, heat, motion transfer, edge support and durability, not in anything health-related. Firmness labels aren't standardized between makers, so the return trial is the real test.

evidence.summary: One well-run double-blind trial of 313 adults with chronic low-back pain found medium-firm mattresses reduced pain in bed and disability compared with firm ones over 90 days, and later systematic reviews of mostly small trials lean the same way. The trial didn't test soft mattresses or specific materials. There is no good evidence that any mattress type improves sleep or health in people without pain, and before-and-after 'new bed' studies can't separate the mattress from novelty.

claims.claim: A firm mattress is best for a bad back
claims.note: In the best trial, medium-firm beat firm on pain and disability. The old 'firmer is better' advice didn't hold up.

claims.claim: Medium-firm reduces low-back pain
claims.note: Shown in adults with chronic low-back pain. A sensible default, but one brand's 'medium-firm' can be another's 'firm'.

claims.claim: Cooling gel or cooling covers keep you cool all night
claims.note: Gel and cool-touch covers feel cool at first, but thick foam still holds heat. Coils and latex let more heat escape.

claims.claim: 'Orthopedic' or zoned designs correct your posture
claims.note: No agreed definition sits behind 'orthopedic', and zoned support hasn't been tested against ordinary designs.

claims.claim: Copper, mineral or 'recovery' infused fabrics help you recover
claims.note: No independent trials show a sleep or health effect.

claims.claim: A better mattress will fix insomnia
claims.note: Unless pain or discomfort is keeping you awake, a new bed won't help. CBT-I is the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia.

look_for: Lie on it in your real sleep position. Side sleepers need give at the shoulders and hips, back and stomach sleepers need the hips held up.
Trial terms: the length, any minimum keep period (often around 30 nights), return or pickup fees, and limits on exchanges.
Heat: if you sleep hot, coil hybrids and latex usually sleep cooler than thick memory foam.
Durability: ask for foam density and coil details. Denser foams resist sagging and body impressions for longer.
Motion isolation and edge support if you share the bed.
Warranty fine print: many cover only sag beyond a stated depth, require a specific base, and are voided by stains.
Emissions certifications (CertiPUR-US for foam, GOLS for organic latex) limit certain chemicals and off-gassing. Useful, but they say nothing about how you'll sleep.
skip: Comparing firmness numbers across brands. The scales aren't standardized.
'Orthopedic', 'doctor-recommended' or 'chiropractor-approved' labels.
Copper, silver, charcoal or 'recovery' fabric infusions sold as health features.
Paying extra for a 'cooling' label on an all-foam bed. Construction matters more than additives.
safety: Don't unzip and remove the inner cover of a foam mattress. Some use a glass-fibre fire barrier that can shed into the room once exposed.
Babies need a firm, flat mattress made for their crib or cot, with a tightly fitted sheet. Never an adult mattress, topper or soft surface.
If back pain comes with leg numbness or weakness, fever, weight loss, or bladder or bowel changes, see a clinician. A mattress won't fix it.
If you have a severe latex allergy, ask your clinician before choosing natural latex, even though it is usually encased.
how_to_use: Give a new mattress 2-4 weeks before judging it. The first nights aren't representative.
Put a protector on from the first night.
Rotate it head-to-foot every few months if the maker recommends it.
Replace it when it sags or holds body impressions, you wake stiff and it eases once you're up, or you sleep clearly better elsewhere. 7-10 years is a rule of thumb, not a tested lifespan.

studies.title: Effect of firmness of mattress on chronic non-specific low-back pain: randomised, double-blind, controlled, multicentre trial
studies.authors: Kovacs FM, Abraira V, Peña A, Martín-Rodríguez JG, Sánchez-Vera M, Ferrer E, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 313 adults with chronic low-back pain were randomly given a firm or a medium-firm mattress. At 90 days the medium-firm group had less pain in bed (odds ratio 2.36) and less disability (odds ratio 2.10) than the firm group.

studies.title: Effect of different mattress designs on promoting sleep quality, pain reduction, and spinal alignment in adults with or without back pain; systematic review of controlled trials
studies.authors: Radwan A, Fess P, James D, Murphy J, Myers J, Rooney M, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 24 controlled trials published since 2000. Mattresses described as medium-firm and custom-inflated (self-adjusted) came out best for sleep comfort, quality and spinal alignment; evidence on mattress temperature was insufficient.

studies.title: What type of mattress should be chosen to avoid back pain and improve sleep quality? Review of the literature
studies.authors: Caggiari G, Talesa GR, Toro G, Jannelli E, Monteleone G, Puddu L
studies.finding_summary: 39 studies up to 2019, classifying mattresses by the European firmness standard. The authors conclude that a medium-firm mattress promotes comfort, sleep quality and spinal alignment.

name: Pillow Protectors & Cases
summary: Protectors keep sweat and stains out of pillows; cases are about feel. Neither treats allergies, and silk's skin and hair claims are untested.
what:
This shelf mixes two things. **Protectors** are zippered encasements, sometimes waterproof or sold as allergen barriers, that go under the pillowcase to keep sweat, skin oils and dust out of the pillow. **Pillowcases** are the outer layer: cotton percale or sateen, linen, lyocell or viscose ('bamboo'), and silk.

A protector extends a pillow's life and makes it easier to keep clean. Which case you choose comes down to feel, warmth and how it washes.

evidence.summary: Allergen-proof encasements do cut dust-mite allergen in bedding, but two large randomized trials found covers alone didn't improve asthma (1,122 adults) or allergic rhinitis (279 people with mite allergy). No good trials show silk or other pillowcases reduce wrinkles, acne or hair breakage; those claims rest on friction and moisture arguments. Comfort and hygiene are the real reasons to buy.

claims.claim: Allergen-barrier covers relieve asthma or hay fever
claims.note: Two large trials found no clinical benefit from impermeable covers used on their own, even though allergen levels fell.

claims.claim: A protector keeps a pillow cleaner and makes it last
claims.note: A washable barrier keeps sweat, oils and stains out of the fill.

claims.claim: Silk pillowcases prevent wrinkles or acne
claims.note: No good trials. 'Anti-aging' claims for silk or copper cases rest on theory.

claims.claim: Silk reduces hair frizz and breakage
claims.note: Plausible because silk is smoother, but not tested in good trials.

look_for: A full zippered encasement, not just an envelope case, if the goal is keeping the pillow clean.
Waterproofing only if you need it. The membrane can sleep warmer; quiet polyurethane is nicer than vinyl.
Washability: whether it can take a hot wash (around 60°C / 140°F) if you have dust-mite allergy.
For cases: percale or linen if you sleep hot; sateen and silk feel smoother but sateen runs warmer and silk needs gentler washing.
The right size. An overstuffed case compresses the pillow.
skip: Anti-aging, anti-acne or 'beauty sleep' claims for silk or copper cases.
'Hypoallergenic' labels. The term has no regulated meaning.
Buying allergen covers as your only allergy treatment.
safety: Asthma or allergic rhinitis: covers alone aren't treatment. Talk to a clinician about medicines or allergen immunotherapy.
Keep pillows and protectors out of a baby's sleep space.

studies.title: Control of exposure to mite allergen and allergen-impermeable bed covers for adults with asthma
studies.authors: Woodcock A, Forster L, Matthews E, Martin J, Letley L, Vickers M, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 1,122 adults with asthma got allergen-impermeable or ordinary bed covers. Mite allergen in mattresses fell at 6 months, but peak flow and the ability to stop inhaled steroids did not differ between groups, including in mite-sensitive patients.

studies.title: Evaluation of impermeable covers for bedding in patients with allergic rhinitis
studies.authors: Terreehorst I, Hak E, Oosting AJ, Tempels-Pavlica Z, de Monchy JG, Bruijnzeel-Koomen CA, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 279 people with mite-allergic rhinitis used impermeable or ordinary covers on mattress, pillow and duvet for a year. Mite allergen in mattresses fell, but symptoms and nasal provocation results did not improve.

studies.title: The role of water temperature and laundry procedures in reducing house dust mite populations and allergen content of bedding
studies.authors: McDonald LG, Tovey E
studies.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
studies.finding_summary: Washing at 55°C or hotter killed all dust mites. A cold wash removed over 90% of mite allergen but left most live mites in the bedding; detergents did not improve killing at lower temperatures.

name: Pillows
summary: Surprisingly little evidence on shape or fill. Match the height to your sleep position so your neck stays level, and judge by how your neck feels in the morning.
what:
A pillow fills the gap between your head and the mattress so your neck stays roughly in line with your spine. That gap depends on position: side sleepers have the biggest gap (shoulder width) and need a higher, firmer pillow; back sleepers a medium one; stomach sleepers a very thin one or none.

Fills differ in feel, heat and upkeep. Down and feather are soft and mouldable; memory foam holds its shape but can sleep warm; latex is springy; shredded foam and buckwheat let you adjust the height; polyester fibre is cheap and washable but flattens fastest.

evidence.summary: A 2021 meta-analysis found small reductions in neck pain and waking pain with latex pillows in people with chronic neck pain, and that pillow height and shape affected neck alignment more than material. A 2025 review of newer trials found no pillow type clearly better. Trials are small and varied, and none show a pillow improves sleep or health in people without neck pain.

claims.claim: The right height depends on how you sleep
claims.note: Alignment studies show height and shape change neck position; side sleepers need the most height.

claims.claim: Latex pillows reduce neck pain
claims.note: Pooled small trials favour latex over standard pillows in chronic neck pain, but the effect is small and a later review found no clear winner.

claims.claim: Contoured 'cervical' pillows fix neck pain
claims.note: Small trials disagree. Some people with neck pain do better on one, others don't; buy with a return policy.

claims.claim: Cooling gel pillows keep you cool all night
claims.note: The cool touch fades as the pillow warms. Breathable fills matter more.

claims.claim: 'Hypoallergenic' pillows prevent allergy symptoms
claims.note: The term isn't regulated, and dust mites colonise any fill. Washability matters more.

look_for: Height (loft) for your position: higher for side sleeping, medium for back, thin for stomach. Adjustable fills let you tune it.
Enough support that you don't need to fold it in half or stack two.
A washable pillow, or at least a removable, washable cover.
Breathable fills (down, latex, buckwheat, shredded foam) if you sleep warm.
A return policy, since comfort is individual.
skip: 'Orthopedic' and 'chiropractor-designed' labels. No standard sits behind them.
Copper-infused or 'recovery' fabrics.
Treating an online 'sleep quiz' as a fitting. It's a sales tool; the return policy is what protects you.
safety: No pillows in a baby's sleep space in the first year.
Neck pain with arm numbness or weakness, severe headache, fever, or pain after an injury needs a clinician, not a new pillow.
how_to_use: Wash pillows (if the label allows) or their covers regularly. A hot wash around 60°C (140°F) kills dust mites; cooler washes remove allergen but leave most mites alive.
Replace a pillow when it stays flat or lumpy after fluffing.

studies.title: The effects of pillow designs on neck pain, waking symptoms, neck disability, sleep quality and spinal alignment in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Chun-Yiu JP, Man-Ha ST, Chak-Lun AF
studies.finding_summary: 35 studies, 9 of high quality (555 people). Latex (rubber) pillows modestly reduced neck pain and waking pain in chronic neck pain; pillow height and shape affected neck alignment more than material.

studies.title: Effect of pillow on pain, disability and sleep quality in patients with chronic neck pain: A systematic review
studies.authors: Ghosh S, Goyal M, Goyal K
studies.finding_summary: Five trials (239 people with chronic neck pain) from 2015-2024. Pain improvements were minor, disability results inconsistent and sleep quality differences not significant; no pillow type (latex, foam or standard) was clearly better.

name: Sheets
summary: Sheets are about feel and heat. Weave and fibre matter more than thread count, and no sheet has health benefits, though a breathable one helps hot sleepers.
what:
The **weave** shapes how a sheet feels more than the fibre does. Percale is a plain, crisp, matte weave that breathes well; sateen is smoother and silkier but denser and warmer; flannel is brushed for winter; jersey is knitted and stretchy. **Fibre** matters too: cotton is the durable default, linen is airy and softens with washing, lyocell and viscose feel cool and smooth, and polyester microfibre is cheap and wrinkle-resistant but holds heat and moisture.

Most 'bamboo' and 'eucalyptus' sheets are regenerated cellulose (viscose/rayon or lyocell) chemically made from plant pulp, not bamboo fibre. US regulators have fined retailers for selling rayon as 'bamboo'.

evidence.summary: No trials show that any sheet improves health. Lab studies show heat and humid heat under the covers disturb sleep, and one small study found people slept better at 17°C than 22°C while wool versus polyester bedding made no difference. So room temperature and overall layer weight matter more than which fibre your sheet is made from. 'Temperature-regulating' fabric claims rest on small, often industry-funded studies.

claims.claim: Higher thread count means better sheets
claims.note: Very high counts are often inflated by counting each strand of multi-ply yarn. Fibre quality and weave matter more, and very dense weaves sleep warmer.

claims.claim: 'Bamboo' sheets are made of bamboo fibre
claims.note: They're usually viscose or lyocell made from bamboo pulp. Lyocell's closed-loop process is cleaner than standard viscose.

claims.claim: Cooling sheets lower your body temperature
claims.note: Crisp percale, linen and smooth lyocell feel cooler and handle moisture; effects on actual sleep are small and little tested.

claims.claim: Organic cotton is healthier to sleep on
claims.note: Organic certification is about farming and processing. There's no evidence of a health difference for the sleeper.

look_for: Weave for your temperature: percale or linen if you run hot, sateen or flannel if you run cold.
Long-staple cotton, which pills less; linen and lyocell handle moisture well.
Pocket depth that fits your mattress plus any topper and protector.
Care: whether it can take a hot wash if you have dust-mite allergy.
OEKO-TEX Standard 100 if you want the finished fabric tested for specific harmful substances.
skip: Thread counts in the high hundreds or thousands.
'Temperature-regulating', 'space technology' or 'smart fabric' claims without a stated test.
Anti-aging or 'infused' finishes.
safety: Babies: only a tightly fitted sheet on a firm crib mattress, with no loose bedding.

studies.title: The effects of fabric for sleepwear and bedding on sleep at ambient temperatures of 17°C and 22°C
studies.authors: Shin M, Halaki M, Swan P, Ireland AH, Chow CM
studies.finding_summary: 17 healthy young adults slept in the lab under different fabric and temperature conditions. Wool sleepwear shortened time to fall asleep versus cotton, there was no effect of wool versus polyester bedding, and people slept better at 17°C than at 22°C.

studies.title: Effects of thermal environment on sleep and circadian rhythm
studies.authors: Okamoto-Mizuno K, Mizuno K
studies.finding_summary: Review of thermal sleep studies: heat exposure increases wakefulness and reduces deep and REM sleep, humid heat makes it worse, and bedding and clothing largely determine how cold affects sleep.

name: Sleep Headphones
summary: Headbands and tiny earbuds for audio or noise masking in bed. Music can modestly improve how well you feel you slept; the gear itself is untested. Keep the volume low.
what:
The options are **headband** headphones with flat speakers in a soft band (comfortable for side sleepers; some double as an eye mask), **sleep earbuds** that sit flush in the ear and play masking sounds or your own audio, **noise-cancelling earbuds**, and open-ear or bone-conduction designs that leave the ear canal open.

People use them to fall asleep to audio, to mask a partner's snoring, or to hear an alarm without waking a partner.

evidence.summary: A 2022 Cochrane review (13 trials, 1,007 adults with sleep complaints) found moderate-certainty evidence that listening to music for 25-60 minutes a day improves self-rated sleep quality, though objective sleep measures changed little. Evidence that continuous masking noise helps is very low quality. No trials test sleep headphones as a product; comfort and fit decide whether you'll use them.

claims.claim: Listening to music helps you sleep
claims.note: Moderate-certainty evidence for better self-rated sleep quality; objective sleep changes were small or absent.

claims.claim: Masking sounds block a partner's snoring
claims.note: Masking can cover some noise, but the evidence is very low quality, and it has to be loud enough to mask.

claims.claim: Noise cancellation removes snoring
claims.note: Active cancellation handles steady low-frequency sound better than irregular snores.

claims.claim: Built-in sensors track your sleep stages
claims.note: Consumer sleep-stage estimates are inconsistent even for tested devices.

look_for: Side-sleeper comfort: flat speakers in a headband, or earbuds that don't stick out.
Battery life for a full night, or a sleep timer and auto-fade if you only need help falling asleep.
Several tip sizes for a secure fit that isn't tight.
An alarm only you can hear, if that's the goal.
A washable headband.
skip: Sleep staging and 'smart' sleep scores.
'Clinically validated' soundtracks without a published trial.
safety: Keep the volume low, just enough to hear or mask, and use a timer. Hours of nightly exposure add to hearing risk.
In-ear devices worn every night can trap moisture and wax. Stop if you get ear pain, itching or discharge.
Sealing or noise-cancelling buds can stop you hearing alarms or a crying baby.
Don't charge batteries under pillows or bedding.

studies.title: Listening to music for insomnia in adults
studies.authors: Jespersen KV, Pando-Naude V, Koenig J, Jennum P, Vuust P
studies.finding_summary: 13 trials (1,007 adults with sleep complaints) of daily music for 25-60 minutes. Moderate-certainty evidence of better self-rated sleep quality (PSQI about 2.8 points); objective sleep measures showed little change.

studies.title: Noise as a sleep aid: A systematic review
studies.authors: Riedy SM, Smith MG, Rocha S, Basner M
studies.finding_summary: 38 studies of continuous white or broadband noise. Findings ranged from improved to disrupted sleep, and by GRADE criteria the evidence that continuous noise improves sleep was very low quality; the authors caution it may harm sleep and hearing.

name: Sleep Masks
summary: A cheap, low-risk way to make your sleep dark. Most evidence comes from hospital wards, but one home study linked masks to better next-day memory.
what:
A mask blocks light at your eyes, which helps when you can't fully darken the room: early summer dawns, streetlights, a partner's reading light, travel. Flat masks are the simplest; **contoured** masks have cups that keep pressure off your eyes and let you blink; weighted masks add gentle pressure that some people find calming.

Fit decides whether it works. Light leaking in at the nose is the usual failure, and a strap that's too tight gives headaches.

evidence.summary: A Cochrane review of intensive-care trials found low-quality evidence that earplugs and/or eye masks improve sleep and may reduce delirium. In a 2023 crossover study, 94 healthy young adults encoded new memories better and were more alert after a week sleeping in a mask than after a week without. Trials in ordinary homes are few, and the benefit depends on how much light your room lets in.

claims.claim: Blocking light helps you sleep in a bright room
claims.note: Light at night suppresses melatonin and can wake you. Trials, mostly in hospitals, show better self-rated sleep with masks.

claims.claim: Wearing a mask improves memory and alertness
claims.note: One well-designed study in young adults found gains after a week; it hasn't been widely replicated.

claims.claim: Silk masks have anti-aging benefits
claims.note: No trials.

claims.claim: Weighted masks relieve anxiety or headaches
claims.note: No good studies.

look_for: Contoured eye cups if you dislike pressure on your eyes or wear lash extensions.
A good seal around the nose, the main source of light leaks.
An adjustable strap that doesn't pull your hair, and a low profile if you sleep on your side.
A washable fabric or removable cover, in a breathable material.
skip: Anti-aging or anti-wrinkle claims for silk.
Bluetooth or 'smart' masks, unless you actually want the audio.
safety: After eye surgery, or with an eye condition, ask your eye doctor before wearing anything that presses on your eyes.
Keep masks and their straps away from babies and young children.
Wash it regularly, and stop if you get skin irritation or an eye infection.
how_to_use: Pair darkness at night with bright light in the morning. The two work together on your body clock.

studies.title: Non-pharmacological interventions for sleep promotion in the intensive care unit
studies.authors: Hu RF, Jiang XY, Chen J, Zeng Z, Chen XY, Li Y, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 30 trials (1,569 ICU adults). Low-quality evidence that earplugs and/or eye masks increased total sleep time and lowered delirium risk (risk ratio 0.55); most studies using objective sleep measures found no benefit.

studies.title: Wearing an eye mask during overnight sleep improves episodic learning and alertness
studies.authors: Greco V, Bergamo D, Cuoccio P, Konkoly KR, Muñoz Lombardo K, Lewis PA
studies.finding_summary: 94 adults aged 18-35 slept a week with an eye mask and a week without. With the mask they encoded new memories better and were more alert; a second study of 35 people linked the gain to time in slow-wave sleep.

studies.title: Effect of the use of earplugs and eye mask on the quality of sleep in intensive care patients: a systematic review
studies.authors: Locihová H, Axmann K, Padyšáková H, Fejfar J
studies.finding_summary: 19 studies (1,379 people). Most found better subjective sleep quality with earplugs and eye masks, and possibly less delirium; objective measures were not clearly improved and study methods varied widely.

name: Smart Mattress Covers
summary: Water- or air-driven covers that cool or warm the bed, often sold with sleep trackers. Cooling has lab support; trackers are fine for trends but poor at sleep stages.
what:
This shelf holds two kinds of product. **Active climate systems** (a cover or pad with water-carrying tubes, or a blower pushing air under the sheets) let you set the bed surface cooler or warmer, often on a schedule and separately for each side. **Sleep trackers** (under-mattress sensor strips, bedside radar units, smart beds and bases, and watches) estimate sleep time, stages, heart rate and breathing without a sleep lab.

Some climate covers include tracking and change the temperature automatically based on it.

evidence.summary: Lab studies show that drawing heat away from the back during sleep modestly increases deep sleep: in a three-centre study of 72 adults, a high-heat-capacity mattress increased stage N3 sleep and lowered heart rate. Heat and humidity reliably disturb sleep. Trials of consumer climate covers are few, short and often company-funded. For trackers, a lab comparison of seven consumer devices found them good at detecting sleep but poor at detecting wake, with inconsistent sleep-stage estimates.

claims.claim: Cooling the bed gives you deeper sleep
claims.note: Lab studies of conductive cooling found more deep sleep; trials of the consumer products are small and mostly industry-funded.

claims.claim: Trackers accurately measure your sleep stages
claims.note: They estimate total sleep reasonably on normal nights, but stage estimates are inconsistent and get worse on disrupted nights.

claims.claim: A nightly sleep score tells you how well you slept
claims.note: Scores are proprietary formulas. Compare trends with how you feel, not single nights.

claims.claim: A tracker can detect sleep apnea
claims.note: A few devices have regulator-cleared features that flag possible apnea. A flag means get tested; no flag doesn't rule it out.

claims.claim: Automatic temperature control improves recovery
claims.note: Recovery and HRV claims haven't been shown in independent trials.

look_for: Temperature range and how quickly it changes, with dual-zone control if partners differ.
Noise from the pump or fan, and where the base unit will sit.
Maintenance: water systems need regular cleaning and refills; check the tubing and any leak protection.
Subscriptions: some features stop working without one, so price it over several years.
For trackers: independent validation against lab sleep studies, data export, and clear privacy terms.
A return window long enough (several weeks) to see whether it actually helps you.
skip: 'Recovery', HRV 'optimisation' and biohacking claims.
Treating a daily sleep score as a target. Chasing the number can make sleep worse, a pattern sleep clinicians call orthosomnia.
Paying for tracking you won't act on.
safety: Heating modes: take care if you have diabetes, neuropathy or reduced sensation, and never use on or near babies.
Loud snoring, gasping or pauses in breathing need a clinical sleep test. A tracker can't rule out sleep apnea.
If tracking data is making you anxious about sleep, take a break from it. CBT-I is the treatment for chronic insomnia.
For water-based systems, follow the setup instructions and check hoses for leaks near electrics.
how_to_use: Start with a cool room, around 18°C (65°F), and use the cover to fine-tune rather than replace room temperature.
Judge it by how you feel over 2-3 weeks, not by the app's scores.

studies.title: Enhanced conductive body heat loss during sleep increases slow-wave sleep and calms the heart
studies.authors: Herberger S, Penzel T, Fietze I, Glos M, Cicolin A, Fattori E, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 72 adults of varied age and weight slept on a high-heat-capacity mattress that draws heat from the back. Deep sleep (N3) increased and heart rate fell, tied to greater heat transfer from core to back skin.

studies.title: Performance of seven consumer sleep-tracking devices compared with polysomnography
studies.authors: Chinoy ED, Cuellar JA, Huwa KE, Jameson JT, Watson CH, Bessman SC, et al.
