studies.finding_summary: In successive drops from a single fingerprick, variation in hemoglobin, white cell and platelet counts was up to 3–8 times greater than in venous blood, so single-drop measurements should be treated with caution.

studies.title: Direct-to-Consumer Testing: Benefits and Concerns of Commercially Accessed Laboratory Tests
studies.authors: Orth M, Sandberg S, Shih P
studies.finding_summary: Laboratory-medicine experts describe how consumer-ordered tests fall outside healthcare protections, how marketing can mislead, and conclude that such testing helps in a few selected situations but risks medicalising healthy people.

name: Blood pressure monitor
summary: The most useful health device you can own. Buy a model on an independent validated list, in your cuff size, and measure by the standard protocol.
what:
A home blood pressure monitor inflates a cuff and senses pressure waves in the artery to estimate **systolic** and **diastolic** pressure. Upper-arm cuffs are the standard; wrist cuffs exist for people who can't use an arm cuff; cuffless watches and rings estimate pressure indirectly.

High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms for years, and it's one of the most treatable risks there is. Home readings catch what clinic visits miss, **white-coat hypertension** (high only in the clinic) and **masked hypertension** (normal in the clinic, high in daily life), which is why guidelines now rely on them for diagnosis and follow-up.

evidence.summary: Lowering blood pressure prevents heart attacks and strokes: across 48 randomized trials and about 345,000 people, each 5 mmHg drop in systolic pressure cut major cardiovascular events by about 10%. Self-monitoring lowers blood pressure when it's paired with medication adjustment, education or counselling; monitoring alone showed no effect. The weak links are the device and the technique: most monitors sold online have never been validated, and the wrong cuff size can add up to about 20 mmHg.

claims.claim: Home readings are accurate enough to guide care
claims.note: With a validated upper-arm device, the right cuff and the standard protocol, yes; guidelines now rely on them.

claims.claim: 'Clinically tested' on the box means it's validated
claims.note: Only independent validation to a recognised standard counts. In one survey of devices sold online, 18% of upper-arm and 8% of wrist-cuff monitors were validated. Check the exact model on validatebp.org or stridebp.org.

claims.claim: Wrist monitors are as good as upper-arm cuffs
claims.note: Some wrist models pass validation, but they're more sensitive to position. Prefer an arm cuff when you can; if you use a wrist cuff, hold it at heart level.

claims.claim: Watches and rings can measure your blood pressure
claims.note: Cuffless devices aren't recommended for diagnosing or managing blood pressure. None of the 532 wristband wearables in the same survey were validated.

claims.claim: Measuring at home lowers your blood pressure
claims.note: Measuring alone didn't; measuring plus acting on the numbers with your clinician lowered systolic pressure by up to about 6 mmHg.

claims.claim: An irregular-heartbeat symbol detects atrial fibrillation
claims.note: It's a prompt to get an ECG, not a diagnosis.

look_for: The exact model on an independent validated list: the US Validated Device Listing (validatebp.org), STRIDE BP (stridebp.org), or your national hypertension society's list.
A cuff that fits: measure around the middle of your upper arm and check it falls inside the range printed on the cuff. Buy a large or extra-large cuff if you need one.
An upper-arm cuff rather than a wrist cuff, unless your arm size or shape rules it out.
Memory that stores and averages readings with dates and times, for two users if needed.
If you're pregnant, or buying for a child, a model validated for that group; STRIDE BP flags these.
Data export or phone syncing, so you can share averages with your clinician.
skip: 'Clinically tested', 'medical grade' or 'hospital grade' as a substitute for independent validation.
Cuffless blood pressure from watches, rings or bands.
Extras that don't improve accuracy, such as colour screens and 'heart health scores'.
safety: If a reading is 180 or higher systolic and/or 120 or higher diastolic, rest briefly and measure again. If it's still that high and you have chest pain, breathlessness, back pain, numbness or weakness, vision changes or trouble speaking, call emergency services. If it's still that high without symptoms, contact your clinician right away.
A home average of 130/80 or above (135/85 under European guidelines) is a reason to book an appointment.
Never start, stop or change blood pressure medication based on home readings without your clinician.
In pregnancy, a reading of 140/90 or higher, or a severe headache, vision changes or upper-belly pain, needs prompt care, because it can signal pre-eclampsia.
Don't take readings on an arm with a dialysis fistula or lymphedema.
how_to_use: For 30 minutes before: no caffeine, exercise or smoking, and empty your bladder.
Sit with your back supported, feet flat and legs uncrossed, and rest quietly for 5 minutes. Don't talk or look at your phone during the reading.
Cuff on your bare upper arm, with the arm resting on a table so the cuff is at heart level. Letting the arm hang at your side added about 6.5 mmHg in a trial.
Take 2 readings a minute apart, morning and evening, for 7 days (at least 3), and average them.
The first time, measure both arms; after that, use the arm that reads higher.

studies.title: Pharmacological blood pressure lowering for primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease across different levels of blood pressure: an individual participant-level data meta-analysis
studies.authors: Blood Pressure Lowering Treatment Trialists' Collaboration
studies.finding_summary: Across 48 randomized trials and 344,716 people, each 5 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure cut the risk of major cardiovascular events by about 10%, with or without prior heart disease, even at normal or high-normal starting pressures.

studies.title: Self-monitoring of blood pressure in hypertension: A systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis
studies.authors: Tucker KL, Sheppard JP, Stevens R, Bosworth HB, Bove A, Bray EP, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Pooling 15 trials with 12-month data (7,138 people with hypertension), self-monitoring lowered clinic systolic pressure by 3.2 mmHg overall: no significant effect when used alone, but about 6.1 mmHg when combined with intensive support such as medication titration, education or counselling.

studies.title: Nonvalidated Home Blood Pressure Devices Dominate the Online Marketplace in Australia: Major Implications for Cardiovascular Risk Management
studies.authors: Picone DS, Deshpande RA, Schultz MG, Fonseca R, Campbell NRC, Delles C, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Of 972 home blood pressure devices sold online, only 18.3% of upper-arm cuffs, 8.0% of wrist cuffs and none of 532 wristband wearables were validated; validated cuffs cost more than non-validated ones.

studies.title: Effects of Cuff Size on the Accuracy of Blood Pressure Readings: The Cuff(SZ) Randomized Crossover Trial
studies.authors: Ishigami J, Charleston J, Miller ER 3rd, Matsushita K, Appel LJ, Brady TM
studies.finding_summary: In 195 adults, using a regular cuff on people who needed a large one raised systolic readings by 4.8 mmHg, and on people who needed an extra-large one by 19.5 mmHg; too-large cuffs on small arms read 3.6 mmHg low.

name: Glucose monitor
summary: Continuous sensors and finger-prick meters. Proven to improve glucose control in diabetes; for people without diabetes, little evidence that wearing one helps.
what:
A **continuous glucose monitor (CGM)** is a small sensor with a thin filament under the skin of your arm or belly that reads glucose in the fluid between cells every few minutes, for 10–15 days per sensor. Its readings trail blood glucose by several minutes. A **blood glucose meter** reads a drop of fingertip blood on a test strip. Both are standard tools in diabetes care.

Since 2024, some CGMs have been sold over the counter in the US to adults who don't use insulin, and they're marketed to people without diabetes as a way to 'see your spikes'. Glucose normally rises after meals and falls back: in healthy adults, sensors show glucose between 70 and 140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L) about 96% of the time.

evidence.summary: In randomized trials, CGM lowered HbA1c by about 0.4–0.6 percentage points more than usual care in adults with type 1 diabetes on injections and type 2 diabetes on basal insulin, and cut time spent with low glucose. For people without diabetes there are no outcome trials: no evidence that tracking or flattening post-meal rises prevents diabetes, helps weight loss or improves health. Finger-prick meters vary too: in an independent test of 18 cleared meters, only 6 met the accuracy standard in all three rounds.

claims.claim: Improves glucose control in diabetes
claims.note: Randomized trials in insulin-treated type 1 and type 2 diabetes showed lower HbA1c and less time low.

claims.claim: Helps people without diabetes lose weight or prevent diabetes
claims.note: No outcome trials exist in people without diabetes.

claims.claim: Post-meal 'spikes' are harming healthy people
claims.note: Brief rises after meals are normal; healthy adults spent a median of about 30 minutes a day above 140 mg/dL. There's no evidence that flattening them improves health.

claims.claim: A CGM can diagnose diabetes or prediabetes
claims.note: Diagnosis uses HbA1c, fasting glucose or a glucose tolerance test from a lab.

claims.claim: A smartwatch or ring can measure blood sugar without a needle
claims.note: In 2024 the FDA warned that no such device is authorized and that wrong readings could lead to dangerous dosing errors.

claims.claim: All finger-prick meters are accurate
claims.note: Cleared meters don't always meet accuracy standards in independent testing; some did every time, some never did.

look_for: Clearance for your use. If you take insulin, you need a system cleared for treatment decisions, with low and high glucose alarms.
Accuracy data: MARD (mean absolute relative difference), where lower is better and current sensors are roughly 8–10%, and whether finger-prick calibration is needed.
Wear length, warm-up time and phone compatibility.
The yearly cost of sensors, and whether insurance covers them for your situation.
For meters: compliance with the ISO 15197:2013 accuracy standard, and affordable strips, since you'll buy far more strips than meters.
Data sharing with your clinician, or with a caregiver for alarms.
skip: Needle-free glucose watches and rings.
'Metabolic health' subscriptions that score your foods by your spikes; there's no evidence this improves health in people without diabetes.
Buying a CGM to diagnose yourself. Get an HbA1c test instead.
safety: Don't change diabetes medicines, especially insulin, based on a wellness CGM or a single reading without your clinician.
Lying on the sensor can cause falsely low overnight readings; confirm lows with a finger-prick if the number doesn't match how you feel.
Some substances can distort readings on certain sensors, such as high-dose vitamin C, paracetamol (acetaminophen) and hydroxyurea; check your sensor's label.
Adhesive can irritate skin, so rotate sites. Remove the sensor before MRI or CT scans unless the maker says otherwise.
If watching your food responses makes you anxious or restrictive, stop; it can feed disordered eating.
Symptoms of very high or low glucose (confusion, sweating, shaking, extreme thirst) need action or care, whatever the device shows.
how_to_use: Curious and without diabetes? A two-week trial is plenty. Compare with healthy reference ranges rather than chasing a flat line.
Allow for the lag: when glucose is changing fast, confirm with a finger-prick before acting.

studies.title: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes Using Insulin Injections: The DIAMOND Randomized Clinical Trial
studies.authors: Beck RW, Riddlesworth T, Ruedy K, Ahmann A, Bergenstal R, Haller S, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 158 adults with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections, 24 weeks of CGM lowered HbA1c by 0.6 percentage points more than usual care and cut time spent below 70 mg/dL from a median of 80 to 43 minutes a day.

studies.title: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Treated With Basal Insulin: A Randomized Clinical Trial
studies.authors: Martens T, Beck RW, Bailey R, Ruedy KJ, Calhoun P, Peters AL, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 175 adults with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes on basal insulin in primary care, 8 months of CGM lowered HbA1c by 0.4 percentage points more than finger-prick monitoring and raised time in range (70–180 mg/dL) from 43% to 59%.

studies.title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring Profiles in Healthy Nondiabetic Participants: A Multicenter Prospective Study
studies.authors: Shah VN, DuBose SN, Li Z, Beck RW, Peters AL, Weinstock RS, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 153 healthy people aged 7–80 without diabetes wearing blinded sensors for up to 10 days, mean glucose was about 98–99 mg/dL (104 over age 60); median time between 70 and 140 mg/dL was 96%, with about 30 minutes a day above 140.

studies.title: Investigation of the Accuracy of 18 Marketed Blood Glucose Monitors
studies.authors: Klonoff DC, Parkes JL, Kovatchev BP, Kerr D, Bevier WC, Brazg RL, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Testing 18 FDA-cleared finger-prick meters in 1,035 people against laboratory reference values, only 6 met the accuracy standard in all three rounds of testing, and 4 met it in none.

name: Heart-rate chest strap
summary: An electrode strap that reads your heart's electrical signal. The reference for heart rate during exercise, and more accurate than any wrist sensor.
what:
A chest strap has two electrodes that pick up your heart's electrical activity, the same signal an ECG records, and sends each beat to a watch, phone or gym machine. Because it times beats electrically rather than optically, it stays accurate where wrist sensors struggle (intervals, lifting, cycling, rowing), and it records precise beat-to-beat intervals, which makes it the better tool for **HRV** readings.

It doesn't diagnose anything. It's a measuring tool for training by heart rate and for checking what your wrist device tells you.

evidence.summary: In a lab comparison against ECG in 50 adults, a chest strap agreed almost perfectly across treadmill, bike and elliptical (concordance 0.996), while optical wrist and forearm monitors ranged from 0.67 to 0.92 and failed on some exercises. Another lab study found wrist-sensor error rose during walking, at higher BMI and with darker skin. That's evidence of accuracy, not of health benefit: whether training by heart-rate zones gets you fitter than training by feel isn't well established.

claims.claim: More accurate than a wrist sensor during exercise
claims.note: Electrode straps are the reference for exercise heart rate; optical sensors vary by device and activity.

claims.claim: Gives reliable HRV readings
claims.note: Electrical beat timing is what HRV needs. Take readings while still, not during exercise.

claims.claim: Calculates the calories you burn
claims.note: Calorie figures still come from a model using heart rate, age and weight; an accurate heart rate doesn't make the estimate accurate.

claims.claim: Heart-rate zone training gets you fitter faster
claims.note: Zones are a useful guide, but they haven't been shown to beat training by effort for most people.

claims.claim: Picks up heart problems
claims.note: A strap reports heart rate, not a diagnostic ECG. Symptoms need a clinician.

look_for: Connectivity that matches your gear: Bluetooth for phones and watches, ANT+ for many bike computers. Many straps do both and connect to several devices at once.
A soft, adjustable strap in your size, with electrodes that stay put without constant re-tightening.
A replaceable coin-cell battery, or a charging routine you'll keep.
If you swim: waterproofing and on-board memory, because Bluetooth barely transmits underwater.
A washable strap; salt and sweat degrade the electrodes and cause dropouts.
skip: Proprietary 'recovery' or 'strain' scores bundled with a subscription.
Premium models for features you won't use. For accurate heart rate, a basic strap does the job.
safety: Moisten the electrodes and rinse the strap after use to avoid chafing and skin irritation.
If you have a pacemaker or implanted defibrillator, check your device maker's guidance before using one.
Stop and seek care for chest pain, fainting, unusual breathlessness or palpitations during exercise, whatever the strap shows.
how_to_use: Wet the electrodes and wear the strap just below the chest muscles, snug enough not to slip.
For HRV, take readings the same way each time (for example lying still on waking) and compare with your own baseline.
Rinse it after every session and unclip the sensor to save the battery.

studies.title: Variable Accuracy of Wearable Heart Rate Monitors during Aerobic Exercise
studies.authors: Gillinov S, Etiwy M, Wang R, Blackburn G, Phelan D, Gillinov AM, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 50 healthy adults exercising on a treadmill, bike and elliptical, an electrode chest strap agreed with ECG almost perfectly (concordance 0.996); optical wrist and forearm monitors ranged from 0.67 to 0.92, and none was accurate on the elliptical with arm levers.

studies.title: Accuracy in Wrist-Worn, Sensor-Based Measurements of Heart Rate and Energy Expenditure in a Diverse Cohort
studies.authors: Shcherbina A, Mattsson CM, Waggott D, Salisbury H, Christle JW, Hastie T, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 60 volunteers, wrist-sensor heart-rate error was lowest during cycling and highest during walking, and was larger with higher BMI and darker skin; no device estimated energy expenditure within 20%.

name: Smart ring
summary: A finger-worn tracker for sleep, resting heart rate, HRV and skin temperature. Fair at sleep timing, shaky on sleep stages; its scores aren't validated.
what:
A smart ring packs optical heart-rate, motion and temperature sensors into a ring you wear day and night. Because it sits on the finger and most people keep it on, it collects overnight data well: **sleep timing, resting heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV)** and **skin-temperature changes** against your own baseline. Most models roll these into a daily 'readiness' or sleep score.

What it measures reasonably well is when and roughly how long you sleep, and how your overnight numbers drift. Sleep stages, and any score built on them, are estimates.

evidence.summary: A 2026 meta-analysis of 28 studies of finger-worn devices found sleep/wake classification about 87% accurate against lab polysomnography, but light, deep and REM staging much weaker, and useful only as a triage tool for severe sleep apnea. A UK Biobank study linked regular sleep timing, something trackers measure well, to lower mortality. No study shows that following a ring's readiness score improves health.

claims.claim: Tracks when and how long you sleep
claims.note: Sleep/wake detection is reasonably accurate on typical nights; it's weaker at spotting quiet wakefulness.

claims.claim: Measures your deep and REM sleep
claims.note: Stage accuracy is well below sleep/wake accuracy. Fine for curiosity, not for decisions.

claims.claim: Its readiness score tells you how hard to train
claims.note: Scores are company-specific blends; no trials show following them improves fitness or health.

claims.claim: Detects sleep apnea
claims.note: Some finger devices can flag severe apnea as a triage step. They don't diagnose it, and mild apnea is often missed.

claims.claim: Spots illness early
claims.note: Resting heart rate and skin temperature often rise around the start of an infection. That's a prompt to rest, not a diagnosis.

claims.claim: Tracks your cycle and ovulation from temperature
claims.note: The rise in temperature after ovulation is real and rings can detect it, but it confirms ovulation after the fact rather than predicting it, and it isn't contraception on its own.

look_for: Correct sizing: use the maker's sizing kit for a day before ordering, because fit affects both readings and comfort.
Battery life (typically several days) and a charging routine you'll keep.
Subscription cost; some rings put scores or history behind a monthly fee.
Independent validation studies for the model, especially for sleep and heart rate.
Data export or syncing to your phone's health app, and a privacy policy you're comfortable with; cycle and temperature data are sensitive.
A durable shell and water resistance for swimming and showers.
skip: Readiness, recovery and sleep scores as health verdicts; they're company-specific blends, not validated clinical measures.
Paying for stage-by-stage sleep breakdowns expecting accuracy.
Using it in place of a sleep study if you snore loudly or stop breathing at night.
safety: Take it off if your fingers swell (injury, heat, pregnancy, fluid retention) or if it becomes tight, hot or misshapen.
Remove it for MRI scans and medical procedures, and consider taking it off for heavy lifting, climbing or work near machinery, where rings can catch.
Snoring with breathing pauses, gasping at night or heavy daytime sleepiness needs a clinician and a proper sleep test, whatever the ring says.
If checking scores makes your sleep worse, hide them.
how_to_use: Wear it every night for two to three weeks to learn your baseline.
Watch seven-day averages of resting heart rate, HRV and sleep timing rather than single nights.
If a score contradicts how you feel, believe how you feel.

studies.title: Performance evaluation of finger-worn devices for sleep stage classification and sleep apnea detection: a systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Jin Y, Xu J, Yue H, Huang Y, Ma W, Fan X, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Across 28 studies of 11 finger-worn devices compared with polysomnography, sleep/wake classification was about 87% accurate, but light, deep and REM staging were less accurate (pooled 0.65, 0.81 and 0.74); the devices worked best as a triage tool for severe sleep apnea and shouldn't replace a sleep study.

studies.title: Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: A prospective cohort study
studies.authors: Windred DP, Burns AC, Lane JM, Saxena R, Rutter MK, Cain SW, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 60,977 UK Biobank participants with accelerometer data, the most regular sleepers had 20–48% lower all-cause mortality than the least regular, and regularity predicted mortality better than sleep duration did.

name: Smart scale
summary: Weighs you accurately and syncs the trend. Its body-fat, muscle and 'metabolic age' numbers are estimates that can be kilograms off for one person.
what:
A smart scale measures your weight and syncs it to an app. Most also send a tiny electrical current through your feet (or hands and feet) to estimate **body composition**: fat, muscle, water, and sometimes 'visceral fat', 'bone mass' or 'metabolic age'. This is **bioimpedance**. Water conducts electricity and fat doesn't, so the scale estimates your body water and converts it using equations built on reference populations.

The weight is the trustworthy part. Composition figures move with hydration, meals, exercise and time of day, often by more than any real change.

evidence.summary: Compared with DEXA scans, three consumer smart scales weighed people to within about 0.3 kg, but underestimated fat mass by a median of about 2–4 kg, and the authors concluded they aren't accurate for body composition. A review of 17 longitudinal studies found regular self-weighing went with more weight loss and wasn't linked to worse psychological outcomes in people trying to lose weight. Nothing shows that tracking bioimpedance numbers improves health.

claims.claim: Tracks your weight accurately
claims.note: Weight errors against a reference were a few hundred grams at most.

claims.claim: Accurately measures body fat and muscle
claims.note: Estimates can be kilograms off for one person and swing with hydration. At best, a rough trend under identical conditions.

claims.claim: Weighing often helps you lose weight
claims.note: In people trying to lose weight, regular self-weighing goes with more weight loss. It isn't for everyone.

claims.claim: 'Metabolic age', 'visceral fat' and 'bone mass' readings
claims.note: These are derived from the same bioimpedance estimate plus your age and height, not measured directly.

claims.claim: Hand-and-foot (8-electrode) models are accurate
claims.note: They often do somewhat better than foot-only scales in validation studies, but they still aren't close to a DEXA scan.

look_for: Repeatable weight: step on three times in a row and the readings should agree closely.
A weight capacity that suits you, and a platform big enough to stand on naturally.
A weight-only mode if you have an implanted device, are pregnant, or simply don't want composition numbers.
Multi-user recognition if your household shares it, and data export or syncing to your phone's health app.
Privacy settings you control; body data is sensitive.
skip: Metabolic age, visceral fat ratings, protein percentage and similar derived numbers.
Paying extra for composition features expecting clinical accuracy. If you need body composition, a DEXA scan on the same machine each time is the reference.
Treating day-to-day swings of 1–2 kg as fat gained or lost.
safety: Don't use bioimpedance if you have a pacemaker, implanted defibrillator or other implanted electronic device; use weight-only mode. Most makers also advise against it in pregnancy.
If weighing triggers restriction, bingeing or distress, or you have a history of an eating disorder, skip the scale and talk to a clinician.
Losing more than 5% of your body weight over 6–12 months without trying is worth a medical check.
how_to_use: Place it on a hard, flat floor; carpet and uneven tiles skew readings.
Weigh at the same time (on waking, after the bathroom, before eating) in the same clothing.
Judge the weekly average, not the day.
If you use composition figures at all, compare only readings taken under identical conditions, over months.

studies.title: Accuracy of Smart Scales on Weight and Body Composition: Observational Study
studies.authors: Frija-Masson J, Mullaert J, Vidal-Petiot E, Pons-Kerjean N, Flamant M, d'Ortho MP
studies.finding_summary: Three commercial smart scales tested against DEXA in about 50 hospital patients each measured weight to within a median of 0–0.3 kg, but fat-mass errors had medians of 2.2–4.4 kg; the authors concluded smart scales are not accurate for body composition.

studies.title: Self-weighing in weight management: a systematic literature review
studies.authors: Zheng Y, Klem ML, Sereika SM, Danford CA, Ewing LJ, Burke LE
studies.finding_summary: Across 17 longitudinal studies of adults seeking weight loss, regular self-weighing was associated with more weight loss and not with adverse psychological outcomes such as depression or anxiety.

name: Tape measure and skinfold calipers
summary: A tape and one division give your waist-to-height ratio, a better risk flag than BMI. Calipers estimate body fat, but only with practice.
what:
These are the cheapest body measurements there are. A **tape measure** gives your waist circumference, and dividing it by your height gives your **waist-to-height ratio**, a stand-in for the fat stored around your organs (visceral fat). **Skinfold calipers** pinch a fold of skin and fat at set sites, and the thicknesses go into equations that estimate body-fat percentage.

The tape is easy to use well on yourself. Calipers need a practised hand, the same sites every time, and ideally someone else doing the pinching.

evidence.summary: A meta-analysis of studies covering more than 300,000 adults found waist-to-height ratio beat both waist size and BMI at flagging diabetes, high blood pressure and cardiovascular risk, and an international consensus statement calls waist circumference a 'vital sign' that adds information to BMI. A 2025 Lancet commission recommended confirming excess fat with a waist measure or direct fat measurement rather than relying on BMI alone. Skinfold equations are population-specific and error-prone in untrained hands, so calipers are best for tracking the same sites over time.

claims.claim: Waist size predicts health risk better than BMI
claims.note: Waist-to-height ratio outperformed BMI and waist alone for cardiometabolic risk in both sexes and several ethnic groups.

claims.claim: Keep your waist under half your height
claims.note: UK NICE guidance classes a ratio of 0.40–0.49 as healthy, 0.50–0.59 as increased risk and 0.60 or more as high risk, for adults with a BMI under 35.

claims.claim: Calipers give an accurate body-fat percentage
claims.note: In trained hands they're a reasonable field estimate; self-measurement and one-size-fits-all equations add several percentage points of error.

claims.claim: App-connected 'smart' tapes are more accurate
claims.note: Technique, not the tape, drives accuracy.

look_for: A non-stretch tape, ideally with a spring-tension or locking end so the pull is the same every time.
Markings in centimetres and inches, long enough to go round your waist and hips with room to spare.
For calipers: jaws that apply a constant pressure, and a clear millimetre scale.
A fixed protocol: the same sites, the same side of the body, and ideally the same person measuring.
skip: Body-fat percentages from a single caliper site or a generic equation.
'Smart' tapes sold as an accuracy upgrade.
Measuring daily. Your waist changes over weeks, so daily checks add worry, not information.
safety: If measuring your body triggers distress or restriction, or you have a history of an eating disorder, skip it and talk to a clinician.
A waist-to-height ratio of 0.5 or more is a reason to ask about a cardiometabolic check (blood pressure, glucose and lipids).
how_to_use: Find the bottom of your ribs and the top of your hip bones, and wrap the tape midway between them, usually just above the belly button.
Breathe out normally, keep the tape level and snug without pressing in, and read it.
Divide by your height in the same units; under 0.5 is the target.
Measure monthly, at the same spot and time of day.
For skinfolds, take each site two or three times and average, and track the sum of skinfolds over time rather than trusting the percentage.

studies.title: Waist-to-height ratio is a better screening tool than waist circumference and BMI for adult cardiometabolic risk factors: systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Ashwell M, Gunn P, Gibson S
studies.finding_summary: In studies covering more than 300,000 adults from several ethnic groups, waist-to-height ratio discriminated diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease and other outcomes significantly better than BMI or waist circumference in both men and women.

studies.title: Waist circumference as a vital sign in clinical practice: a Consensus Statement from the IAS and ICCR Working Group on Visceral Obesity
studies.authors: Ross R, Neeland IJ, Yamashita S, Shai I, Seidell J, Magni P, et al.
studies.finding_summary: An international expert group concluded that waist circumference adds independent information to BMI for predicting illness and death, recommended measuring it routinely, and noted that exercise and diet can reduce it meaningfully.

studies.title: Definition and diagnostic criteria of clinical obesity
studies.authors: Rubino F, Cummings DE, Eckel RH, Cohen RV, Wilding JPH, Brown WA, et al.
studies.finding_summary: A commission of 58 experts recommended that BMI be used only for population screening and that excess fat be confirmed by a direct body-fat measurement or at least one measure such as waist circumference, waist-to-hip or waist-to-height ratio (except when BMI is above 40).

name: Thermometer
summary: For fever, digital oral or rectal readings are the most reliable; ear and forehead models are faster but miss more fevers. 'Normal' isn't exactly 37°C.
what:
Home thermometers come in two broad kinds. **Digital contact** thermometers (oral, underarm, rectal) read the temperature where the tip sits. **Infrared** thermometers read heat radiated from the eardrum or forehead: fast and easy on a sleeping child, but more sensitive to technique, sweat, room temperature and distance. Basal thermometers read to two decimal places for cycle tracking.

A fever is generally **38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher**. 'Normal' varies: in 35,488 clinic patients, average oral temperature was 36.6°C, and individuals had their own baselines.

evidence.summary: Taking a temperature is simple, but the site matters. In a meta-analysis of 75 studies, mostly in hospital patients, ear, forehead, underarm and oral thermometers often differed from core temperature by more than 0.5°C and caught only about 64% of fevers, though they rarely reported fevers that weren't there. In children, ear readings differed from rectal ones by up to about 1°C either way. Non-contact forehead devices picked up about 81% of fevers in a separate meta-analysis. For babies, a rectal digital reading remains the reference.

claims.claim: A no-touch forehead reading is as reliable as a digital thermometer
claims.note: Non-contact infrared thermometers detected about 81% of fevers found by conventional thermometers. Fine for quick screening; confirm with a digital thermometer when it matters.

claims.claim: Ear thermometers are accurate for children
claims.note: The average difference from rectal readings is small, but individual readings can be off by about 1°C either way. Fine for a quick check in older children, not when precision matters.

claims.claim: Normal body temperature is 37.0°C
claims.note: Average adult oral temperature is about 36.6°C, and people have their own baselines.

claims.claim: Basal temperature charting confirms ovulation
claims.note: Progesterone raises resting temperature by roughly 0.2–0.5°C after ovulation, which shows, after the fact, that it happened.

claims.claim: Temperature tracking works as contraception
claims.note: Used perfectly with other fertility signs it can work, but typical-use failure rates are much higher than for IUDs, implants or the pill.

look_for: For fever: a digital thermometer for oral, underarm or rectal use; for babies, one with a flexible tip suitable for rectal readings.
For speed with children: an ear or forehead model used exactly as the manual says, with a digital thermometer to confirm when it matters.
The age range the device is designed for; ear thermometers aren't recommended for babies under about 6 months.
A clear display, a fever alert and memory for recent readings.
For cycle tracking: a basal thermometer that reads to 0.01°C, or a wearable that tracks overnight skin temperature.
Easy cleaning: probe covers or a washable tip. Label a rectal thermometer and never use it by mouth.
skip: Mercury glass thermometers. They break and spill mercury, and digital ones are just as good.
Phone apps that claim to take your temperature without a sensor.
App features that promise to predict illness or fertility from a single reading.
safety: Get medical care right away for a baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher.
At any age, seek urgent care for a fever with a stiff neck, severe headache, confusion, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, trouble breathing, or a seizure.
See a clinician for a fever that keeps climbing or lasts more than a few days.
Symptoms outrank the number: someone who looks very unwell with a 'normal' forehead reading still needs care.
Don't rely on temperature-based cycle tracking as contraception without discussing its typical-use failure rate with a clinician.
how_to_use: Wait 15–30 minutes after eating, drinking or exercise before an oral reading.
Follow the positioning instructions exactly for ear and forehead models, and repeat the reading if it seems off.
For basal temperature, measure on waking, before getting up, at the same time each day.

studies.title: Individual differences in normal body temperature: longitudinal big data analysis of patient records
studies.authors: Obermeyer Z, Samra JK, Mullainathan S
studies.finding_summary: In 35,488 outpatients without infections (243,506 measurements), mean oral temperature was 36.6°C (95% of readings 35.7–37.3°C). Individuals had their own baselines, which varied with age, sex and health.

studies.title: Accuracy of peripheral thermometers for estimating temperature: a systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Niven DJ, Gaudet JE, Laupland KB, Mrklas KJ, Roberts DJ, Stelfox HT
studies.finding_summary: Across 75 studies (8,682 patients), ear, forehead (temporal artery), underarm and oral thermometers had limits of agreement with core temperature outside ±0.5°C; they detected fever with 64% sensitivity and 96% specificity.

studies.title: Infrared ear thermometry compared with rectal thermometry in children: a systematic review
studies.authors: Craig JV, Lancaster GA, Taylor S, Williamson PR, Smyth RL
studies.finding_summary: In 31 comparisons covering 4,441 children, ear readings averaged 0.29°C below rectal ones, but individual differences ranged from about −0.7 to +1.3°C, too wide for situations that need precise measurement.

studies.title: Diagnostic accuracy of non-contact infrared thermometers and thermal scanners: a systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Aggarwal N, Garg M, Dwarakanathan V, Gautam N, Kumar SS, Jadon RS, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Pooling 19 studies, non-contact infrared thermometers detected fever with about 81% sensitivity and 92% specificity compared with conventional thermometers.

name: Watch or fitness tracker
summary: Wrist devices that log heart rate, steps and sleep. Good for resting heart rate and movement; rough for calories, VO₂ max and sleep stages.
what:
Wrist trackers and smartwatches use motion sensors and **optical heart-rate sensors** (light shone into the skin to detect each pulse) to estimate steps, heart rate and sleep, and on some models blood oxygen, skin temperature, fitness (VO₂ max) and heart rhythm. A few features, such as an ECG app or irregular-rhythm notifications, may be cleared by regulators; most of the rest are wellness estimates never reviewed for medical accuracy.

The value is in trends against your own baseline: resting heart rate, daily movement, and when you sleep.

evidence.summary: An umbrella review of 39 meta-analyses (about 164,000 people) found activity trackers raised physical activity by roughly 1,800 steps a day, with small effects on weight and fitness. In a study of 419,297 smartwatch users, 34% of those who got an irregular-pulse alert had atrial fibrillation confirmed on a later ECG patch. Accuracy depends on the metric: heart rate is good at rest and worse during movement, no tested device estimated calories within 20%, and VO₂ max estimates can be off by about ±10 mL/kg/min for an individual.

claims.claim: Helps you move more
claims.note: Across many trials, trackers added about 1,800 steps a day, with benefits that lasted.

claims.claim: Measures resting heart rate and steps accurately
claims.note: Good enough for tracking trends. Slow walking or pushing a cart or stroller can undercount steps.

claims.claim: Counts the calories you burn
claims.note: In a lab test of seven wrist devices, none estimated energy use within 20%. Don't 'eat back' exercise calories from your watch.

claims.claim: Detects atrial fibrillation
claims.note: Cleared rhythm features can flag it. An alert means get an ECG, and no alert doesn't rule it out.

claims.claim: Tells you your VO₂ max
claims.note: Right on average across groups, but individual readings can be off by about ±10 mL/kg/min, and heat, hills and fatigue shift the estimate.

claims.claim: Measures blood pressure from the wrist band
claims.note: Cuffless readings aren't recommended for diagnosing or managing blood pressure. Use a validated upper-arm cuff.

claims.claim: Tracks your deep and REM sleep
claims.note: Timing and total sleep are fair; stage breakdowns are inconsistent, and sleep or 'readiness' scores aren't validated clinical measures.

look_for: Independent validation studies for the metrics you care about (search the model name plus 'validation'), not the marketing page.
Comfort and battery life you'll live with; gaps break trends.
Regulatory clearance for any medical-style feature you'll rely on, such as ECG or irregular-rhythm alerts. Clearance applies feature by feature.
Data export or syncing to your phone's health app, so years of history aren't trapped if you switch.
Any subscription cost, and a privacy policy that lets you delete your data and limits sharing with advertisers.
If exercise heart rate matters to you (intervals, zones), plan to pair it with a chest strap.
skip: Calorie-burn numbers as a basis for how much to eat.
'Stress', 'body battery' and readiness scores as verdicts on your health; they're proprietary blends.
Cuffless blood pressure features.
Paying extra for sensors whose readings you won't act on.
safety: An irregular-rhythm alert is a reason to book an ECG. A watch can't detect a heart attack: call emergency services for chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness or signs of stroke, whatever the watch says.
Blood-oxygen readings from light sensors can overestimate oxygen on darker skin, and wrist SpO₂ is a wellness feature. Symptoms outrank the number.
See a clinician if your resting heart rate is consistently above 100, or below 50 with dizziness, fainting or unusual fatigue.
If tracking makes you anxious or you find yourself chasing sleep scores, hide the scores or take a break.
Keep the skin under the band clean and dry, and loosen it if it irritates.
how_to_use: Learn your baseline over two to three weeks before reading anything into a number.
Review weekly averages, not daily scores.
Wear it the same way (same wrist, same snug fit) so trends stay comparable.

studies.title: Effectiveness of wearable activity trackers to increase physical activity and improve health: a systematic review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
studies.authors: Ferguson T, Olds T, Curtis R, Blake H, Crozier AJ, Dankiw K, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Pooling 39 systematic reviews covering 163,992 people, activity trackers increased physical activity by about 1,800 steps a day and reduced body weight by about 1 kg; effects on blood pressure, cholesterol and HbA1c were small and often not significant.

studies.title: Large-Scale Assessment of a Smartwatch to Identify Atrial Fibrillation
studies.authors: Perez MV, Mahaffey KW, Hedlin H, Rumsfeld JS, Garcia A, Ferris T, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Of 419,297 smartwatch wearers, 0.52% received an irregular-pulse notification; among those who then wore an ECG patch (on average 13 days later), 34% had atrial fibrillation, and 84% of alerts during patch wear coincided with it. The study was funded by the device maker.

studies.title: Accuracy in Wrist-Worn, Sensor-Based Measurements of Heart Rate and Energy Expenditure in a Diverse Cohort
studies.authors: Shcherbina A, Mattsson CM, Waggott D, Salisbury H, Christle JW, Hastie T, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 60 volunteers tested against ECG and indirect calorimetry, six of seven wrist devices measured heart rate within 5% during cycling, but none estimated energy expenditure within 20%. Errors were larger during walking and with higher BMI and darker skin.

studies.title: Validity of Estimating the Maximal Oxygen Consumption by Consumer Wearables: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis and Expert Statement of the INTERLIVE Network
studies.authors: Molina-Garcia P, Notbohm HL, Schumann M, Argent R, Hetherington-Rauth M, Stang J, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Across 14 validation studies, exercise-based watch estimates of VO₂ max were unbiased on average but individual errors spanned about ±10 mL/kg/min; estimates from resting data overestimated by about 2.2 mL/kg/min with wider error.

name: Cold plunge
summary: Tubs and chillers for short cold-water dips. Real short-term effects on alertness and soreness, no long-term health data, and bad timing can blunt muscle gains.
what:
A cold plunge is a tub or barrel of cold water, kept cold with ice or a **chiller**, that you sit in up to your neck for a few minutes. Home units range from pop-up tubs and barrels to insulated tubs with built-in chillers, filtration and sanitation.

The jolt is real: immersion triggers a big stress-hormone surge, a gasp and fast breathing, then a lingering alertness many people enjoy. But the evidence base is much thinner than for sauna, and no long-term studies show that people who plunge live longer.

evidence.summary: A Cochrane review found cold-water immersion modestly reduced muscle soreness after exercise, but in 17 small, low-quality trials. A 2025 meta-analysis of 11 trials found a delayed dip in stress and small quality-of-life gains, with no clear effect on mood. In a trial of 3,018 adults, cold-finished showers cut self-reported sick leave but not days of illness. Cold right after strength training reduced muscle and strength gains in a 12-week trial. Long-term health effects are unknown.

claims.claim: Reduces muscle soreness after exercise
claims.note: Pooled trials favour cold water over resting, but the effect is modest and the trials are small and low quality.

claims.claim: Boosts your immune system
claims.note: In the large cold-shower trial, people took less sick leave but weren't ill on fewer days, and they knew which group they were in.

claims.claim: Improves mood and lowers stress
claims.note: A meta-analysis found lower stress 12 hours after immersion and small quality-of-life gains, but no clear effect on mood, from few small trials.

claims.claim: Burns fat and helps weight loss
claims.note: Brown fat can be recruited by hours of mild cold a day. A few minutes of plunging burns a modest amount of energy and isn't a weight-loss tool.

claims.claim: A plunge after every strength session helps you build muscle
claims.note: Cold within minutes of lifting led to smaller muscle and strength gains in a 12-week trial, and muscle biopsies showed weaker growth signalling. Keep plunges away from strength sessions.

claims.claim: Helps you live longer
claims.note: No long-term outcome studies exist.

look_for: A chiller that reliably holds about 10–15°C (50–59°F), the range most studies used. A lower minimum isn't a feature you need.
Filtration plus sanitation (such as ozone or UV, with a changeable filter); standing water fouls quickly.
Electrical safety: a GFCI/RCD-protected outlet and a safety-certified chiller rated for wet locations.
A lockable, insulated cover. Children and pets can drown in a tub.
A size and shape you can get into and out of safely, with handles or a step if you need them.
A thermometer you trust and an easy way to drain and clean it.
skip: Near-freezing minimum temperatures as a selling point.
'Dopamine boost' percentages. The famous figure came from an hour of immersion at 14°C, not a 2-minute plunge.
Fat-loss, immune-boosting and longevity promises.
Water treatments sold as health benefits for you; sanitation is for the water.
safety: Cold shock is the real danger: an involuntary gasp and runaway breathing in the first minute. Enter slowly, keep your head out of the water, and breathe out slowly.

Skip it, or get medical advice first, if you have coronary heart disease, a heart-rhythm problem, uncontrolled high blood pressure, a past stroke, Raynaud's, cold urticaria (hives from cold), sickle cell disease, or you're pregnant.
Never plunge alone or after alcohol, and never combine it with breath-holds or hyperventilation breathing; blacking out in water can be fatal.
Get out if you're shivering hard, numb or confused, or can't settle your breathing. Rewarm gradually, because core temperature can keep falling after you get out.
Keep the lid locked when the tub isn't in use.
how_to_use: Try it free first: a 30–90 second cold finish to your shower shows whether you like it.
Start mild, around 15°C (59°F) for 1–2 minutes. Repeated short exposures blunt the cold shock.
Recovery studies mostly used about 10–15°C for 5–15 minutes; there's no evidence you need colder or longer.
If muscle growth is a goal, keep plunges off strength days or well away from lifting.
Plunge earlier in the day; cold is alerting.

studies.title: Cold-water immersion (cryotherapy) for preventing and treating muscle soreness after exercise
studies.authors: Bleakley C, McDonough S, Gardner E, Baxter GD, Hopkins JT, Davison GW
studies.finding_summary: Across 17 small trials (366 people), immersion in water below 15°C after exercise reduced muscle soreness at 24 to 96 hours compared with rest. Study quality was low and most trials didn't monitor for adverse events.

studies.title: Post-exercise cold water immersion attenuates acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training
studies.authors: Roberts LA, Raastad T, Markworth JF, Figueiredo VC, Egner IM, Shield A, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 21 active men strength training twice a week for 12 weeks, 10 minutes of cold-water immersion after each session led to smaller gains in strength and muscle mass than an active cool-down, with blunted muscle growth signalling in biopsies.

studies.title: The Effect of Cold Showering on Health and Work: A Randomized Controlled Trial
studies.authors: Buijze GA, Sierevelt IN, van der Heijden BC, Dijkgraaf MG, Frings-Dresen MH
studies.finding_summary: In 3,018 Dutch adults, finishing showers with 30–90 seconds of cold for 30 days reduced self-reported sickness absence from work by 29%, but not the number of illness days.

studies.title: Effects of cold-water immersion on health and wellbeing: A systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Cain T, Brinsley J, Bennett H, Nelson M, Maher C, Singh B
studies.finding_summary: Across 11 trials (3,177 healthy adults) of water at or below 15°C, immersion caused a short-term rise in inflammation and lowered stress 12 hours later but not at other times; sleep and quality of life improved, mood did not. The authors noted few, small trials.

name: Cryotherapy
summary: Chambers that expose you to air at −110°C or colder for 2–3 minutes. The evidence is very low quality, it isn't shown to beat an ice bath, and it has real risks.
what:
**Whole-body cryotherapy** exposes you to extremely cold, dry air, typically **−110 to −140°C (−166 to −220°F)**, for about **2–3 minutes**, either in an electrically cooled chamber you walk into or in a nitrogen-cooled 'cryosauna' that leaves your head outside. **Localised** cryotherapy blows very cold air or nitrogen vapour onto one area. Because the air is dry and the exposure short, your skin cools sharply while your core temperature changes little.

It's sold for recovery, inflammation, pain, mood, weight loss and skin. In the US, the FDA has not cleared any whole-body cryotherapy device to treat any medical condition.

evidence.summary: A Cochrane review found only four small trials (64 mostly young men) on muscle soreness, all at high risk of bias, and rated the evidence 'very low' quality, too little to say whether it works. Broader recovery meta-analyses suggest cold exposure trims soreness a little, but whole-body and partial-body cryo performed the same, and there's no evidence it beats a far cheaper cold-water tub. There are no good trials for weight loss, anti-ageing or treating medical conditions.

claims.claim: Reduces muscle soreness
claims.note: Small trials hint at less soreness, but the evidence is very low quality, and cold water does similar things for a fraction of the cost.

claims.claim: Burns 500–800 calories a session
claims.note: No measurement supports this for a 2–3 minute exposure.

claims.claim: Treats arthritis, pain, depression, anxiety or skin conditions
claims.note: The FDA hasn't cleared any whole-body device for these uses and has warned that the claims lack evidence.

claims.claim: Works better than an ice bath
claims.note: No trials show an advantage over cold-water immersion.

claims.claim: Tightens skin and slows ageing ('cryofacials')
claims.note: No good controlled trials support it.

look_for: A trained operator present for the whole session, with an emergency stop you can reach.
Electrically cooled walk-in chambers where you breathe normal air, or, for nitrogen cryosaunas, your head held above the vapour and oxygen monitoring in the room.
Screening before your first session, including a blood pressure check and health questions.
Dry gloves, socks, ear covers and a mask provided, and a strict 2–3 minute limit.
A price you can justify against a cold shower or ice bath, which have at least as much evidence.
skip: Calorie-burn and weight-loss claims.
Treating arthritis, fibromyalgia, depression, anxiety or migraine with cryotherapy.
'Cryofacial' and 'cryo-slimming' packages.
Longer or colder sessions. More isn't shown to help, and it raises frostbite risk.
safety: Nitrogen cryosaunas can displace oxygen, and people have died from asphyxiation, including a spa worker who used a chamber alone in 2015. Never use one alone or with your head below the rim.
Frostbite and cold burns happen, especially on damp or sweaty skin or under jewellery. Be completely dry and remove metal.
Skip it if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart disease or a rhythm problem, Raynaud's, cold urticaria, peripheral artery disease, or you're pregnant; it isn't for children.
Blood pressure jumps during exposure, so anyone with heart or circulation problems should ask a clinician first.
Get out immediately if you feel faint, numb or panicky.

studies.title: Whole-body cryotherapy (extreme cold air exposure) for preventing and treating muscle soreness after exercise in adults
studies.authors: Costello JT, Baker PR, Minett GM, Bieuzen F, Stewart IB, Bleakley C
studies.finding_summary: Four small laboratory trials in 64 active, mostly male young adults, all at high risk of bias, gave very low-quality evidence on soreness after whole-body cryotherapy; the reviewers found insufficient evidence to say whether it reduces soreness or improves recovery, and no data in women.

studies.title: Different Cryotherapy Modalities Demonstrate Similar Effects on Muscle Performance, Soreness, and Damage in Healthy Individuals and Athletes: A Systematic Review with Metanalysis
studies.authors: Azevedo KP, Bastos JAI, de Sousa Neto IV, Pastre CM, Durigan JLQ
studies.finding_summary: In six studies (120 people) comparing whole-body and partial-body cryotherapy after muscle-damaging exercise, both produced similar effects on performance, soreness and muscle-damage markers.

studies.title: An Evidence-Based Approach for Choosing Post-exercise Recovery Techniques to Reduce Markers of Muscle Damage, Soreness, Fatigue, and Inflammation: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
studies.authors: Dupuy O, Douzi W, Theurot D, Bosquet L, Dugué B
studies.finding_summary: Across 99 studies of recovery methods, massage was most effective for soreness and perceived fatigue; cold exposure, compression garments and water immersion gave small-to-large reductions in soreness, and massage and cold exposure lowered inflammation markers.

name: Hyperbaric chamber
summary: Breathing oxygen under pressure. A proven hospital treatment for specific conditions like decompression sickness; home soft chambers aren't that, and longevity use is unproven.
what:
**Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT)** means breathing close to 100% oxygen while the pressure around you is raised, usually to **2–3 times normal atmospheric pressure**, in a hospital-grade chamber. That drives far more oxygen into your blood, and it's an established treatment for a short list of conditions, from decompression sickness to carbon monoxide poisoning and some non-healing wounds.

Most chambers sold for homes and wellness clinics are different. **Soft-sided 'mild' chambers** reach about **1.3 atmospheres**, usually with ordinary air or oxygen from a concentrator. Breathing air at 1.3 atmospheres raises your oxygen intake only about as much as a little supplemental oxygen at sea level, a small fraction of a clinical dose. In the US, soft chambers have been cleared for acute mountain sickness, not for wellness or anti-ageing.

evidence.summary: In hospitals, recompression with oxygen is the standard treatment for decompression sickness and gas embolism, and the US FDA has cleared hyperbaric chambers for about a dozen specific conditions. Even there, trial evidence varies: a Cochrane review found diabetic foot ulcers healed faster at six weeks but not at one year. For healthy people, the widely cited 'anti-ageing' study had 35 older adults, no control group, and measured telomeres in blood cells rather than ageing itself. Home soft chambers deliver a much smaller dose and have no outcome trials for wellness uses.

claims.claim: Treats decompression sickness and gas embolism
claims.note: Recompression breathing 100% oxygen is the definitive treatment for divers' decompression illness, as an emergency, in a medical chamber.

claims.claim: Treats carbon monoxide poisoning
claims.note: A double-blind trial found three sessions cut cognitive problems at six weeks (25% vs 46%), but other trials disagree. It's a hospital decision for serious poisoning: call emergency services, don't use a home chamber.

claims.claim: Heals chronic wounds
claims.note: For diabetic foot ulcers, HBOT improved healing at six weeks but not at one year, and the trials had design flaws. It's an add-on to specialist wound care.

claims.claim: Reverses ageing and lengthens telomeres
claims.note: The headline study gave 60 sessions to 35 older adults with no comparison group and measured blood-cell telomeres, not health or lifespan.

claims.claim: Helps autism, stroke recovery, brain injury or sports injuries
claims.note: The FDA has warned that HBOT hasn't been proven for these and many other conditions; small positive studies haven't been confirmed.

claims.claim: A home soft chamber gives the same benefits as hospital HBOT
claims.note: About 1.3 atmospheres of air versus 2–3 atmospheres of pure oxygen is a very different dose, and the clinical evidence comes from the latter.

look_for: For a medical condition: treatment at an accredited hyperbaric facility with a physician trained in hyperbaric medicine (in the US, look for Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society accreditation).
Confirmation that your condition is on the approved list; insurers generally cover only those uses.
For a home soft chamber: the regulatory clearance and its actual indication, the maximum pressure, and emergency pressure-release valves you can operate from inside.
Another person present for every session, and a plan for ear pain or panic.
Plain claims. A seller who lists autism, cancer or anti-ageing is selling beyond any clearance.
skip: Anti-ageing, telomere and 'stem-cell boosting' protocols.

Oxygen concentrators sold with soft chambers. The chambers weren't cleared for use with added oxygen, which raises fire risk inside an enclosure not built for it, for a benefit that's never been shown.
Hard-shell 'home' chambers marketed for wellness. Clinical pressures carry clinical risks and need clinical supervision.
Wellness-clinic packages of dozens of sessions for conditions not on the approved list.
safety: Ear and sinus pressure injury is the most common problem. Don't go in with a cold, blocked sinuses or after recent ear surgery, and stop if you can't equalize.
An untreated collapsed lung (pneumothorax) rules HBOT out; severe lung disease with air trapping, uncontrolled seizures and some chemotherapy drugs need specialist review.
Fire is the catastrophic risk in oxygen-rich chambers: no electronics, hand warmers, lighters or oil-based products inside. A child died in a hyperbaric chamber fire at a US clinic in 2025.
Many sessions at clinical pressures can temporarily change your eyesight (short-sightedness), and oxygen toxicity can rarely cause seizures.
Discuss it first if you're pregnant, claustrophobic, or struggle to clear your ears.
For suspected carbon monoxide poisoning or decompression sickness, call emergency services. Don't treat it at home.

studies.title: Decompression illness
studies.authors: Vann RD, Butler FK, Mitchell SJ, Moon RE
studies.finding_summary: Reviews decompression illness in divers, aviators and others: first aid is 100% oxygen, definitive treatment is recompression breathing 100% oxygen, and treatment is usually effective, though serious cases can leave lasting deficits.

studies.title: Hyperbaric oxygen for acute carbon monoxide poisoning
studies.authors: Weaver LK, Hopkins RO, Chan KJ, Churchill S, Elliott CG, Clemmer TP, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 152 patients with symptomatic carbon monoxide poisoning, three hyperbaric oxygen sessions within 24 hours reduced cognitive problems at six weeks (25% vs 46% with normal-pressure oxygen), with a benefit still seen at 12 months.

studies.title: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy for chronic wounds
studies.authors: Kranke P, Bennett MH, Martyn-St James M, Schnabel A, Debus SE, Weibel S
studies.finding_summary: Across 12 trials (577 people), HBOT improved healing of diabetic foot ulcers at six weeks (RR 2.35) but not at one year, with no significant difference in major amputations; trial flaws limited confidence.

studies.title: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy increases telomere length and decreases immunosenescence in isolated blood cells: a prospective trial
studies.authors: Hachmo Y, Hadanny A, Abu Hamed R, Daniel-Kotovsky M, Catalogna M, Fishlev G, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Thirty-five healthy adults aged 64 and over received 60 daily HBOT sessions; telomere length in several blood immune-cell types rose by more than 20% and some senescent T-cell counts fell. There was no control group, and no clinical outcomes were measured.

name: Infrared sauna
summary: Panels warm your skin directly while the air stays around 45–65°C. Gentler than a Finnish sauna, with a much smaller evidence base of its own.
what:
An **infrared sauna** uses carbon or ceramic panels that emit infrared radiation, warming your skin directly while the air stays much cooler than in a traditional sauna, usually around **45–65°C (113–150°F)**. 'Near', 'mid' and 'far' describe the wavelength band; 'full-spectrum' cabins combine them, often adding red or near-infrared LEDs. The category also covers portable pods and **infrared blankets** you lie in.

It feels gentler, which is the appeal, and it's also why the big Finnish sauna findings don't transfer automatically. Those came from ~80°C rooms; minute for minute, an infrared session is usually a lighter heat load.

evidence.summary: The best-studied infrared protocol is Japanese 'Waon therapy' (15 minutes at 60°C, then 30 minutes resting under blankets) in people with heart failure. Small trials and one multicentre randomized trial reported better symptoms and walking distance, though the main blood-marker endpoint didn't reach significance. A 2018 review of 40 dry-sauna studies found mostly small, varied trials. There are no long-term outcome studies of infrared use in healthy people; a Japanese cohort linking near-daily hot baths to less cardiovascular disease hints that heat dose, not the device, is what matters.

claims.claim: Gives the same benefits as a traditional sauna
claims.note: The mortality and stroke data come from ~80°C Finnish saunas. Infrared heat is real, but it's a different and usually lighter dose, with no comparable long-term studies.

claims.claim: Penetrates deeper, so it's healthier
claims.note: Infrared warms the outer layers of skin and your core heats through circulation, as in any sauna. No study shows depth of penetration adds a health benefit.

claims.claim: Detoxifies heavy metals and toxins
claims.note: Sweat carries only small amounts of metals and chemicals; your liver and kidneys do the real clearing, and no good trial shows sauna 'detox' improves health.

claims.claim: Burns up to 600 calories a session
claims.note: No measurement supports this. The weight you lose is water.

claims.claim: Helps heart failure
claims.note: Supervised Waon therapy improved symptoms and walking distance in small trials of patients. That's a medical protocol, done with a cardiologist, not evidence of heart benefits for healthy people.

claims.claim: 'Full-spectrum' LEDs add red-light therapy benefits
claims.note: The heat is real; extra cellular benefits from lights inside a hot cabin are largely untested.

look_for: The air temperature it actually reaches and holds (many cabins top out around 60–65°C), and how long it takes to heat up.
Heater coverage: panels at your back, sides, front and calves heat you more evenly than a single back panel.
Electrical safety certification (UL or ETL listing, CE or UKCA) and whether it runs on a standard outlet or needs a dedicated circuit.
Materials: solid wood and low-VOC glues and finishes. Run a new cabin empty a few times to air it out.
For blankets and pods: reliable temperature control, an automatic shut-off timer and a washable inner liner.
Room to sit upright, or lie down, the way you'll actually use it.
skip: 'Low EMF' or 'zero EMF' premiums. There's no evidence the fields from heater wiring harm health, so treat it as a preference, not a health feature.
Detox, calorie-burn and 'deeper penetration' claims.
Colour-light therapy, crystals and negative-ion generators.
Paying more for 'full-spectrum' or built-in red light expecting extra health benefits; they're untested in a sauna.
safety: Same precautions as a traditional sauna: no alcohol, extra care with heart disease, low blood pressure, heat-sensitive medicines and medication patches, pregnancy and fever.
If you have reduced skin sensation (diabetic neuropathy, spinal cord injury), be careful with panels close to the skin and with blankets, which can burn skin you can't feel.
Don't fall asleep in a blanket or pod; set the timer.
Heat can lower sperm counts, so pause regular use if you're trying to conceive.
Heart failure: use infrared heat only with your cardiologist's guidance, as in the studied Waon protocol.
how_to_use: A studied starting point is about 15 minutes at around 60°C, as in Waon therapy, then rest and cool down gradually.
Build up slowly and drink water before and after.
Several moderate sessions a week fit the heat evidence better than one long one.
Get out if you feel dizzy, nauseous or unwell, and stand up slowly.

studies.title: Waon Therapy for Managing Chronic Heart Failure - Results From a Multicenter Prospective Randomized WAON-CHF Study
studies.authors: Tei C, Imamura T, Kinugawa K, Inoue T, Masuyama T, Inoue H, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 149 hospitalized patients with advanced heart failure, 10 days of daily far-infrared sauna (60°C for 15 minutes, then 30 minutes under blankets) improved symptom class, 6-minute walk distance and heart size on X-ray versus controls; the change in the primary blood marker (BNP) was not statistically significant. No serious adverse events.

studies.title: Clinical Effects of Regular Dry Sauna Bathing: A Systematic Review
studies.authors: Hussain J, Cohen M
studies.finding_summary: Across 40 studies with 3,855 participants, only 13 were randomized trials and most were small (under 40 people). Outcomes were varied and mostly reported benefits; the authors called for larger, higher-quality studies to establish effects and safe doses.

studies.title: Habitual tub bathing and risks of incident coronary heart disease and stroke
studies.authors: Ukai T, Iso H, Yamagishi K, Saito I, Kokubo Y, Yatsuya H, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 30,076 Japanese adults aged 40–59 followed for about 20 years, near-daily hot tub bathing was associated with 28% lower risk of cardiovascular disease than bathing 0–2 times a week (HR 0.72), with no association for sudden cardiac death.

name: Light therapy box
summary: Bright white light for your eyes in the morning. About 10,000 lux for 30 minutes treats winter depression; it's the best-supported device on this shelf.
what:
A **light box** works through your eyes, not your skin. Bright light reaches light-sensitive cells in the retina that report straight to your brain's master clock, shifting circadian timing and acting on mood pathways. That makes it a different tool from a red-light panel, which acts (if at all) on the skin it reaches.

The category also includes **dawn simulators**, which brighten gradually in your bedroom before you wake. The best-studied dose is about **10,000 lux at your eyes for about 30 minutes soon after waking**. A bright indoor room is only a few hundred lux, so a lamp that looks bright isn't necessarily delivering that dose.

evidence.summary: For seasonal (winter) depression, randomized trials against dim-light or sham devices show a clear benefit: a 2020 meta-analysis of 19 trials found bright light beat placebo, and in one trial it matched fluoxetine. It has also beaten placebo in non-seasonal depression. The limits are study size and quality (mostly small trials with moderate-to-high risk of bias), and the evidence for jet lag, energy or general wellness is much thinner.

claims.claim: Treats seasonal affective disorder (winter depression)
claims.note: The best-studied use: about 10,000 lux for 30 minutes each morning. In a Canadian trial it worked as well as fluoxetine and acted faster.

claims.claim: Helps non-seasonal depression
claims.note: In a placebo-controlled trial, light alone and light plus fluoxetine both beat placebo. The evidence base is smaller than for seasonal depression, and it belongs alongside care, not instead of it.

claims.claim: Dawn simulators treat winter low mood
claims.note: A meta-analysis pooled five small positive trials, but the evidence is thinner than for a light box.

claims.claim: Shifts your body clock for jet lag or late sleep timing
claims.note: Morning light moves your clock earlier and evening light later, which is solid physiology, but trials of light boxes for jet lag and sleep problems are few and mixed.

claims.claim: Blue-enriched light works better than white
claims.note: The key trials used white light; blue-enriched boxes haven't been shown to do better.

claims.claim: Any bright 'daylight' bulb or mood lamp will do
claims.note: Trials used about 10,000 lux at the eyes for 30 minutes, or about 2,500 lux for 2 hours. Most lamps deliver far less at a normal sitting distance.

look_for: 10,000 lux at a stated, practical distance (for example 40–60 cm, 16–24 in). A lamp that only reaches 10,000 lux a few centimetres from your face is a poor buy.
White light with UV filtered out. You don't need 'full-spectrum' or UV.
A lit surface large enough that small head movements don't take you out of the beam.
Flicker-free output and a stand that places the light slightly above eye level, angled down.
For a dawn simulator: a gradual brightening ramp (typically 30 minutes or more) and a light you can place near the bed.
A timer, so a morning session becomes a routine you keep.
skip: Colour-changing 'mood' lamps and ordinary daylight bulbs sold as therapy lights.
Blue-only or 'blue-enriched' premiums; they aren't shown to beat white light.
Energy, focus or 'productivity' claims for healthy people, which are barely tested.
Tiny lamps whose rated lux is only reached a few centimetres from the face.
safety: See a clinician before starting if you have bipolar disorder: bright light can trigger hypomania or mania.
Check first if you have eye disease (such as macular degeneration or diabetic retinopathy), a light-sensitive condition, or take light-sensitising medicines.
Headache, eye strain, nausea or feeling wired are common at first and usually settle; shorten the session if they don't.
Depression is a medical condition. Use light alongside care, not instead of it, and get urgent help if you have thoughts of self-harm.
Avoid late-evening sessions unless advised, because they can push your sleep later.
how_to_use: Use it within about an hour of waking: roughly 30 minutes at 10,000 lux, or as your clinician advises.
Sit at the distance where your box actually delivers 10,000 lux; check the manual.
Keep your eyes open with the light in view, slightly above and in front of you. Read or eat breakfast rather than staring into it.
If winter low mood returns every year, start as the days shorten and continue through the dark months.
Give it a couple of weeks. If you're not improving, or feel worse, see a clinician.

studies.title: The Efficacy of Light Therapy in the Treatment of Seasonal Affective Disorder: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
studies.authors: Pjrek E, Friedrich ME, Cambioli L, Dold M, Jäger F, Komorowski A, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Across 19 randomized trials of bright light (at least 1,000 lux) against dim light or sham devices, light therapy reduced depression scores (SMD −0.37) and raised response rates (RR 1.42) in seasonal affective disorder; studies were small with moderate-to-high risk of bias.

studies.title: The Can-SAD study: a randomized controlled trial of the effectiveness of light therapy and fluoxetine in patients with winter seasonal affective disorder
studies.authors: Lam RW, Levitt AJ, Levitan RD, Enns MW, Morehouse R, Michalak EE, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 96 patients with winter depression, 8 weeks of 10,000-lux light for 30 minutes each morning (plus a placebo pill) worked as well as fluoxetine (plus dim placebo light): 67% responded in both groups. Light worked faster and caused fewer side effects such as agitation and sleep disturbance.

studies.title: Efficacy of Bright Light Treatment, Fluoxetine, and the Combination in Patients With Nonseasonal Major Depressive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial
studies.authors: Lam RW, Levitt AJ, Levitan RD, Michalak EE, Cheung AH, Morehouse R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 122 adults with non-seasonal major depression, 8 weeks of morning 10,000-lux light beat an inactive placebo device, alone (effect size 0.80) and combined with fluoxetine (1.11); fluoxetine alone did not beat placebo.

studies.title: The efficacy of light therapy in the treatment of mood disorders: a review and meta-analysis of the evidence
studies.authors: Golden RN, Gaynes BN, Ekstrom RD, Hamer RM, Jacobsen FM, Suppes T, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Only 13% of studies met quality criteria. Among those, bright light (effect size 0.84) and dawn simulation (0.73) reduced symptoms of seasonal depression, and bright light helped non-seasonal depression (0.53); effects were similar to antidepressant drug trials.

name: PEMF device
summary: Mats, pads and coils that pulse a magnetic field into tissue. A few prescription uses exist; evidence for wellness mats is weak, and implants rule them out.
what:
**Pulsed electromagnetic field** devices send pulsing current through coils to create a changing magnetic field, which induces tiny electrical currents in tissue. Consumer versions are mats, pads, belts and chair covers sold for relaxation, sleep, recovery or 'cellular energy', often combined with heat or LEDs.

The acronym covers very different things: prescription bone-growth stimulators for fractures that won't heal, cleared devices for post-operative pain and swelling, and the far stronger clinic treatment **transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)** for depression. Evidence for one says little about another. A wellness mat borrows the name, not the data.

evidence.summary: For fractures that failed to heal, a Cochrane review of four small blinded trials found a possible benefit that wasn't statistically significant. For knee osteoarthritis, a meta-analysis of 8 sham-controlled trials found some improvement in physical function but no clear effect on pain or stiffness. There are no good trials behind the sleep, stress, 'detox' or frequency-specific claims made for consumer mats, which is telling, because PEMF is easy to test against a sham device.

claims.claim: Helps broken bones heal
claims.note: Prescription bone stimulators are used for fractures that won't heal, but a Cochrane review called the evidence inconclusive. Consumer mats aren't those devices.

claims.claim: Eases knee osteoarthritis pain
claims.note: Pooled sham-controlled trials showed a small gain in function but no clear pain relief, and settings varied widely.

claims.claim: Improves sleep, stress or energy
claims.note: No good controlled trials support these claims for consumer mats.

claims.claim: Treats depression
claims.note: Clinic TMS, a far stronger, focused magnetic pulse, is FDA-cleared for depression. Home mats are orders of magnitude weaker and don't share that evidence.

claims.claim: Tuned to the Earth's natural frequency or to 'brainwaves'
claims.note: Frequency-specific claims aren't backed by good human evidence.

claims.claim: Recharges cells and boosts circulation
claims.note: Cell and animal studies show PEMF can affect signalling, but consumer devices rarely publish the settings needed to compare, and no human trials show these benefits.

look_for: Published field intensity (microtesla or gauss) and frequency or waveform, not just named 'presets', so you can compare with studies.
If clearance is claimed, the 510(k) number and its actual indication.
A generous return window: set a 4–6 week trial and judge it by something concrete, like a pain score or a walk you can manage.
For heated mats: adjustable temperature and an automatic shut-off.
Plain claims. A seller who promises to treat named diseases is a reason to walk away.
skip: Amethyst, tourmaline, 'chakra' and 'photon' layers; there's no evidence they add anything.
'Earth frequency', 'Schumann resonance' and brainwave-tuning presets.
Borrowed credibility: bone-stimulator, TMS or space-agency research doesn't transfer to a consumer mat.
High prices justified by 'medical-grade' language without a cleared indication.
safety: Don't use one if you have a pacemaker, implanted defibrillator, cochlear implant, neurostimulator, insulin pump or any other implanted electronic device.
Avoid it during pregnancy.
Check with a clinician first if you have epilepsy, a bleeding disorder or cancer.
Heated mats can burn skin you can't feel; take care with diabetic neuropathy or reduced sensation.
Don't let a mat replace care for persistent pain, low mood, sleep problems or a bone injury.
how_to_use: Rule out implants and pregnancy first.
Treat it as a comfort aid and test it honestly: record a pain or sleep measure for a week before and throughout a 4–6 week trial.

studies.title: Electromagnetic field stimulation for treating delayed union or non-union of long bone fractures in adults
studies.authors: Griffin XL, Costa ML, Parsons N, Smith N
studies.finding_summary: Four small blinded randomized trials (125 people) of electromagnetic stimulation for long-bone fractures that hadn't healed showed a possible benefit that was not statistically significant (RR 1.96, 95% CI 0.86–4.48). The authors judged the evidence inconclusive.

studies.title: Effects of pulsed electromagnetic field therapy on pain, stiffness and physical function in patients with knee osteoarthritis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
