studies.authors: Chen L, Duan X, Xing F, Liu G, Gong M, Li L, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 8 placebo-controlled trials with 421 people with knee osteoarthritis, PEMF improved physical function scores but showed no significant advantage for pain or stiffness.

name: Pneumatic compression
summary: Inflatable boots, sleeves and pumps that squeeze limbs in sequence. Proven medical uses (clots, lymphedema); for sports recovery, mostly a short-term feel-good.
what:
**Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC)** devices inflate chambers in a boot or sleeve, usually squeezing from the foot or hand toward the body, then release. The category covers recovery boots sold to athletes, arm and leg sleeves and the pumps that drive them, alongside simpler graduated compression garments.

In medicine, IPC helps prevent blood clots in people who can't move and manages **lymphedema**, usually with a prescription and set pressures. Consumer recovery boots apply the same idea to tired legs, and the evidence for that use is far thinner.

evidence.summary: In a UK trial of 2,876 immobile stroke patients, hospital IPC cut deep-vein clots from 12.1% to 8.5%, and a 2025 meta-analysis found IPC reduced lymphedema after breast-cancer surgery. Graduated compression stockings on flights over five hours sharply reduced symptomless clots in a Cochrane review. For recovery, a randomized trial in ultramarathon runners found a 20-minute session made people feel less fatigued straight afterward, with no effect on soreness or running performance over the following week.

claims.claim: Speeds recovery and next-day performance
claims.note: In the ultramarathon trial, soreness and running performance over the next 1–7 days were no different from simply lying down.

claims.claim: Flushes out lactic acid and toxins
claims.note: Lactate clears on its own within about an hour after exercise, and it isn't what causes next-day soreness.

claims.claim: Makes tired legs feel better
claims.note: A short-term drop in how fatigued people feel is the most consistent finding, which may be all you want from it.

claims.claim: Prevents blood clots
claims.note: In hospital, IPC lowers clot risk in people who can't walk, and graduated stockings reduce symptomless clots on long flights. Recovery boots aren't a clot-prevention device.

claims.claim: Reduces lymphedema
claims.note: IPC helps prevent and manage lymphedema as part of therapy supervised by a lymphedema specialist, usually at modest pressures.

claims.claim: Improves circulation for better health
claims.note: Blood flow rises while the device runs; no study shows lasting health benefits in healthy people.

look_for: Adjustable pressure that starts low, with a clear display of the setting in mmHg.
Sequential, overlapping chambers that inflate from the far end toward the body.
Boots or sleeves sized to your leg length and girth; too loose does little, too tight is uncomfortable.
For lymphedema or another medical need: a device prescribed and set up with a lymphedema therapist or clinician, not a sports model.
A session timer, cleanable liners, and noise and battery life you can live with.
If 'FDA cleared' is claimed, check the indication, which is often temporary relief of minor aches or a temporary increase in circulation.
skip: Lactic-acid 'flushing' and detox language.
'Used by pro teams': that's an endorsement, not evidence.
Maximum-pressure bragging. Higher pressure isn't shown to work better and can be uncomfortable or harmful.
'FDA registered', which means the company filed paperwork, not that anyone checked whether it works.
safety: Don't use it on a leg with a known or suspected deep-vein clot (pain, swelling or warmth in one calf); see a clinician urgently instead.
Avoid it with decompensated heart failure or fluid on the lungs, severe peripheral artery disease, or a skin infection, open wound or recent fracture in the limb.
Take care with diabetic neuropathy or reduced sensation, where you may not feel excess pressure.
Stop if you get numbness, tingling, pain, or skin marks that don't fade.
Lymphedema, leg ulcers and clot prevention are medical uses: follow your clinician's settings.
how_to_use: Start at the lowest pressure for about 20 minutes, and increase only if it's comfortable.
Treat it as a comfort tool after hard sessions. Sleep, food and sensible training load do the real recovery work.

studies.title: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Massage and Pneumatic Compression for Ultramarathon Recovery
studies.authors: Hoffman MD, Badowski N, Chin J, Stuempfle KJ
studies.journal: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
studies.finding_summary: Among 72 finishers of a 161-km race randomized to 20 minutes of massage, pneumatic compression or rest, compression lowered overall fatigue ratings immediately afterward, but there were no differences in soreness, fatigue or 400-m run times over the next 1–7 days.

studies.title: Effectiveness of intermittent pneumatic compression in reduction of risk of deep vein thrombosis in patients who have had a stroke (CLOTS 3): a multicentre randomised controlled trial
studies.authors: Dennis M, Sandercock P, Reid J, Graham C, Forbes J, Murray G
studies.finding_summary: In 2,876 immobile stroke patients in 94 UK hospitals, IPC reduced proximal deep-vein thrombosis within 30 days from 12.1% to 8.5%; skin breaks on the legs were more common with IPC (3% vs 1%).

studies.title: Compression stockings for preventing deep vein thrombosis in airline passengers
studies.authors: Clarke MJ, Broderick C, Hopewell S, Juszczak E, Eisinga A
studies.finding_summary: In 12 trials (2,918 passengers) on flights over five hours, graduated compression stockings reduced symptomless deep-vein thrombosis (3 vs 47 cases; OR 0.10, high-certainty evidence) and ankle swelling. No symptomatic clots, pulmonary emboli or deaths were reported in either group.

studies.title: Intermittent pneumatic compression devices for the prevention and treatment of breast cancer-related lymphedema-a systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Su L, Huang H, Tong Y, Dong L, Gu C, Zhuang S, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Across 14 randomized trials (1,397 patients), IPC reduced the incidence of lymphedema after breast-cancer surgery (RR 0.36); pressures of 40 mmHg or less and earlier treatment did better, and effects on established chronic lymphedema were limited.

name: Red light therapy
summary: LED panels, masks and caps that shine red and near-infrared light on skin. Modest evidence for hair loss and fine lines; weak for whole-body claims.
what:
Red-light therapy, properly called **photobiomodulation (PBM)**, shines low-power red (about **630–680 nm**) and near-infrared (about **800–880 nm**) light onto the body. It isn't meant to heat you like a sauna or set your body clock like a light box. The claim is that the light acts on the cells it reaches, mainly through a light-absorbing enzyme in mitochondria.

The category spans full-body panels, face masks, laser and LED hair caps, handheld wands, belts and blankets. Red light is absorbed mostly in the skin and near-infrared a little deeper, so the more targeted the claim (scalp, face, a mouth sore), the more plausible it is.

evidence.summary: It depends entirely on the use. Sham-controlled trials show modest gains in hair density for pattern hair loss, and controlled trials report smoother skin and fewer fine lines, though many studies are small or industry-linked. Clinician-delivered PBM is guideline-recommended to prevent mouth sores during some cancer treatments. For whole-body claims (testosterone, fat loss, thyroid, immunity, longevity) there is little or no good human evidence, and dose matters: too little light does nothing, and too much can cancel the effect.

claims.claim: Regrows hair in pattern hair loss
claims.note: In double-blind trials against sham devices, home laser devices added more hairs over 26 weeks, and several are FDA-cleared for this use. Gains are modest and take months.

claims.claim: Reduces fine lines and wrinkles
claims.note: Controlled trials report smoother skin and denser collagen on ultrasound, but effects are modest, studies are small and many are industry-funded.

claims.claim: Relieves pain and speeds sports recovery
claims.note: Some trials in neck pain, tendon problems and exercise recovery are positive and others aren't; protocols vary widely.

claims.claim: Prevents mouth sores during cancer treatment
claims.note: International supportive-care guidelines recommend specific clinician-delivered protocols for some treatments, such as stem-cell transplant. Not a home-panel use.

claims.claim: Boosts testosterone, burns fat or 'detoxes'
claims.note: No good human trials support whole-body claims like these.

claims.claim: More LEDs or watts means a stronger dose
claims.note: What counts is irradiance at your skin (mW/cm²) at the distance you use, and it falls quickly as you move away from the panel.

look_for: Wavelengths stated in nanometres that match the studies for your goal: red around 630–680 nm, near-infrared around 800–880 nm.
Irradiance (mW/cm²) at a stated, realistic distance such as 15 cm (6 in), not only at the panel surface.
How irradiance was measured. Spectroradiometer data is more trustworthy than cheap solar-meter readings, which can overstate LED output.
For hair loss: a device cleared for androgenetic alopecia, and a schedule you can keep for six months (the trials used about three sessions a week).
If 'FDA cleared' is claimed, the 510(k) number and its indication, which is often temporary relief of minor muscle and joint pain rather than skin or longevity.
A timer, flicker-free output, and eye protection rated for the device's wavelengths.
A device that matches the target: a mask or cap for face or scalp beats a big panel you stand far away from.
skip: LED count, total 'watts' and 'clinical grade' as stand-ins for dose.
Whole-body claims: hormones, fat loss, detox, thyroid, immunity and 'cellular energy'.
Acupressure spikes, PEMF or 'photon' add-ons bundled into the same device; each needs its own evidence.
Pulsed or 'frequency' modes sold as superior. Comparisons with continuous light are few and inconsistent.
safety: Protect your eyes. Near-infrared is invisible, so your blink reflex won't help. Don't look into the LEDs, and wear goggles rated for the device's wavelengths, especially for face treatments.

Check with a clinician first if you take light-sensitising medicines, have a light-sensitive condition (such as lupus or porphyria) or eye disease, or would be treating over a known or suspected skin cancer.
Pregnancy: safety hasn't been established, so ask your clinician first.
High-power panels warm the skin up close. If you have reduced sensation, keep your distance and use the timer.
If you have photosensitive epilepsy, avoid pulsing or flashing modes.
how_to_use: Pick one goal and match the device and dose to the studies for that goal.
Dose is irradiance × time: at 50 mW/cm², a 10-minute session delivers 30 J/cm². Longer isn't automatically better.
Keep the distance and session length the same each time, on clean skin.
Give it a fair trial (about six months for hair, three to four months for skin) and compare photos taken in the same light.

studies.title: Efficacy and safety of a low-level laser device in the treatment of male and female pattern hair loss: a multicenter, randomized, sham device-controlled, double-blind study
studies.authors: Jimenez JJ, Wikramanayake TC, Bergfeld W, Hordinsky M, Hickman JG, Hamblin MR, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Across four sham-controlled trials in 269 men and women with pattern hair loss, three home sessions a week for 26 weeks increased terminal hair counts by about 18–26 hairs/cm², versus about 2–9 with sham devices. No serious adverse events.

studies.title: A controlled trial to determine the efficacy of red and near-infrared light treatment in patient satisfaction, reduction of fine lines, wrinkles, skin roughness, and intradermal collagen density increase
studies.authors: Wunsch A, Matuschka K
studies.finding_summary: In 136 volunteers, twice-weekly red or broad-spectrum light for 30 sessions improved skin roughness, collagen density on ultrasound and blinded photo ratings compared with untreated controls; the broader spectrum was no better than red light alone.

studies.title: Systematic review of photobiomodulation for the management of oral mucositis in cancer patients and clinical practice guidelines
studies.authors: Zadik Y, Arany PR, Fregnani ER, Bossi P, Antunes HS, Bensadoun RJ, et al.
studies.finding_summary: The MASCC/ISOO mucositis group recommends specific photobiomodulation protocols to prevent oral mucositis in stem-cell transplant and head-and-neck radiotherapy patients, but found too little evidence to recommend it for treating established mucositis.

studies.title: Biphasic dose response in low level light therapy
studies.authors: Huang YY, Chen AC, Carroll JD, Hamblin MR
studies.finding_summary: Reviews cell, animal and clinical work showing that low doses of red and near-infrared light often work better than higher doses, and that inconsistent choices of wavelength, dose and timing explain many conflicting trial results.

name: Sauna
summary: A hot, dry room at 80–100°C. Frequent use is linked to fewer heart deaths in Finnish studies: the best long-term data on this shelf, but observational.
what:
A traditional sauna heats the air and stones to about **80–100°C (176–212°F)** at low humidity; throwing water on the stones briefly raises the steam. The category covers indoor cabins and outdoor barrels and cubes, with electric or wood-fired heaters.

A session works a bit like light exercise for your circulation: heart rate climbs to roughly 100–150 beats per minute, blood vessels widen, and blood pressure dips afterward. The long-term evidence comes from Finland, where sauna use is ordinary rather than a wellness trend.

evidence.summary: In 2,315 Finnish men followed for about 20 years, using a sauna 4–7 times a week was linked to about 40% lower all-cause mortality than once a week, and the same research group has linked frequent use to less stroke, hypertension and dementia. Small randomized trials of repeated heat show better artery function and blood pressure, which fits. But these are observational data, mostly from one research group in one region, using hot traditional saunas (~79°C, ~14-minute sessions); no trial shows sauna use itself extends life.

claims.claim: Linked to fewer heart deaths and a longer life
claims.note: The association is large and held after adjusting for fitness, smoking and income. It is observational, though: frequent users may differ in ways that weren't measured, so 'adds years to your life' goes beyond the data.

claims.claim: Lowers blood pressure
claims.note: Pressure dips for a while after each session, an 8-week heat trial lowered it modestly, and cohort data link frequent use to less hypertension. It isn't a treatment for high blood pressure.

claims.claim: Protects against dementia
claims.note: One Finnish cohort of men linked 4–7 sessions a week to lower dementia risk. Interesting, not confirmed.

claims.claim: Detoxes your body through sweat
claims.note: Sweat is mostly water and salt with trace amounts of anything else; your liver and kidneys do the clearing. No trial shows sauna 'detox' improves health.

claims.claim: Burns hundreds of calories and helps weight loss
claims.note: The weight you lose in a session is water, and it comes straight back when you drink.

claims.claim: Speeds muscle recovery
claims.note: Plenty of athletes like it, but there's little controlled evidence on soreness or performance.

look_for: A heater sized to the room's volume (the maker should state the range) so it actually reaches 80°C or more and recovers quickly after the door opens.
Enough stones to throw water on, if you want the traditional bursts of steam.
Electrical safety certification (a UL or ETL listing in North America, CE or UKCA in Europe). Larger electric heaters usually need a dedicated circuit fitted by an electrician.
Ventilation: a fresh-air inlet and an outlet, so the air doesn't go stale.
Benches high enough that your head sits in the hot air, made of wood that stays comfortable to touch, and a thermometer at head height so you know your dose.
For outdoor barrels and cubes: insulation and weatherproofing for the seasons you'll use it in.
A size and location you'll use often. In the Finnish data, frequency mattered more than anything else.
skip: 'Detox' and calorie-burn claims: neither holds up.
Salt walls, colour-light therapy and 'negative ions': atmosphere at most, with no health outcome shown.
Paying extra for built-in red-light or 'full-spectrum' add-ons in a traditional sauna. The heat is the part with evidence.
Very high maximum temperatures as a selling point. The studied sessions averaged about 79°C, and hotter isn't shown to be better.
safety: Alcohol is the biggest avoidable risk: about half of people who died in Finnish saunas between 1990 and 2002 had been drinking. Don't drink before or during.

Get your doctor's go-ahead first if you have unstable angina, a recent heart attack, severe aortic stenosis, decompensated heart failure, uncontrolled or very low blood pressure, or a history of fainting. Many people with stable heart disease can use a sauna, but that's a decision to make with your cardiologist.

Medicines that lower blood pressure or fluid (diuretics, beta-blockers, nitrates, alpha-blockers) raise fainting risk, and some drugs impair sweating. Heat can make medication patches, especially fentanyl, release a dangerous dose.
Pregnancy: avoid raising your core temperature to about 39°C (102°F) or higher, especially early on, and talk to your clinician before any use.
Trying to conceive: in a small study, twice-weekly saunas for three months lowered sperm counts, which took about six months to recover.
Supervise children and keep their sessions shorter and cooler. Skip it when you're feverish or acutely ill.
how_to_use: Start with 5–10 minutes on a lower bench and build toward 15–20 minutes over a few weeks.
Aim for frequency over length: the Finnish associations were strongest at 4–7 sessions a week.
Drink water before and after; a session can sweat out around half a litre.
Get out straight away if you feel dizzy, nauseous or confused, or get palpitations or a headache.
Stand up slowly at the end, because blood pressure dips right after a session. Cool down gradually, and skip icy plunges if you have heart disease.
If you use it in the evening, finish an hour or two before bed.

studies.title: Association between sauna bathing and fatal cardiovascular and all-cause mortality events
studies.authors: Laukkanen T, Khan H, Zaccardi F, Laukkanen JA
studies.finding_summary: In 2,315 middle-aged Finnish men followed for a median of about 20 years, sauna use 4–7 times a week was associated with lower sudden cardiac death, fatal heart disease and all-cause mortality than once a week, after adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors.

studies.title: Sauna bathing reduces the risk of stroke in Finnish men and women: A prospective cohort study
studies.authors: Kunutsor SK, Khan H, Zaccardi F, Laukkanen T, Willeit P, Laukkanen JA
studies.finding_summary: In 1,628 Finnish men and women aged 53–74 followed for a median of 14.9 years, 4–7 sauna sessions a week was associated with a 61% lower risk of stroke than one session (HR 0.39), after adjusting for risk factors, physical activity and socioeconomic status.

studies.title: Passive heat therapy improves endothelial function, arterial stiffness and blood pressure in sedentary humans
studies.authors: Brunt VE, Howard MJ, Francisco MA, Ely BR, Minson CT
studies.finding_summary: In 20 young sedentary adults, 8 weeks of repeated hot-water immersion (4–5 times a week, raising core temperature to at least 38.5°C) improved artery dilation, arterial stiffness and mean blood pressure (83 to 78 mmHg) compared with thermoneutral immersion.

studies.title: Death in sauna
studies.authors: Kenttämies A, Karkola K
studies.finding_summary: Reviewing deaths that occurred in saunas in Finland from 1990 to 2002, the annual rate was under 2 per 100,000 people; half of those who died were under the influence of alcohol.

name: Cleanser & soap
summary: Removes dirt, oil and sunscreen. Gentle beats strong for skin; for hands, plain soap and 20 seconds of scrubbing is what prevents infection.
what:
Cleansers use surfactants, detergent molecules that lift oil and dirt so water can rinse them away. Face cleansers, body washes, shower gels, bar soaps and hand soaps differ mainly in how strong the surfactants are and how much they strip. Traditional bar soap is alkaline (often pH 9 to 10), while synthetic-detergent ('syndet') bars and most liquid cleansers sit closer to skin's own slightly acidic pH, around 4.7.

A cleanser is on your skin for under a minute, so any 'active' in it (vitamin C, peptides, most extracts) is mostly rinsed away. Exceptions that do work in a wash-off format: salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide washes for acne, and anti-dandruff actives on the scalp.

evidence.summary: For hands, a meta-analysis of 30 community trials found hand-hygiene programs cut gastrointestinal illness by 31% and respiratory illness by 21%, and antibacterial soap added little over plain soap. For face and body, evidence is mostly about harm avoidance: alkaline and harsh cleansers raise skin pH and disturb the barrier. There is no good evidence that expensive or 'active' cleansers improve skin health.

claims.claim: Handwashing with soap prevents infections
claims.note: Community trials show fewer stomach and respiratory infections with better hand hygiene.

claims.claim: Antibacterial soap protects better than plain soap
claims.note: Triclosan soaps were no more effective than plain soap in community studies, and the US banned triclosan from consumer antiseptic washes in 2016.

claims.claim: pH-balanced cleansers are kinder to skin
claims.note: Skin in better barrier condition tends to have a surface pH below 5; alkaline soaps raise it for hours. Matters most for dry, sensitive or eczema-prone skin.

claims.claim: Sulfate-free is safer
claims.note: Sulfates can irritate dry or sensitive skin with long contact, but they are not a cancer or hormone concern. It's a comfort choice.

claims.claim: Cleanser actives (vitamin C, collagen, peptides) treat your skin
claims.note: Contact time is too short for most actives; salicylic acid and benzoyl peroxide washes are the main exceptions.

look_for: Gentle, fragrance-free face cleanser, or just water in the morning if your skin is dry.
Syndet bars or mild liquid washes rather than traditional soap if your skin is dry, sensitive or eczema-prone.
Salicylic acid (0.5 to 2%) or benzoyl peroxide washes if you have acne and want a wash-off active.
Plain soap for hands. The scrubbing and rinsing do the work, not the antibacterial label.
An oil or balm cleanser, or a second cleanse, only if you wear water-resistant sunscreen or heavy makeup.
skip: Antibacterial and 'sanitizing' soaps for everyday home use; plain soap works as well.
Cleansers sold on anti-aging or brightening actives that rinse off in seconds.
Cleansing brushes and daily scrubbing, which strip the barrier and irritate.
Heavily fragranced washes if your skin reacts; fragrance is a leading contact allergen.
safety: Tight, stinging or flaky skin after washing means the cleanser is too harsh or you are washing too often or too hot.
Benzoyl peroxide washes bleach towels and pillowcases.
Essential oils and fragrance in soaps are common allergens; a recurring rash where a product touches warrants a dermatologist's patch test.
Frequent handwashers (healthcare, food, cleaning work) should moisturize after washing to prevent hand dermatitis.
how_to_use: Use lukewarm water and pat dry rather than rub.
Wash hands for about 20 seconds, covering backs, between fingers and under nails, then rinse and dry.
Cleanse the face once or twice a day; in the evening it removes sunscreen and the day's grime.
Moisturize within a few minutes of washing if your skin tends to be dry.

studies.title: Effect of hand hygiene on infectious disease risk in the community setting: a meta-analysis
studies.authors: Aiello AE, Coulborn RM, Perez V, Larson EL
studies.finding_summary: Across 30 community trials, improved hand hygiene reduced gastrointestinal illness by 31% and respiratory illness by 21%. Education with non-antibacterial soap was the most beneficial intervention; antibacterial soap added little benefit.

studies.title: Consumer antibacterial soaps: effective or just risky?
studies.authors: Aiello AE, Larson EL, Levy SB
studies.finding_summary: Across 27 studies, soaps with triclosan at consumer concentrations (0.1 to 0.45%) were no more effective than plain soap at preventing infectious symptoms or reducing bacteria on hands, while lab studies raised concerns about antibiotic cross-resistance.

studies.title: Natural skin surface pH is on average below 5, which is beneficial for its resident flora
studies.authors: Lambers H, Piessens S, Bloem A, Pronk H, Finkel P
studies.finding_summary: In 330 people, skin surface pH averaged about 4.7 once soap and products were withheld. Skin with pH below 5 had better barrier function, moisture and less scaling; soaps and even tap water raised pH for hours. The study was run by a consumer-products company.

name: Conditioner & leave-in
summary: Coats the hair shaft to cut friction, tangles and breakage. A cosmetic job it does well; it cannot repair or grow hair.
what:
Hair is dead keratin. Once the protective outer cuticle is chipped by brushing, heat, bleach or sun, the shaft cannot heal itself. Conditioner works by leaving a thin film of positively charged ingredients (cationic surfactants such as behentrimonium, silicones such as dimethicone, and oils) on the negatively charged, damaged surface. That smooths the cuticle, reduces static, and cuts the friction of combing, which is where much breakage happens.

Rinse-out conditioners deposit a light layer; leave-ins deposit more and suit dry, curly, coily or bleached hair. Proteins, amino acids and plant oils in the formula mainly add feel and shine.

evidence.summary: Lab studies consistently show conditioners reduce combing force and friction, and dermatology reviews describe them as the main way to limit mechanical breakage. There are few trials on outcomes people notice over months, and none showing conditioner affects hair growth or scalp health. Claims to 'repair' hair describe a temporary coating that washes out.

claims.claim: Reduces tangles, frizz and breakage
claims.note: Coating the shaft lowers combing friction and static; this is the core, well-understood effect.

claims.claim: Repairs split ends
claims.note: Some polymers temporarily glue split ends together; they return after washing. Trimming is the only fix.

claims.claim: Silicones suffocate or damage hair
claims.note: Hair doesn't breathe. Heavy silicones can build up and weigh fine hair down, which a clarifying wash removes.

claims.claim: Makes hair grow faster or thicker
claims.note: Conditioner acts on the shaft, not the follicle.

look_for: Weight to match your hair: light rinse-out for fine or oily hair, richer conditioner or leave-in for thick, curly, coily, bleached or heat-styled hair.
Silicones (dimethicone, amodimethicone) or cationic conditioners if breakage and frizz are the problem.
A leave-in or detangler if you comb or brush wet hair, when it's most fragile.
Fragrance-free if you get rashes along the hairline, ears or neck.
skip: 'Bond repair' or 'rebuilding' claims on ordinary conditioners.
Biotin, collagen and caffeine conditioners marketed for growth.
Paying extra for exotic oils; common silicones and cationic surfactants do the conditioning work.
safety: Rinse-off and leave-in products can cause contact allergy on the scalp edges, face and neck; stop a new product if a rash appears there.
Heavy leave-ins and oils on the hairline and forehead can worsen acne there; keep them to the lengths.
Conditioner cannot fix hair loss; see a dermatologist for thinning, shedding or patches.
how_to_use: Apply mainly to the mid-lengths and ends after shampooing; leave for a minute or two, then rinse.
Detangle with a wide-tooth comb while conditioner is in, starting at the ends.

studies.title: Hair cosmetics: an overview
studies.authors: Gavazzoni Dias MF
studies.finding_summary: A dermatology review of how shampoos, conditioners, straighteners and dyes are formulated and act on the hair shaft, and their possible side effects, to help clinicians advise on hair and scalp care.

name: Deodorant & antiperspirant
summary: Deodorant masks odor; antiperspirant reduces sweat. The cancer and Alzheimer's scares haven't held up; irritation and fragrance allergy are the real issues.
what:
Fresh sweat is nearly odorless. Underarm smell comes from skin bacteria breaking down compounds in sweat from apocrine glands. A **deodorant** is a cosmetic that curbs those bacteria or masks the smell, using alcohol, antimicrobials, fragrance, acids, magnesium or baking soda. An **antiperspirant** is an over-the-counter drug in the US: aluminum salts form temporary plugs in sweat ducts and must reduce sweat by at least 20% in standardized tests (30% for 'extra effective'). Many products are both.

Genes matter too: a common variant of the ABCC11 gene, frequent in East Asian populations, almost eliminates the typical underarm odor.

evidence.summary: Antiperspirants reduce sweat by a tested, regulated amount. A population case-control study of 813 women with breast cancer and 793 controls found no link with antiperspirant or deodorant use, and the US National Cancer Institute reports no established link. One smaller case-control study reported higher risk with very frequent use from a young age, based on recalled use. Evidence that 'natural' deodorants perform as well, or that switching requires a 'detox', is lacking.

claims.claim: Antiperspirants cause breast cancer
claims.note: A larger case-control study found no association; a smaller one found an association only with very frequent early use, relying on recall. No causal link is established.

claims.claim: Aluminum in antiperspirant causes Alzheimer's
claims.note: The suspected link hasn't held up in later research.

claims.claim: Your armpits need to 'detox' when switching to natural deodorant
claims.note: There is no detox process; you simply sweat normally again without aluminum plugs.

claims.claim: Antiperspirant works best at night
claims.note: Applying to dry skin at bedtime lets plugs form while sweat glands are quiet; it still works after a morning shower.

claims.claim: Natural deodorants are gentler
claims.note: Baking soda is alkaline and a common underarm irritant, and essential oils are fragrance allergens.

look_for: Antiperspirant (aluminum chlorohydrate or similar, listed under Drug Facts in the US) if wetness is your concern; deodorant alone if only odor bothers you.
Fragrance-free if you have sensitive skin or recurring underarm rashes.
Baking-soda-free formulas if you've had redness or darkening with 'natural' deodorants.
Clinical-strength antiperspirants for heavier sweating before moving to prescription options.
skip: 'Detox' underarm masks and cleanses.
Paying extra for 'aluminum-free' as a safety upgrade; it's a preference, not a proven safety gain.
Crystal or 'mineral salt' deodorants sold as aluminum-free; alum is itself an aluminum salt.
safety: People with kidney disease should ask a doctor before using antiperspirants, as US labels say, because weak kidneys clear aluminum poorly.
Don't apply to broken or freshly shaved, irritated skin; wait or switch to a gentler product.
A rash that keeps coming back where you apply a product may be fragrance or preservative allergy; a dermatologist's patch test can pinpoint it.
See a clinician if sweating soaks through clothes or disrupts daily life (it's treatable), or for new night sweats, especially with fever or weight loss.
how_to_use: Apply antiperspirant to clean, completely dry skin at bedtime; reapply deodorant in the morning if you like.
Give a new antiperspirant a few nights to reach full effect.

studies.title: Antiperspirant use and the risk of breast cancer
studies.authors: Mirick DK, Davis S, Thomas DB
studies.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
studies.finding_summary: 813 women with breast cancer and 793 controls: breast cancer risk did not increase with antiperspirant (OR 0.9) or deodorant use, with blade shaving, or with applying products within an hour of shaving.

studies.title: Use of Underarm Cosmetic Products in Relation to Risk of Breast Cancer: A Case-Control Study
studies.authors: Linhart C, Talasz H, Morandi EM, Exley C, Lindner HH, Taucher S, Egle D, Hubalek M, Concin N, Ulmer H
studies.finding_summary: 209 women with breast cancer and 209 controls: self-reported use of underarm products several times daily starting before age 30 was associated with higher risk (OR 3.88, wide CI), and breast-tissue aluminum was higher in cases. Small study relying on recalled use.

studies.title: A functional ABCC11 allele is essential in the biochemical formation of human axillary odor
studies.authors: Martin A, Saathoff M, Kuhn F, Max H, Terstegen L, Natsch A
studies.finding_summary: Underarm odor forms when bacteria act on precursors secreted by apocrine glands. A common ABCC11 variant, frequent in East Asian populations, nearly abolishes secretion of the main odor precursors. The work was done by a personal-care company.

name: Exfoliant & scrub
summary: Loosens dead surface cells for smoother, brighter skin. Chemical exfoliants have modest trial evidence; overdoing any exfoliant damages the barrier.
what:
Exfoliants remove or loosen the outermost layer of dead skin cells. **Chemical** exfoliants dissolve the bonds between cells: alpha-hydroxy acids (AHAs) such as glycolic, lactic and mandelic acid work on the surface; salicylic acid (a BHA) is oil-soluble and gets into pores, which is why it suits acne and blackheads; polyhydroxy acids such as gluconolactone are gentler. **Physical** exfoliants are scrubs, grains and brushes.

On the body, urea, lactic acid and salicylic acid lotions are often gentler and more effective than gritty scrubs for rough, bumpy skin (keratosis pilaris) and thick heels. The actives pages cover glycolic acid and salicylic acid in detail.

evidence.summary: A 22-week double-blind trial found 8% glycolic and 8% lactic acid creams modestly improved sun-damaged skin compared with a plain cream. Salicylic acid is an approved non-prescription acne active with a conditional recommendation in the 2024 US acne guideline. A randomized study showed 10% glycolic acid increases UV sensitivity, reversing within a week of stopping. Evidence for scrubs is thin, and none of the trials are long.

claims.claim: Smoother, brighter skin
claims.note: AHAs have vehicle-controlled evidence for modest improvement in roughness, sallowness and mottled pigment.

claims.claim: Clears blackheads and acne
claims.note: Salicylic acid 0.5 to 2% helps mild comedonal acne; benzoyl peroxide and retinoids are stronger options.

claims.claim: Reverses aging like a retinoid
claims.note: Effects are smaller and more superficial than retinoids'; exfoliants mainly improve texture and tone.

claims.claim: Daily scrubbing keeps skin clear
claims.note: Frequent scrubbing and stacked acids break down the barrier and cause dryness, redness and irritation.

claims.claim: Exfoliated skin needs no extra sun care
claims.note: Glycolic acid measurably increases sunburn damage; the effect lasts about a week after stopping.

look_for: A chemical exfoliant with a stated percentage: glycolic or lactic acid up to about 10% for home use, salicylic acid 0.5 to 2%.
Lactic acid, mandelic acid or gluconolactone if your skin is sensitive; they are gentler than glycolic acid.
Salicylic acid if you have oily skin, blackheads or acne.
For rough, bumpy arms or thick heels, a lotion with urea, lactic acid or salicylic acid rather than a harsh scrub.
If you prefer a scrub, fine, rounded particles rather than crushed shells or pits.
skip: High-strength 'peeling solutions' (25 to 30% acid) used at home without experience; save strong peels for a clinician.
Daily scrubs, stiff brushes and exfoliating mitts on the face.
Walnut-shell and other jagged scrubs, which can cause micro-tears.
Combining several acids with a retinoid in one routine.
safety: Wear broad-spectrum sunscreen daily while using acids and for a week after stopping.
Don't exfoliate broken, sunburned or eczema-affected skin; for eczema-prone skin, often the right amount is none.
Stop and let skin recover if you get stinging, persistent redness or a shiny, tight surface.
Salicylic acid over large body areas is not advised in pregnancy or for young children without clinical advice, and people with aspirin allergy should ask a clinician first.
how_to_use: Start 2 to 3 times a week, in the evening, on nights you don't use a retinoid.
A couple of times a week is a sensible ceiling for most people.
Follow with moisturizer, and with sunscreen the next morning.

studies.title: Topical 8% glycolic acid and 8% L-lactic acid creams for the treatment of photodamaged skin. A double-blind vehicle-controlled clinical trial
studies.authors: Stiller MJ, Bartolone J, Stern R, Smith S, Kollias N, Gillies R, Drake LA
studies.finding_summary: 74 women with moderately photodamaged skin used 8% glycolic acid, 8% lactic acid or plain cream twice daily for 22 weeks. At least one grade of facial improvement occurred in 76% and 71% of the acid groups versus 40% on vehicle; the authors called the effect modest.

studies.title: Topical glycolic acid enhances photodamage by ultraviolet light
studies.authors: Kaidbey K, Sutherland B, Bennett P, Wamer WG, Barton C, Dennis D, Kornhauser A
studies.finding_summary: In 29 adults, four weeks of 10% glycolic acid increased UV-induced sunburn cells and lowered the dose needed to redden skin. The sensitivity was gone a week after stopping.

name: Eye cream
summary: A moisturizer in a smaller, pricier jar. Useful if your regular products sting around the eyes; it cannot fix dark circles or bags.
what:
Eye creams are moisturizers formulated for the thin skin around the eyes, usually with fewer fragrances and irritants. Many add caffeine, peptides, vitamin C or a retinoid. The skin there is thin and easily irritated, which is the real case for a separate product: a gentler formula for people whose face cream or retinoid stings near the eyes.

Dark circles come mostly from genetics, pigment, thin skin showing blood vessels, and hollows that cast shadows. Puffy bags come from fluid, fat pads and aging support tissue. Creams do little for the structural causes. Sunscreen and a retinoid, applied carefully, do more for crow's-feet than most eye creams.

evidence.summary: Independent trials of eye creams are scarce. Retinoids have evidence for fine lines on sun-damaged skin generally, which is why retinoid eye products are the most credible. Caffeine can briefly tighten and de-puff, but lasting reductions in dark circles or bags are not shown. Most claims rest on small company-run studies with self-rated results.

claims.claim: Reduces fine lines around the eyes
claims.note: Retinoid formulas have indirect support from facial trials; plain eye moisturizers only smooth lines temporarily through hydration.

claims.claim: Erases dark circles
claims.note: Most dark circles are genetic, pigment- or shadow-related; creams make little lasting difference. Concealer and sleep are more reliable.

claims.claim: De-puffs bags
claims.note: Caffeine and cold can briefly reduce morning puffiness; structural bags need a clinician's options.

claims.claim: You need a separate eye product
claims.note: A fragrance-free face moisturizer works fine for most people unless it stings.

look_for: Fragrance-free and essential-oil-free; eyelid skin is one of the most allergy-prone sites.
A gentle retinoid (low retinol or retinal) if your aim is crow's-feet and you tolerate it.
Mineral sunscreen or sunglasses in the day, which protect this area better than any cream.
Small, airless or tube packaging for retinoid or vitamin C formulas.
skip: Paying several times more per gram than your face moisturizer for similar ingredients.
Metal 'cooling' applicators and roller balls as a feature; a cold spoon does the same.
Promises to remove dark circles or bags.
safety: Swelling, itching or scaling of the eyelids is often allergic contact dermatitis; stop new products and see a dermatologist if it persists.
Keep retinoids and acids off the lid margin and out of the eyes.
Avoid retinoid eye creams if pregnant or breastfeeding unless a clinician approves.
New puffiness on waking that affects both eyes and your ankles, or one-sided swelling with pain, warrants a medical check.
how_to_use: Tap a rice-grain amount along the orbital bone, not on the lids.
Introduce retinoid eye products 2 to 3 nights a week at first.

name: Face mask
summary: A treat, not a treatment. Sheet and sleeping masks hydrate for a while; clay masks absorb oil. No mask has lasting health effects.
what:
Face masks come in a few types. **Sheet masks** are fabric soaked in a watery serum that sits on the face for 10 to 20 minutes. **Sleeping masks** are thick overnight creams, essentially rich moisturizers. **Clay masks** (kaolin, bentonite) absorb surface oil, sometimes with salicylic acid or sulfur for breakouts. **Peel-off** masks lift a film and some dead cells with it.

The short contact time and one-off use mean a mask behaves like a single dose of whatever it contains. Hydration makes skin look plumper for hours. If an ingredient in a mask is worth using, it is usually more useful in a product you apply every day.

evidence.summary: There are no good independent trials showing masks produce lasting improvements in skin health. Temporary hydration is real and easy to measure. Clay masks with salicylic acid or sulfur contain recognised acne actives, but their evidence comes from daily-use products, not occasional masks. Most mask claims come from small company-run panels.

claims.claim: Instant glow and plumpness
claims.note: Hydration makes skin look smoother for a few hours; the effect does not last.

claims.claim: Detoxes or draws out impurities
claims.note: Skin does not store toxins for a mask to pull out. Clay absorbs surface oil, which is all 'drawing out' means.

claims.claim: Clay masks help oily or acne-prone skin
claims.note: They reduce shine briefly; sulfur and salicylic acid versions add real acne actives, but daily treatments work better.

claims.claim: Peel-off masks remove blackheads
claims.note: They pull off surface debris and fine hairs; blackheads return quickly and the peel can irritate.

look_for: A mask you'd enjoy using; that is the main benefit.
Fragrance-free and essential-oil-free options if your skin reacts easily.
Kaolin or bentonite with salicylic acid or sulfur if you want a mask for oily or breakout-prone skin.
For a sleeping mask, the same things you'd look for in a moisturizer: humectants plus occlusives.
skip: 'Detox', charcoal-cleansing and 'pore vacuum' claims.
Paying a premium for single-use sheet masks as an anti-aging step.
Peel-off masks on sensitive skin or near the eyebrows and hairline.
safety: Sheet masks soaked in fragranced serum can trigger contact allergy; stop if you get itching or redness.
Don't use acid or clay masks on the same night as a retinoid or other exfoliants.
Sulfur masks can irritate and have a noticeable smell.
how_to_use: Use on clean skin, follow the time on the pack, and moisturize afterwards.
Once or twice a week is plenty for clay or acid masks.

name: Floss & interdental cleaning
summary: Cleans where a toothbrush can't reach. The trials are short and low-certainty, but the habit is cheap, low-risk and targets where gum disease starts.
what:
Plaque between teeth inflames the gums (gingivitis), and in susceptible people years of that inflammation become periodontitis, which destroys the bone holding teeth in place. A toothbrush can't reach the gaps, so something else has to: **floss** or floss picks for tight contacts, **interdental brushes** for wider gaps (many adults have them), and **water flossers** for braces, implants or limited dexterity.

The choice of floss matters less than using it daily. Waxed, tape or coated floss slides more easily; flavors and coatings are comfort features.

evidence.summary: A 2019 Cochrane review of 35 trials found low-certainty evidence that adding floss to brushing reduces gingivitis, and that interdental brushes may work better than floss; water-flosser evidence was limited and no trial measured decay between teeth. That reflects short, small trials in people with mild inflammation, not proof that interdental cleaning fails. The classic 1965 experiment showed plaque causes gingivitis within weeks of stopping cleaning, and treating periodontitis lowers blood sugar in people with diabetes.

claims.claim: Flossing reduces gum inflammation
claims.note: Low-certainty but consistent evidence of less gingivitis when floss is added to brushing.

claims.claim: Interdental brushes beat floss
claims.note: They may reduce gingivitis more where they fit; floss is still the tool for tight contacts.

claims.claim: Flossing prevents cavities between teeth
claims.note: Plausible, but no trial in the review measured decay between teeth.

claims.claim: Water flossers replace floss
claims.note: Short-term gingivitis benefits in some trials but inconsistent evidence; best for braces, implants or people who won't floss.

claims.claim: Healthy gums protect your heart
claims.note: Gum disease and heart disease are associated, but treating gums hasn't been shown to prevent heart attacks or strokes. The diabetes link is firmer.

look_for: Interdental brushes sized to your gaps (a dentist or hygienist can size them) if you have space between teeth.
Waxed or tape floss if contacts are tight or floss shreds.
Floss picks or a water flosser if dexterity, braces, bridges or implants make string floss hard.
Whatever tool you'll actually use every day.
skip: Paying extra for charcoal, infused or 'whitening' floss.
Skipping interdental cleaning because the evidence is 'weak'; the uncertainty is about size of effect, and harms are minimal.
safety: Some bleeding in the first week or two is common when you start; if it continues after two weeks of daily cleaning, see a dentist.
Don't snap floss into the gums; guide it gently and curve it around each tooth.
Choose PTFE floss or interdental brushes if you have many fillings that catch or shred floss.
Bleeding gums with easy bruising, nosebleeds or unusual tiredness should be checked by a doctor.
how_to_use: Clean between teeth once a day, before or after brushing.
Curve the floss into a C around each tooth and slide it just under the gumline.
Use interdental brushes with a gentle in-and-out motion without forcing them.

studies.title: Home use of interdental cleaning devices, in addition to toothbrushing, for preventing and controlling periodontal diseases and dental caries
studies.authors: Worthington HV, MacDonald L, Poklepovic Pericic T, Sambunjak D, Johnson TM, Imai P, Clarkson JE
studies.finding_summary: 35 trials (3,929 adults): floss or interdental brushes added to brushing may reduce gingivitis or plaque (low certainty), and interdental brushes may beat floss. Evidence on sticks and water flossers was limited and inconsistent, and no trial assessed decay between teeth.

studies.title: Experimental gingivitis in man
studies.authors: Löe H, Theilade E, Jensen SB
studies.finding_summary: A classic experiment in which volunteers with healthy gums stopped all oral hygiene. All developed gingivitis within about 9 to 21 days as plaque accumulated, and gums returned to health once cleaning resumed. (PubMed lists no abstract; summary from the published paper.)

studies.title: Treatment of periodontitis for glycaemic control in people with diabetes mellitus
studies.authors: Simpson TC, Clarkson JE, Worthington HV, MacDonald L, Weldon JC, Needleman I, Iheozor-Ejiofor Z, Wild SH, Qureshi A, Walker A, Patel VA, Boyers D, Twigg J
studies.finding_summary: 35 trials (3,249 people with diabetes and periodontitis): professional gum treatment lowered HbA1c by 0.43 percentage points at 3 to 4 months versus no treatment or usual care (moderate-certainty evidence).

name: Fragrance & body mist
summary: Pure pleasure, no health benefit. The one real health issue is contact allergy, which affects a few percent of people and is usually lifelong.
what:
Perfumes are fragrance oils dissolved in alcohol. The names describe concentration and longevity, not quality: **eau de parfum** is roughly 15 to 20% fragrance oil, **eau de toilette** about 5 to 15%, **cologne** and **body mists** less. A single 'parfum' on a label can stand for dozens of undisclosed components, natural or synthetic.

Fragrance is one of the most common causes of allergic skin reactions to cosmetics. Allergy develops after repeated exposure, often after years of trouble-free use, and once you're sensitized it usually lasts for life. 'Natural' essential oils contain the same allergens, and some components (linalool, limonene) become more allergenic as they oxidize in air.

evidence.summary: Fragrance has no health benefit to evaluate; the evidence is about harm. A five-country European study patch-testing 3,119 adults found about 2 to 3% reacted to fragrance mixes, with women affected about twice as often as men. A meta-analysis of general-population studies ranked fragrance mix I as the second most common contact allergen after nickel. Claims about hormone effects of fragrance ingredients such as some phthalates rest on limited human evidence.

claims.claim: Natural perfumes and essential oils are safer
claims.note: They contain the same allergens and can cause the same reactions.

claims.claim: Fragrance allergy is common
claims.note: A few percent of adults are patch-test positive to fragrance; it's among the top allergens, especially in leave-on products.

claims.claim: Pheromone perfumes attract partners
claims.note: No reliable human pheromone has been shown to work this way.

claims.claim: Perfume disrupts hormones
claims.note: Some fragrance-related chemicals show hormone activity in lab and animal studies; effects at real-world exposure in people aren't established.

look_for: Test on a blotter or the inside of your wrist and wait a few hours; the scent changes as it dries.
Eau de toilette or body mist for lighter wear; eau de parfum for longer-lasting scent with fewer sprays.
In the EU, the named allergens on the label (such as linalool, limonene, citronellol, geraniol) if you've reacted before.
Storage away from heat and light, which slows the oxidation that makes some components more allergenic.
skip: Pheromone and 'aphrodisiac' fragrances.
Spraying directly on skin you have reacted on; spray on clothes instead (test fabric first).
Assuming 'unscented' products are fragrance-free; look for 'fragrance-free'.
safety: Citrus oils such as bergamot plus sun can cause streaky brown marks (berloque dermatitis); don't spray on sun-exposed skin before going out.
A recurring itchy rash on the neck, wrists or behind the ears where you apply perfume may be fragrance allergy; a dermatologist's patch test can confirm it.
Perfume is flammable and toxic if swallowed; keep it away from flames and young children.
Strong scents can trigger symptoms in some people with asthma or migraine; go light in shared spaces.
how_to_use: One to three sprays is enough; apply to clothes or hair if your skin reacts.
Choose fragrance-free lotions and skincare if you want to keep total fragrance exposure down but still wear perfume.

studies.title: Prevalence of fragrance contact allergy in the general population of five European countries: a cross-sectional study
studies.authors: Diepgen TL, Ofenloch R, Bruze M, Cazzaniga S, Coenraads PJ, Elsner P, Goncalo M, Svensson Å, Naldi L
studies.finding_summary: 3,119 randomly sampled adults in five European countries were patch tested. 2.6% reacted to fragrance mix I and 1.9% to fragrance mix II; clinically relevant fragrance allergy was estimated at 0.8 to 1.9%, about twice as common in women as in men.

studies.title: Prevalence of contact allergy in the general population: A systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Alinaghi F, Bennike NH, Egeberg A, Thyssen JP, Johansen JD
studies.finding_summary: 28 studies with 20,107 people from the general population: about 20% had at least one contact allergy. Nickel was most common (11.4%), followed by fragrance mix I (3.5%).

name: Hair treatment & mask
summary: Masks, bond repair and scalp serums condition damaged hair. For thinning, only minoxidil (and prescription options) has strong trial evidence.
what:
This shelf mixes two different kinds of product. **Hair-shaft treatments** (masks, bond-repair treatments, leave-in serums and oils) aim at bleached, heat-damaged or dry hair. They are intensive conditioners: they coat and smooth, and bond-building products aim to re-link some broken bonds inside the shaft. They change how hair looks, feels and breaks, not how it grows.

**Scalp and regrowth treatments** aim at thinning. Here the evidence is narrow: **topical minoxidil** is the non-prescription first-line option for pattern hair loss in men and women, and oral finasteride is a prescription option for men. Most 'growth serums' use caffeine, biotin, peptides or plant extracts without controlled evidence; rosemary oil has one small trial. Name the type of hair loss first; the hair lesson covers how.

evidence.summary: For regrowth, the evidence is strong but narrow: 5% topical minoxidil beat 2% and placebo in a 48-week trial of 393 men, and finasteride increased hair counts over two years in 1,553 men. The rosemary-oil claim rests on one small trial against 2% minoxidil with no placebo. For masks and bond repair, independent trials are largely absent; benefits are cosmetic and measured in the lab. A large cohort linked frequent chemical straightener use with higher uterine cancer rates, an observational finding.

claims.claim: Minoxidil regrows hair in pattern hair loss
claims.note: Randomized, placebo-controlled trials in men and women; 5% outperformed 2%. Gains fade within months of stopping.

claims.claim: Growth serums with caffeine, biotin or peptides regrow hair
claims.note: Lab and small company studies only. Biotin helps only if you are deficient, which is rare.

claims.claim: Rosemary oil works as well as minoxidil
claims.note: One 100-person trial found similar hair counts to 2% minoxidil at six months, with no placebo group and against the weaker strength.

claims.claim: Masks and bond builders repair damaged hair
claims.note: They improve feel, shine and breakage in lab tests; damaged hair still can't regenerate, and independent trials are scarce.

claims.claim: Keratin smoothing treatments are harmless
claims.note: Some release formaldehyde when heated with a flat iron, a known carcinogen when inhaled at high exposures, and FDA has warned about them.

look_for: For thinning: topical minoxidil, 5% foam or solution for men; for women, the 2% solution or 5% foam sold for women, used as labeled.
For bleached or heat-damaged hair: a rich mask or bond-building treatment used weekly, plus less heat and gentler handling.
Ingredient lists without formaldehyde, formalin, methylene glycol or glyoxylic-acid 'smoothing' chemistry if you want to avoid formaldehyde-releasing treatments.
Realistic timing: minoxidil needs about 4 months for first results and 6 to 12 months for a fair verdict.
skip: Hair gummies, biotin and collagen for growth unless a test shows you are deficient.
Growth serums and 'follicle activators' priced like medicine without trials.
Scalp 'detox' treatments.
Stacking several masks and oils; one conditioning treatment a week is enough.
safety: Don't use minoxidil while pregnant or breastfeeding. Expect a temporary increase in shedding in the first weeks; it can cause scalp itch and unwanted facial hair, and is toxic to cats if they lick treated skin or bedding.
Finasteride and oral minoxidil are prescription drugs; use them only under a clinician's care, including through telehealth services.
Formaldehyde-releasing smoothing treatments can cause eye, nose and throat irritation; avoid them, especially in pregnancy, and ask salons what they use.
Frequent use of chemical straighteners and relaxers has been linked with uterine cancer in a large cohort; it is observational, but a reason to use them less.
See a dermatologist for sudden, patchy or rapid hair loss, or a painful, red or scaly scalp; blood tests for iron and thyroid may be worth doing.
how_to_use: Minoxidil: apply to a dry scalp twice daily (solution) or as labeled (foam), and keep going; the benefit lasts only as long as you use it.
Masks: apply to clean, damp mid-lengths and ends for the labeled time, then rinse.

studies.title: A randomized clinical trial of 5% topical minoxidil versus 2% topical minoxidil and placebo in the treatment of androgenetic alopecia in men
studies.authors: Olsen EA, Dunlap FE, Funicella T, Koperski JA, Swinehart JM, Tschen EH, Trancik RJ
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: 393 men with pattern hair loss used 5% minoxidil, 2% minoxidil or placebo twice daily for 48 weeks. 5% was superior to both, with 45% more regrowth than 2% and an earlier response, but more itching and irritation.

studies.title: Finasteride in the treatment of men with androgenetic alopecia. Finasteride Male Pattern Hair Loss Study Group
studies.authors: Kaufman KD, Olsen EA, Whiting D, Savin R, DeVillez R, Bergfeld W, Price VH, Van Neste D, Roberts JL, Hordinsky M, Shapiro J, Binkowitz B, Gormley GJ
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: In two one-year trials of 1,553 men, finasteride 1 mg daily increased hair counts versus placebo (107 hairs at 1 year and 138 at 2 years in a 1-inch circle), while placebo users kept losing hair. The trials were run by the manufacturer.

studies.title: Rosemary oil vs minoxidil 2% for the treatment of androgenetic alopecia: a randomized comparative trial
studies.authors: Panahi Y, Taghizadeh M, Marzony ET, Sahebkar A
studies.finding_summary: 100 people with pattern hair loss used rosemary oil or 2% minoxidil for six months. Both groups had more hairs at six months with no difference between them; scalp itching was more frequent with minoxidil.

studies.title: Use of Straighteners and Other Hair Products and Incident Uterine Cancer
studies.authors: Chang CJ, O'Brien KM, Keil AP, Gaston SA, Jackson CL, Sandler DP, White AJ
studies.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
studies.finding_summary: Among 33,947 women followed for about 11 years, using hair straighteners in the prior year was associated with higher uterine cancer rates (HR 1.80), and frequent use more so (HR 2.55). Dyes and perms were not associated.

name: Hand cream
summary: A thicker moisturizer for hands that take a beating from washing. Helps prevent chapped, cracked skin and hand eczema, especially if you wash often.
what:
Hands are washed far more than the rest of the body, and every wash strips some barrier lipids. Hand creams are moisturizers tuned for that: usually richer, with occlusives (petrolatum, dimethicone, shea butter) and humectants (glycerin, urea) that survive a few hand movements without feeling greasy.

For people who wash or glove up all day, such as healthcare, food and cleaning workers, parents of young children, and hairdressers, a hand cream is a real preventive step against irritant hand eczema, not just a comfort item.

evidence.summary: A Cochrane review of workplace trials found moisturizers may lower the risk of irritant hand dermatitis (13% vs 19% developing it) but the evidence was low quality and imprecise. A year-long trial in 501 healthcare workers found better access to cream helped mild hand eczema but not the primary outcomes, and was industry-funded. Claims for anti-aging hand creams are not supported beyond sunscreen's role.

claims.claim: Prevents dry, cracked hands
claims.note: Moisturizers restore barrier comfort; the preventive effect on hand eczema has low-quality evidence but consistent direction.

claims.claim: Barrier creams protect like gloves
claims.note: Barrier creams alone showed little benefit in trials; gloves for wet work and moisturizer after are the combination.

claims.claim: Anti-aging hand creams reverse age spots
claims.note: Sunscreen on the backs of hands prevents spots; fading them needs actives like retinoids or a clinician.

look_for: An occlusive-rich formula (petrolatum, dimethicone, shea butter) for very dry or cracked hands; lighter creams for daytime.
Fragrance-free, since fragrance is a top cause of hand allergic dermatitis.
Urea or glycerin for rough, thickened skin on fingertips and knuckles.
A tube or pump to keep at the sink, in a bag and at work, so you actually use it.
SPF on the backs of the hands if you drive or are outdoors a lot.
skip: Luxury fragrance-led hand creams if your hands are cracked or itchy.
Barrier creams sold as a substitute for gloves.
'Anti-aging' premiums; the ingredients are the same as ordinary creams.
safety: Stinging on cracked skin is common with urea and some preservatives; use a plain ointment on fissures.
Wear gloves for wet work and cleaning products; cotton liners under rubber gloves reduce sweating.
See a dermatologist if hand eczema lasts more than a few weeks, cracks and bleeds, or keeps returning; patch testing can find an allergen.
how_to_use: Apply after every wash and before bed; thicker ointment under cotton gloves overnight for cracked hands.
Rub into cuticles and knuckles, where cracks start.

studies.title: Interventions for preventing occupational irritant hand dermatitis
studies.authors: Bauer A, Rönsch H, Elsner P, Dittmar D, Bennett C, Schuttelaar MLA, Lukács J, John SM, Williams HC
studies.finding_summary: Nine workplace trials (2,888 workers). Moisturizers may have a clinically important protective effect (13% vs 19% developing irritant hand dermatitis), barrier creams alone had little effect, and all estimates were low quality and imprecise.

studies.title: Effectiveness of a skin care programme for the prevention of contact dermatitis in healthcare workers (the Healthy Hands Project): A single-centre, cluster randomized controlled trial
studies.authors: Soltanipoor M, Kezic S, Sluiter JK, de Wit F, Bosma AL, van Asperen R, Rustemeyer T
studies.finding_summary: 501 healthcare workers on 19 wards; the intervention supplied cream dispensers with monitored use and feedback for a year. Primary outcomes did not differ significantly, but relative improvement in hand eczema was greater (56% vs 44%), especially in mild cases. The project was funded by a skin-care company.

name: Intimate care & lubricant
summary: Personal lubricants reduce friction and discomfort. What matters is the base, condom compatibility and osmolality; 'feminine hygiene' washes and douches aren't needed.
what:
Intimate-care products include **personal lubricants** and **washes, wipes and sprays** for the genital area. Lubricants come in three bases: **water-based** (easy to clean, condom-safe, can dry out and get sticky), **silicone-based** (long-lasting, condom-safe, harder to wash off) and **oil-based** (long-lasting, but they weaken latex condoms).

For the vagina, formulation matters because the lining is thin and relies on protective lactobacilli. Very **hyperosmolar** lubricants (high in glycerin or propylene glycol) draw water out of cells and have damaged tissue in lab tests; the WHO suggests keeping osmolality below about 1,200 mOsm/kg. The vagina cleans itself, so scented washes, wipes and douches aren't needed and can upset its balance.

evidence.summary: Lab studies show hyperosmolar water-based lubricants damage vaginal and rectal tissue explants and some are toxic to lactobacilli, while near-iso-osmolar and silicone lubricants were the gentlest; human outcome data are limited. Mineral oil weakens latex condoms within 60 seconds in burst tests. Spermicide nonoxynol-9 did not prevent HIV or other STIs in trials and increased genital lesions.

claims.claim: Lubricant reduces pain and dryness during sex
claims.note: Reduced friction is the core, well-accepted benefit; especially useful after menopause, while breastfeeding or with some medicines.

claims.claim: Any lubricant is safe with condoms
claims.note: Oil-based products, including lotions and baby oil, rapidly weaken latex; use water- or silicone-based with latex condoms.

claims.claim: Spermicidal lubricants protect against STIs
claims.note: Nonoxynol-9 did not reduce HIV or STIs in trials of more than 5,000 women and increased genital lesions.

claims.claim: Feminine washes keep the vagina clean and balanced
claims.note: The vagina is self-cleaning; douching is associated with bacterial vaginosis and other infections. Plain water on the outside is enough.

claims.claim: 'Body-safe' or 'natural' means gentler
claims.note: Unregulated wording. Osmolality, pH and ingredient list tell you more.

look_for: Water- or silicone-based if you use latex condoms or diaphragms.
A water-based lubricant with a short list and low glycerin/propylene glycol, or a stated iso-osmolar formula, if you are prone to irritation or infections.
Silicone-based for longer-lasting glide (not with silicone toys unless the maker allows it).
Fragrance-, flavor- and warming-agent-free if you have sensitive skin.
For ongoing dryness after menopause, a vaginal moisturizer used regularly, not only at sex.
skip: Nonoxynol-9 spermicidal lubricants for STI protection.
Douches, scented washes, wipes and 'feminine deodorant' sprays.
Oil-based products, lotions and petroleum jelly with latex condoms.
Warming, tingling and flavored lubricants if you react easily.
safety: Lubricant does not protect against pregnancy or STIs; use condoms for that.
Some lubricants can lower sperm movement; if trying to conceive, ask about fertility-friendly products.
Itching, burning, unusual discharge or odor warrant a clinician visit rather than a new wash; these can be infections that need treatment.
Persistent dryness or pain with sex, or bleeding after sex, should be checked by a clinician; after menopause, prescription vaginal estrogen may help.
how_to_use: Apply to both partners or the condom's outside, and reapply as needed.
Wash the outer genital area with water or a mild unscented cleanser only.

studies.title: Is wetter better? An evaluation of over-the-counter personal lubricants for safety and anti-HIV-1 activity
studies.authors: Dezzutti CS, Brown ER, Moncla B, Russo J, Cost M, Wang L, Uranker K, Kunjara Na Ayudhya RP, Pryke K, Pickett J, Leblanc MA, Rohan LC
studies.study_type: Laboratory study (cell lines and tissue explants)
studies.finding_summary: Of 14 over-the-counter lubricants, hyperosmolar water-based gels reduced tissue viability and caused epithelial damage in ectocervical and colorectal tissue, and some were toxic to lactobacilli. Near-iso-osmolar and silicone-based lubricants were the safest.

studies.title: Mineral oil lubricants cause rapid deterioration of latex condoms
studies.authors: Voeller B, Coulson AH, Bernstein GS, Nakamura RM
studies.finding_summary: Sixty seconds of exposure to mineral oil cut the burst volume of latex condoms by about 90%; mineral-oil lotions and baby oil also weakened them. Glycerol and water-based spermicide had no significant effect.

studies.title: Nonoxynol-9 spermicide for prevention of vaginally acquired HIV and other sexually transmitted infections: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials including more than 5000 women
studies.authors: Wilkinson D, Tholandi M, Ramjee G, Rutherford GW
studies.finding_summary: Nine trials in 5,096 women: nonoxynol-9 did not reduce HIV, gonorrhoea, chlamydia or other infections versus placebo, and genital lesions were more common (RR 1.18). The authors concluded it cannot be recommended for HIV and STI prevention.

name: Lip balm
summary: Seals moisture into chapped lips. Choose one with SPF for outdoors; lips burn, and sun is the main risk factor for lip cancer.
what:
Lips have a thin outer layer and no oil glands, so they dry and chap easily in wind, cold and sun. Lip balms are mostly occlusives (petrolatum, beeswax, plant butters, lanolin) that slow water loss. Some add **sunscreen filters** (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, avobenzone, octisalate, octocrylene); tinted balms and lip products add pigment.

The lower lip gets a lot of sun, and long-term sun exposure is the main risk factor for lip cancer, alongside smoking. An SPF balm is the lip equivalent of sunscreen.

evidence.summary: Occlusive balms reliably reduce dryness; this is basic skin physiology rather than trial evidence. A small case-control study of women in Los Angeles found lip cancer risk rose steeply with lifetime sun exposure and that frequent lip protection was associated with lower risk. There are no randomized trials of SPF lip balm and lip cancer.

claims.claim: Heals chapped lips
claims.note: Occlusive balms protect and let the lip surface recover; reapply often.

claims.claim: SPF lip balm lowers lip cancer risk
claims.note: Consistent with sunscreen biology and one case-control study, but not tested in trials.

claims.claim: Lip balm is addictive
claims.note: There's no dependence. Irritating ingredients (menthol, camphor, phenol, fragrance) or licking can keep lips dry, which feels like needing more.

claims.claim: Plumping lip products add lasting volume
claims.note: They irritate the lips to swell them temporarily.

look_for: A plain occlusive base (petrolatum, beeswax, shea) for chapped lips.
Broad-spectrum SPF 30 for outdoor use, sport and skiing.
Fragrance-, flavor- and menthol-free if your lips stay irritated; flavors and fragrance can cause allergic cheilitis.
A zinc oxide or titanium dioxide balm if you react to organic sunscreen filters.
skip: Tingling, cooling or 'plumping' balms for chapped lips; menthol, camphor and cinnamon irritate.
Heavily flavored balms for children who lick them off.
Paying extra for collagen or peptide lip treatments.
safety: Stop lip licking; saliva dries lips further and causes lip-licker's dermatitis around the mouth.
Persistent peeling, cracking at the corners or swelling that doesn't improve in two weeks can be allergy, infection or eczema; see a clinician.
See a doctor for a scaly, rough patch on the lower lip that doesn't heal, or any lip sore lasting 3 weeks; it can be sun damage that needs treatment.
Some lip products contain sunscreen filters or fragrance allergens; patch test if you react.
how_to_use: Apply often, especially before bed and before going outside.
Reapply SPF balm every 2 hours outdoors and after eating or drinking.

studies.title: Solar radiation, lip protection, and lip cancer risk in Los Angeles County women (California, United States)
studies.authors: Pogoda JM, Preston-Martin S
studies.finding_summary: 74 women with lip cancer and 105 controls: risk rose strongly with lifetime sun exposure (OR 13.5 for the highest quartile). Among highly exposed women, those using lip protection once a day or less had about twice the risk of those using it more often.

name: Moisturizer
summary: Draws water into skin and seals it in. Useful for dry skin and eczema; cheap basic formulas work as well as luxury ones.
what:
Moisturizers combine three kinds of ingredients. **Humectants** (glycerin, urea, hyaluronic acid, lactic acid) pull water into the outer skin layer. **Emollients** (squalane, plant oils, fatty alcohols) smooth the rough edges between cells. **Occlusives** (petrolatum, dimethicone, mineral oil, shea butter) form a film that slows water loss; petrolatum is among the most effective and allergy to it is very rare. Ceramides, cholesterol and fatty acids resemble the skin's own barrier lipids.

Face creams, body lotions, ointments and foot creams differ mostly in how much oil versus water they contain: lotions are light, creams heavier, ointments the most occlusive. Foot creams usually add high-strength urea or salicylic acid to soften thick skin.

evidence.summary: A Cochrane review of 77 trials found moisturizers reduce eczema severity, prevent flares and reduce steroid use, but found no reliable evidence that any one moisturizer beats another. For ordinary dry skin the evidence is mostly short, small and industry-run. A large trial found daily emollient from birth did not prevent eczema in high-risk babies. Anti-aging claims for moisturizers themselves rest on temporary plumping, not lasting change.

claims.claim: Relieves dry skin and eczema
claims.note: Moisturizers reduce eczema severity and flares in randomized trials, and work better alongside prescribed treatment.

claims.claim: Expensive creams work better
claims.note: Trials have not found one moisturizer reliably better than another; the working ingredients are inexpensive.

claims.claim: Reverses wrinkles
claims.note: Hydration temporarily smooths fine lines. Lasting change comes from sunscreen and retinoids, not the moisturizer base.

claims.claim: Daily emollient in newborns prevents eczema
claims.note: The BEEP trial of 1,394 high-risk infants found no reduction in eczema at age 2 and a small rise in skin infections.

claims.claim: Urea softens rough, thick skin
claims.note: Urea creams improved dryness in trials; higher strengths (10% and up) are used for heels, elbows and rough, bumpy skin.

look_for: A texture for your skin: gel or lotion for oily skin, cream for dry, ointment for very dry or cracked skin.
Both a humectant (glycerin, urea, hyaluronic acid) and an occlusive (petrolatum, dimethicone) for real water retention.
Fragrance-free if you are sensitive or have eczema; 'unscented' can still contain masking fragrance.
Urea (about 10% or more) or lactic acid for rough heels, elbows and bumpy upper arms.
Pump or tube packaging for larger family-size tubs, which keeps fingers out and lasts longer.
For the face in the morning, a moisturizer with broad-spectrum SPF 30 can replace a step, but only if you use a full dose.
skip: Luxury price tags and exotic extracts. Glycerin, petrolatum, dimethicone and ceramides are cheap and effective.
Separate day, night and 'neck' creams unless the texture difference matters to you.
'Firming' and 'lifting' claims, which describe temporary tightening from film-forming ingredients.
Essential-oil-heavy 'natural' creams if you are prone to rashes; they are common allergens.
safety: Stinging on eczema or broken skin is common with urea and lactic acid; use a plain ointment on cracked areas instead.
Babies and people with eczema can react to fragrance, lanolin and preservatives such as methylisothiazolinone; check the list.
Paraffin-based emollients soak into fabric and make it flammable; keep away from open flame if you use large amounts.
See a clinician if dryness comes with widespread itching, thick scaly plaques, weeping or cracking that does not heal, or sudden onset without an obvious cause.
how_to_use: Apply within a few minutes of bathing, while skin is still slightly damp.
Keep showers short and warm rather than hot.
Reapply to hands after washing and to lips and dry patches as often as needed.
For eczema, use generously and often, alongside any prescribed treatment rather than instead of it.

studies.title: Emollients and moisturisers for eczema
studies.authors: van Zuuren EJ, Fedorowicz Z, Christensen R, Lavrijsen A, Arents BWM
studies.finding_summary: 77 trials (6,603 people with eczema): moisturizers lowered investigator-rated severity and reduced flares (RR 0.33) versus no moisturizer or vehicle, and worked better combined with active treatment. There was no reliable evidence that one moisturizer is better than another.

studies.title: Daily emollient during infancy for prevention of eczema: the BEEP randomised controlled trial
studies.authors: Chalmers JR, Haines RH, Bradshaw LE, Montgomery AA, Thomas KS, Brown SJ, Ridd MJ, Lawton S, Simpson EL, Cork MJ, Sach TH, Flohr C, Mitchell EJ, Swinden R, Tarr S, Davies-Jones S, Jay N, Kelleher MM, Perkin MR, Boyle RJ, Williams HC
studies.finding_summary: 1,394 newborns at high risk of eczema were randomized to daily emollient for a year or standard care. Eczema at age 2 was 23% vs 25% (no significant difference), and skin infections were somewhat more common with emollient.

name: Mouthwash
summary: Fluoride rinses help people prone to decay; antiseptic rinses reduce plaque short-term. Neither replaces brushing, and daily antiseptic use has trade-offs.
what:
Mouthwashes do different jobs depending on the active. **Fluoride rinses** (sodium fluoride) add decay protection. **Antiseptic rinses** reduce mouth bacteria: essential oils (thymol, eucalyptol, menthol), cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC), and prescription chlorhexidine. **Cosmetic rinses** freshen breath with flavor and alcohol. **Dry-mouth rinses** are lubricants, and **peroxide rinses** are sold for minor mouth sores.

Know which kind you are buying: a fluoride rinse and an antiseptic rinse are not interchangeable. The actives pages cover sodium fluoride, CPC and the essential-oil actives.

evidence.summary: A Cochrane review found supervised fluoride rinsing cut decay in children's permanent teeth by about 27%. Chlorhexidine sharply reduces plaque, but its effect on mild gingivitis was judged not clinically relevant and it stains teeth. Industry-run trials show essential-oil rinses reduce plaque and gingivitis over six months. Small studies show antiseptic rinsing suppresses nitrate-reducing mouth bacteria and nudged blood pressure up by 2 to 3.5 mmHg; an observational study linked twice-daily use with prediabetes. The long-term meaning of these findings is unknown.

claims.claim: Fluoride mouthwash prevents cavities
claims.note: Strong in children using supervised rinsing; also recommended for adults at higher decay risk.

claims.claim: Antiseptic mouthwash reduces plaque and gingivitis
claims.note: Essential-oil and chlorhexidine rinses reduce plaque; gingivitis benefits are modest, and much of the essential-oil evidence is industry-sponsored.

claims.claim: Mouthwash can replace brushing or flossing
claims.note: Rinses don't remove the sticky plaque film between teeth; mechanical cleaning is the foundation.

claims.claim: Mouthwash cures bad breath
claims.note: Masks odor for a few hours. Persistent bad breath usually comes from gum disease, the tongue, dry mouth or a medical cause.

claims.claim: Daily antiseptic mouthwash raises blood pressure
claims.note: A one-week study in 19 people found a 2 to 3.5 mmHg rise with chlorhexidine; long-term effects of everyday rinses are not established.

claims.claim: Alcohol mouthwash causes mouth cancer
claims.note: Studies are inconsistent. Alcohol-free rinses are a reasonable choice, especially if you have a dry mouth.

look_for: A fluoride rinse if you are prone to cavities, have exposed roots, braces or a dry mouth.
Alcohol-free formulas if you have a dry or sensitive mouth.
Essential-oil or CPC rinses if a dentist suggests extra plaque control.
A dedicated dry-mouth rinse if medicines or conditions leave your mouth dry.
