skip: Daily antiseptic rinsing without a reason, given the unresolved blood-pressure and oral-microbiome questions.
Rinses marketed as 'healthy gums' as a substitute for seeing a dentist about bleeding gums.
Oil pulling as a replacement for brushing or flossing.
safety: Keep mouthwash away from young children; alcohol-containing rinses can poison a child who drinks them, and children under 6 should not use them unless a dentist advises.
Chlorhexidine stains teeth, alters taste and can irritate the mouth; it is a short-term tool a dentist recommends, not a daily product.
Use a fluoride rinse at a different time from brushing (for example after lunch) so you don't wash off toothpaste fluoride.
Persistent bad breath, bleeding gums or a mouth sore lasting 3 weeks warrant a dentist visit.
how_to_use: Swish for the time on the label, spit, and don't eat or drink for about 30 minutes after a fluoride rinse.
Don't swallow.

studies.title: Fluoride mouthrinses for preventing dental caries in children and adolescents
studies.authors: Marinho VC, Chong LY, Worthington HV, Walsh T
studies.finding_summary: 37 trials (15,813 children), mostly supervised school rinsing: fluoride mouthrinse reduced decayed, missing or filled surfaces in permanent teeth by 27% (moderate-quality evidence).

studies.title: Chlorhexidine mouthrinse as an adjunctive treatment for gingival health
studies.authors: James P, Worthington HV, Parnell C, Harding M, Lamont T, Cheung A, Whelton H, Riley P
studies.finding_summary: 51 trials: chlorhexidine added to brushing produced a large reduction in plaque, but the small reduction in mild gingivitis was not considered clinically relevant. Rinsing for 4 weeks or longer caused tooth staining, and taste changes and mouth irritation were reported.

studies.title: Physiological role for nitrate-reducing oral bacteria in blood pressure control
studies.authors: Kapil V, Haydar SM, Pearl V, Lundberg JO, Weitzberg E, Ahluwalia A
studies.finding_summary: In 19 healthy volunteers, a week of chlorhexidine mouthwash cut oral nitrite production by 90% and plasma nitrite by 25%, and systolic and diastolic blood pressure rose by 2 to 3.5 mmHg within a day.

studies.title: Over-the-counter mouthwash use and risk of pre-diabetes/diabetes
studies.authors: Joshipura KJ, Muñoz-Torres FJ, Morou-Bermudez E, Patel RP
studies.finding_summary: Among 945 overweight adults aged 40 to 65 followed for 3 years, using mouthwash at least twice daily was associated with a higher risk of developing prediabetes or diabetes (IRR 1.49 vs non-users); less frequent use showed no association. Observational, so causation is not shown.

name: Serum
summary: A light, concentrated delivery vehicle for an active. Worth buying only for an active with evidence, at a disclosed strength.
what:
A serum is a thin water- or oil-based product meant to carry a higher concentration of an active ingredient than a cream. The format itself does nothing special. What matters is which active is in it, at what strength, and whether it stays stable in the bottle.

The actives with controlled human trials behind them are few: **retinoids** (retinol, retinal, and prescription tretinoin), **vitamin C** as L-ascorbic acid, **niacinamide**, **azelaic acid**, and exfoliating acids. Hydrating serums built on hyaluronic acid or glycerin are simply light moisturizers. Most serums in the aisle are built around extracts, peptides or ferments with little independent evidence. The actives pages cover each ingredient in detail.

evidence.summary: Evidence depends entirely on the active. Tretinoin has vehicle-controlled trials for sun-damaged skin going back to 1988, and retinol reduced fine wrinkles versus vehicle in a small 24-week trial. Niacinamide trials show modest gains in blotchiness and fine lines over 12 weeks, mostly manufacturer-funded. Vitamin C only reaches skin from acidic formulas, and many derivatives did not raise skin vitamin C in lab tests. For most botanical, peptide and ferment serums, there are no good trials.

claims.claim: Retinoid serums reduce wrinkles
claims.note: Tretinoin has the best evidence; retinol works more slowly and gently, with smaller trials. Expect 3 to 6 months.

claims.claim: Vitamin C serum brightens and protects
claims.note: Modest effects in small trials, and only for stable, acidic L-ascorbic acid formulas. It never replaces sunscreen.

claims.claim: Niacinamide evens tone and redness
claims.note: Trials at about 5% show modest improvements over 8 to 12 weeks; most were funded by manufacturers. Higher percentages mainly add irritation.

claims.claim: Hyaluronic acid adds lasting plumpness
claims.note: It hydrates the surface temporarily, like any humectant; it does not replace lost volume.

claims.claim: Peptide and growth-factor serums rebuild collagen
claims.note: Mostly lab and small company-run studies with self-rated outcomes.

claims.claim: Visible results in days
claims.note: Any change from a real active takes weeks to months; instant effects are hydration or light-reflecting particles.

look_for: One evidence-backed active, named with its percentage. A concentration on the label tells you more than a long list of extracts.
Retinol roughly 0.1 to 1%, starting low; retinal or prescription tretinoin if you want stronger effects.
Vitamin C as L-ascorbic acid at about 10 to 20% in an acidic formula, in opaque or airless packaging. Discard it once it turns dark orange-brown.
Niacinamide at 2 to 5%; higher strengths add irritation risk without clear extra benefit.
Fragrance-free, with a short ingredient list, so you can tell what caused a reaction.
Opaque, airless or pump packaging for retinoids and vitamin C, which degrade with light and air.
skip: Stacking several actives at once. It multiplies irritation and makes reactions impossible to trace.
Serums sold on 'stem cells', exotic ferments or trademarked complexes without independent trials.
Very high niacinamide (10% and up) or very high acid strengths as a 'stronger is better' upgrade.
Paying for 'clinically proven' when the proof is a small company panel rating how their skin 'felt'.
safety: Avoid retinoids (retinol, retinal, adapalene, tretinoin) if pregnant, trying to conceive or breastfeeding, unless a clinician approves.
Retinoids and acids make skin more sun-sensitive; wear sunscreen daily while using them.
Expect dryness and peeling for the first 2 to 4 weeks of a retinoid; cut frequency rather than stopping. Stop and see a clinician for swelling, blistering or a spreading rash.
Patch test new serums on the inner arm for 7 to 10 days if you react easily.
how_to_use: Add one new active at a time and wait 2 to 4 weeks before adding another.
Retinoids at night, starting 2 to 3 nights a week with a pea-sized amount for the whole face.
Vitamin C in the morning under sunscreen.
Apply thinnest to thickest: serum first, then moisturizer, then sunscreen in the morning.

studies.title: Topical tretinoin improves photoaged skin. A double-blind vehicle-controlled study
studies.authors: Weiss JS, Ellis CN, Headington JT, Tincoff T, Hamilton TA, Voorhees JJ
studies.finding_summary: In a 16-week double-blind trial of 30 adults, tretinoin-treated forearms improved while vehicle-treated forearms did not, and 14 of 15 faces treated with tretinoin improved versus none on vehicle. Side effects were limited to irritation.

studies.title: Improvement of naturally aged skin with vitamin A (retinol)
studies.authors: Kafi R, Kwak HS, Schumacher WE, Cho S, Hanft VN, Hamilton TA, King AL, Neal JD, Varani J, Fisher GJ, Voorhees JJ, Kang S
studies.finding_summary: In 36 elderly adults (mean age 87), 0.4% retinol applied to one arm up to 3 times a week for 24 weeks reduced fine wrinkling versus vehicle, with increased collagen markers in biopsies.

studies.title: Niacinamide: A B vitamin that improves aging facial skin appearance
studies.authors: Bissett DL, Oblong JE, Berge CA
studies.finding_summary: 50 women applied 5% niacinamide to half the face and vehicle to the other for 12 weeks; the niacinamide side showed less fine lines, hyperpigmented spots, red blotchiness and sallowness. The study was run by a manufacturer.

studies.title: Topical L-ascorbic acid: percutaneous absorption studies
studies.authors: Pinnell SR, Yang H, Omar M, Monteiro-Riviere N, DeBuys HV, Walker LC, Wang Y, Levine M
studies.finding_summary: L-ascorbic acid entered skin only when formulated below pH 3.5, with absorption peaking at 20%. Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, ascorbyl palmitate and dehydroascorbic acid did not raise skin vitamin C levels.

name: Shampoo
summary: Cleans scalp and hair. Anti-dandruff actives have real evidence; 'growth', 'thickening' and 'detox' claims mostly don't.
what:
Shampoo is a detergent for your scalp. Its job is to remove oil, sweat, flakes and product build-up. The main choices are how strong the cleansing is (sulfate shampoos lather and clean hard; milder or 'low-poo' formulas suit dry, curly or color-treated hair) and whether it carries a medicated active.

**Anti-dandruff** shampoos are where the evidence is. Dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis are driven partly by an overreaction to *Malassezia*, a yeast on everyone's scalp. Ketoconazole, ciclopirox, zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide, salicylic acid and coal tar all target flaking. Everything else on the label, from biotin to caffeine to rosemary, spends a minute or two on your scalp before being rinsed away.

evidence.summary: A Cochrane review of 51 trials found ketoconazole and ciclopirox clear seborrheic dermatitis better than placebo over about four weeks, with low- to moderate-quality evidence and little long-term data. Other anti-dandruff actives have supportive but smaller trials. There is no good evidence that 'growth' shampoos regrow hair; a small ketoconazole study in pattern hair loss is a hint, not proof.

claims.claim: Anti-dandruff shampoo controls flaking
claims.note: Ketoconazole and ciclopirox beat placebo in trials; zinc pyrithione and selenium sulfide are also established actives.

claims.claim: Shampoo can regrow hair
claims.note: Growth claims rest on ingredients without controlled evidence. Topical minoxidil is the non-prescription product with trials.

claims.claim: 'Thickening' shampoo makes hair fuller
claims.note: Coating polymers can make strands look fuller; it's cosmetic and washes out, not regrowth.

claims.claim: Sulfates damage hair or are toxic
claims.note: Strong sulfates can dry out curly or color-treated hair and irritate a sensitive scalp, but they are not a cancer or hormone concern.

claims.claim: Washing too often causes hair loss
claims.note: Hairs shed in the shower were already coming out. Wash as often as your scalp needs; daily is fine for an oily scalp.

look_for: For dandruff or itchy flaking: ketoconazole (1 to 2%), zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide, ciclopirox or salicylic acid.
Rotate two anti-dandruff actives if one stops working.
Milder, sulfate-free cleansers if your hair is dry, curly, coily or color-treated, or your scalp is sensitive.
Fragrance-free if you get scalp or neck rashes; fragrance and cocamidopropyl betaine are known allergens.
A clarifying shampoo occasionally if you use a lot of styling product.
skip: Growth, anti-hair-loss and 'follicle-stimulating' shampoos priced for regrowth; they don't have the evidence.
Biotin, collagen and keratin shampoos for hair growth; they don't reach or feed the follicle.
'Scalp detox' claims; product residue does not cause pattern hair loss.
Paying extra for 'natural' or 'clean' labels, which have no legal meaning.
safety: Keep medicated shampoos out of the eyes; selenium sulfide can discolor light or chemically treated hair.
Coal-tar shampoos can stain and increase sun sensitivity; ask a clinician before using them on children or in pregnancy.
See a dermatologist for sudden or patchy hair loss, a painful, red or scaly scalp, or flaking that doesn't respond to anti-dandruff shampoo within a few weeks.
A rash on the scalp edges, neck or ears after a new product may be contact allergy; stop it and consider patch testing.
how_to_use: Focus shampoo on the scalp; the lather rinsing through is enough for the lengths.
Leave anti-dandruff lather on for 3 to 5 minutes before rinsing.
Use anti-dandruff shampoo 2 to 3 times a week for flare-ups, then once a week to keep it controlled.

studies.title: Topical antifungals for seborrhoeic dermatitis
studies.authors: Okokon EO, Verbeek JH, Ruotsalainen JH, Ojo OA, Bakhoya VN
studies.finding_summary: 51 trials with 9,052 people. Topical ketoconazole 2% cut the risk of failed clearance by 31% versus placebo at four weeks, and ciclopirox 1% also beat placebo. Evidence was low to moderate quality, few trials lasted longer than four weeks, and about half had industry ties.

name: Shaving & beard care
summary: Gels, creams, balms and beard oils reduce friction and irritation. Comfort products with no health claims; technique matters more than the can.
what:
Shaving creams and gels soften hair with water and let the blade glide, reducing nicks and razor burn. After-shave balms soothe; alcohol-based splashes sting and dry. Beard oils and balms condition the beard and the skin under it.

The main shaving-related condition is **razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae)**: sharp, cut hairs curl back into the skin and inflame it. It is most common in people with tightly curled hair. Technique, not product, is the main lever: shave less closely, with the grain, with a sharp blade, or switch to clippers.

evidence.summary: There are no good trials showing any shaving cream, gel or beard oil improves skin health. Reviews of pseudofolliculitis barbae agree that prevention through technique (less close shaving, with the grain, or not shaving) is the mainstay, with laser hair removal and topical treatments for persistent cases. Product claims are mostly about comfort.

claims.claim: Shaving gel prevents razor burn
claims.note: Lubrication reduces friction and nicks; blade sharpness, pressure and direction matter more.

claims.claim: More blades give a better, safer shave
claims.note: Multi-blade razors cut closer, which can worsen razor bumps in curly hair.

claims.claim: Beard oil makes beards grow
claims.note: It conditions hair and skin; it doesn't affect growth.

claims.claim: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker
claims.note: The blunt tip feels coarser, but shaving doesn't change the follicle.

look_for: Fragrance-free and low-alcohol gels, creams and balms if you have sensitive skin.
A clear gel if you shape edges and want to see the skin.
For razor bumps: a single-blade or guarded razor, or clippers that leave a little stubble.
A simple unscented oil or balm for beard itch and flaking.
skip: Alcohol-heavy aftershave splashes, which sting and dry.
Heavily fragranced beard oils if the skin underneath gets itchy or red.
Paying for 'growth' beard serums.
safety: Don't share razors; nicks can spread blood-borne infections.
Persistent razor bumps, scarring or dark marks deserve a dermatologist visit; prescription treatments and laser hair removal help.
Itchy, flaky skin under a beard is often seborrheic dermatitis, which responds to anti-dandruff washes.
Stop a product that causes a spreading rash; fragrance and some preservatives in shaving products are common allergens.
how_to_use: Shave after a warm shower, leave the gel on for a minute, and shave with the grain using light pressure.
Rinse the blade often and replace it when it drags.
Apply an unscented balm or moisturizer afterwards.

studies.title: Defining pseudofolliculitis barbae in 2001: a review of the literature and current trends
studies.authors: Perry PK, Cook-Bolden FE, Rahman Z, Jones E, Taylor SC
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: Razor bumps are a chronic inflammatory condition most common in people with tightly curled hair who shave or tweeze often; hair shape and growth direction drive it. Prevention and early intervention are the mainstays, and no treatment is fully curative.

name: Spot & skin treatment
summary: Targeted products for acne, dark marks, rough bumpy skin and eczema patches. A few actives have real evidence; many products are gentle extras.
what:
This shelf covers products aimed at one problem: acne spot treatments and pads, post-acne marks and uneven pigment, rough and bumpy skin (keratosis pilaris) and thick patches, and soothing creams for eczema-prone skin. It also includes lip-repair balms.

The ingredient decides whether a treatment can work. For acne, **benzoyl peroxide**, **adapalene** and other retinoids, **salicylic acid** and **azelaic acid** have trial evidence. For dark marks and melasma, **azelaic acid**, retinoids, **niacinamide** and, by prescription, hydroquinone combinations have the most support, always alongside daily sunscreen. For rough, bumpy skin, **urea**, **lactic acid** and **salicylic acid** lotions help. For eczema, **colloidal oatmeal** creams and plain moisturizers are the baseline. Centella, tea tree and other extracts are mostly soothing extras. The actives pages go into each one.

evidence.summary: The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline strongly recommends benzoyl peroxide and topical retinoids and conditionally recommends salicylic and azelaic acid. A three-trial comparison found 2.5% benzoyl peroxide worked as well as 5% and 10% on inflamed acne with less irritation than 10%. For melasma and dark marks, a Cochrane review found treatments work only modestly and trials are generally poor. Evidence for most botanical spot products is thin.

claims.claim: Benzoyl peroxide clears acne
claims.note: Strongly recommended in guidelines; 2.5% is about as effective as higher strengths with less irritation.

claims.claim: Fades dark spots and post-acne marks
claims.note: Azelaic acid, retinoids and niacinamide help modestly over months; without daily sunscreen, gains are lost.

claims.claim: Hydrocolloid patches heal pimples overnight
claims.note: They protect a spot from picking and absorb fluid from opened lesions; they don't treat acne.

claims.claim: Tea tree and centella treat acne as well as drugs
claims.note: Small trials only. Pleasant soothing extras, not substitutes for evidence-based actives.

claims.claim: Urea and acid lotions smooth rough, bumpy arms
claims.note: Keratolytic moisturizers soften the plugs of keratosis pilaris; the bumps return if you stop.

look_for: For acne: benzoyl peroxide 2.5 to 5%, adapalene 0.1%, or salicylic acid 0.5 to 2%, used on the whole affected area, not just visible spots.
For dark marks and melasma: azelaic acid, a retinoid or niacinamide, plus a daily broad-spectrum sunscreen (tinted mineral for melasma).
For rough, bumpy skin and thick heels: urea (10% or more), lactic acid or salicylic acid lotion.
For eczema-prone patches: fragrance-free colloidal oatmeal or ceramide creams.
The active and its percentage on the label; in the US, acne products list them in a Drug Facts box.
skip: Spot treatments with long lists of extracts and no recognised acne active.
Strong multi-acid 'peels' used at home on top of other actives.
Skin-lightening creams bought online from unverified sellers, which can contain mercury or undisclosed steroids.
Toothpaste, lemon juice or baking soda on pimples; they irritate without treating.
safety: Avoid retinoids (including adapalene) if pregnant, trying to conceive or breastfeeding unless a clinician approves; azelaic acid is often considered compatible, but confirm.
Benzoyl peroxide bleaches fabric and can irritate; start every other day. Stop and seek care for swelling, hives or trouble breathing, which are rare but serious reactions.
Hydroquinone has not been legally sold without a prescription in the US since 2020; long-term misuse can cause blue-black darkening (ochronosis).
See a dermatologist for acne that scars, is deep and painful, or doesn't improve after 2 to 3 months of consistent treatment, and for pigment that is new, changing or one-sided.
A 'breakout' that is really persistent redness, flushing or scaly patches may be rosacea or dermatitis and needs a diagnosis.
how_to_use: Apply acne treatments to the whole area prone to breakouts, not just existing spots.
Introduce one active at a time; give it 8 to 12 weeks before judging.
Pair any acne or pigment treatment with a moisturizer and daily sunscreen.

studies.title: Guidelines of care for the management of acne vulgaris
studies.authors: Reynolds RV, Yeung H, Cheng CE, Cook-Bolden F, Desai SR, Druby KM, Freeman EE, Keri JE, Stein Gold LF, Tan JKL, Tollefson MM, Weiss JS, Wu PA, Zaenglein AL, Han JM, Barbieri JS
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: The AAD's acne guideline makes strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline, and conditional recommendations for salicylic acid and azelaic acid, among others. It advises combining topical treatments with different mechanisms.

studies.title: Comparing 2.5%, 5%, and 10% benzoyl peroxide on inflammatory acne vulgaris
studies.authors: Mills OH Jr, Kligman AM, Pochi P, Comite H
studies.finding_summary: In 153 people with mild to moderately severe acne, 2.5% benzoyl peroxide beat its vehicle and matched 5% and 10% gels for reducing inflamed spots, with less peeling, redness and burning than 10%.

studies.title: Interventions for melasma
studies.authors: Rajaratnam R, Halpern J, Salim A, Emmett C
studies.finding_summary: 20 trials (2,125 people) covering 23 treatments. Triple-combination cream (hydroquinone, tretinoin, a steroid) lightened melasma more than hydroquinone alone, and 20% azelaic acid beat 2% hydroquinone. Study quality was generally poor and treatments were judged inadequate.

name: Styling product
summary: Creams, gels and sprays that shape and hold hair. Purely cosmetic; the health questions are heat damage, tight styles and the odd allergen.
what:
Styling products (curl creams, gels, custards, mousses, pomades, smoothing lotions, hairsprays and heat protectants) use film-forming polymers, oils and silicones to hold shape, define curls and control frizz. They don't change the health of the scalp or the growth of hair.

What affects hair health is how you style. **Heat** from flat irons, curling tongs and very hot dryers damages the cuticle. **Tight styles** worn for long periods, such as tight ponytails, braids, weaves and extensions, can cause traction alopecia, hair loss along the hairline that is reversible early and permanent if it continues for years.

evidence.summary: Lab studies show hair-surface damage rises with drying temperature, and that a dryer used on low heat at a distance does less harm than very hot tools. Heat protectants reduce damage in manufacturer lab tests, but independent trials are scarce. Reviews of traction alopecia consistently link long-term tight styling, extensions and chemical relaxing to hairline loss that can become permanent.

claims.claim: Heat protectant prevents heat damage
claims.note: Lab tests show some reduction; the bigger levers are lower temperatures and fewer passes.

claims.claim: Curl creams and gels are bad for your scalp
claims.note: Most are inert on the scalp; heavy build-up is a cosmetic issue fixed by washing.

claims.claim: Tight styles can cause permanent hair loss
claims.note: Traction alopecia is well documented; loosening styles early lets hair recover.

claims.claim: Styling products nourish or strengthen hair
claims.note: Vitamins, proteins and oils in stylers affect feel and shine, not the strength of new growth.

look_for: A product matched to your hair type and goal: light mousse or spray for fine hair, creams and custards for curls and coils, gels for hold.
A heat protectant if you use hot tools, together with the lowest temperature that works.
Fragrance-free options if you get rashes on the hairline, forehead or neck.
Non-aerosol sprays if you are sensitive to inhaled sprays.
skip: 'Strengthening' and 'growth' claims on stylers.
Very high flat-iron temperatures on wet or damp hair.
Products sold as 'damage erasing' in one use.
safety: Loosen or vary tight ponytails, braids, weaves and extensions, especially if you notice thinning, bumps or tenderness at the hairline.
Use aerosol hairspray in a ventilated room and keep it away from flames and eyes.
Oily pomades and heavy creams near the hairline can cause forehead acne.
See a dermatologist early for hairline thinning; traction alopecia becomes permanent if tension continues.
how_to_use: Air-dry partly, then use a dryer on medium heat, kept moving, about 15 cm from the hair.
Keep flat irons and tongs to the lowest effective setting and a single pass per section.

studies.title: Hair shaft damage from heat and drying time of hair dryer
studies.authors: Lee Y, Kim YD, Hyun HJ, Pi LQ, Jin X, Lee WS
studies.finding_summary: Hair tresses washed and dried 30 times showed more surface damage as drying temperature rose, up to 95°C. Using a dryer at 15 cm with continuous motion caused less damage than letting hair dry naturally.

studies.title: All hairstyles are not created equal: What the dermatologist needs to know about black hairstyling practices and the risk of traction alopecia (TA)
studies.authors: Haskin A, Aguh C
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: A review that ranks common styling practices into high-, moderate- and low-risk categories for traction alopecia and outlines diagnosis and conservative management, aiming to stop hair loss before it becomes permanent.

studies.title: Traction alopecia: the root of the problem
studies.authors: Billero V, Miteva M
studies.finding_summary: Traction alopecia affects about one-third of women of African descent who wear tight styles long-term; risk rises with tension, duration and chemical relaxing. Tight buns, ponytails, weaves, extensions and tight braids carry the highest risk, and late disease can become irreversible scarring.

name: Sunscreen
summary: The one skincare product with randomized-trial evidence for fewer skin cancers and slower skin aging, if you apply enough of it every day.
what:
Sunscreen absorbs (and to a small degree scatters) ultraviolet light before it damages skin cells. **SPF** measures protection against UVB, the burning rays; **broad spectrum** (US), the circled UVA logo (EU) or a PA+ to PA++++ rating (Asia) tells you it also covers UVA, which reaches deeper, passes through window glass and drives much of photoaging.

Filters come in two families. **Mineral** filters are zinc oxide and titanium dioxide. **Organic** ("chemical") filters include avobenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate, oxybenzone and newer ones such as bemotrizinol and bisoctrizole, which are sold in Europe and Asia. Both families work. The actives pages cover each filter; zinc oxide and avobenzone are the two most worth knowing.

evidence.summary: In the Nambour randomized trial (1,621 Australian adults, 4.5 years), daily sunscreen cut the number of squamous-cell carcinomas by about 39% and slowed measurable skin aging; basal-cell carcinoma was not reduced. Long-term follow-up found half as many melanomas in the daily group, a borderline result based on small numbers. The trial tested SPF 15+ on the head, arms and hands in a sunny region, so the size of benefit elsewhere is extrapolated. FDA studies show several organic filters are absorbed into the blood; that triggers further safety testing but is not evidence of harm.

claims.claim: Prevents skin cancer
claims.note: Randomized evidence for squamous-cell carcinoma and, less certainly, melanoma. No reduction in basal-cell carcinoma was shown.

claims.claim: Prevents wrinkles and sun spots
claims.note: Daily users in the Nambour trial showed no detectable increase in photoaging over 4.5 years and 24% less aging than occasional users.

claims.claim: Higher SPF is always much better
claims.note: SPF 30 blocks about 97% of UVB and SPF 50 about 98% at the tested dose, but real users apply far less, so a higher number buys margin for under-application.

claims.claim: Chemical filters are toxic because they get into your blood
claims.note: Absorption above FDA's screening threshold is shown; harm in people is not. It is a reason for more data, and a reason some people prefer mineral filters, not a reason to skip sunscreen.

claims.claim: Mineral sunscreen reflects UV while chemical absorbs it
claims.note: Zinc oxide and titanium dioxide also protect mainly by absorbing UV; only a few percent is reflected.

claims.claim: Reef safe
claims.note: An unregulated label. Reef concerns about oxybenzone and octinoxate come mostly from lab studies at high concentrations.

claims.claim: Sunscreen causes vitamin D deficiency
claims.note: Real-world studies find little effect on vitamin D levels. If you are worried, test your level rather than skip protection.

look_for: Broad spectrum (or the circled UVA logo, or PA+++ or higher) so UVA is covered, not just UVB.
SPF 30 or higher for daily use; SPF 50 for long outdoor days, fair skin or a history of skin cancer.
A texture you will actually wear every day in a full dose. This predicts protection better than price or brand.
Zinc oxide (alone or with titanium dioxide) if your skin is sensitive, for children, or if you want the filters with the most regulatory certainty.
Water resistant (40 or 80 minutes) for swimming and sport, and a plan to reapply after that time.
A tinted mineral formula with iron oxides if you have melasma, since visible light also darkens it.
An expiry date, or a recent purchase. Heat degrades filters, so don't keep a bottle in a hot car.
skip: SPF above 50+ as a reason to apply less or stay out longer. The gain on paper is small and people burn by under-applying, not by choosing SPF 50 over 70.
Paying extra for "reef safe", "clean" or "non-toxic" labels. None is regulated.
Relying on SPF in makeup or tinted moisturizer. You would need a thick layer to reach the labeled number.
Sprays and powders as your only product. It is hard to get an even, full dose, and sprays should not be inhaled.
Sunscreen "pills" and supplements marketed as oral sun protection. They are not a substitute for a topical filter.
safety: Keep babies under 6 months out of direct sun rather than relying on sunscreen, and ask a pediatrician before using it on them.
Oxybenzone and octocrylene are among the more common sunscreen allergens. If a rash appears where you applied it, switch to a zinc-oxide formula and see a dermatologist if it persists.
Some medicines make you burn much faster, including doxycycline and other tetracyclines, hydrochlorothiazide, isotretinoin and topical retinoids. Ask your pharmacist and be stricter with protection.
No sunscreen makes a tanning bed safe; UV tanning devices are classified as carcinogenic to humans.
See a clinician for any new or changing mole, or a sore that does not heal within a few weeks.
how_to_use: Apply as the last morning step on any day the UV index is 3 or above, which in many places is most of the year.
Use about a quarter to half a teaspoon for face and neck, and roughly 30 mL (a shot glass) for an adult body in swimwear.
Don't miss ears, the back of the neck, the backs of hands and any scalp part.
Reapply at least every 2 hours outdoors, and after swimming, heavy sweating or towelling.
Treat it as one layer: shade around midday, a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses and clothing do much of the work.

studies.title: Daily sunscreen application and betacarotene supplementation in prevention of basal-cell and squamous-cell carcinomas of the skin: a randomised controlled trial
studies.authors: Green A, Williams G, Neale R, Hart V, Leslie D, Parsons P, Marks GC, Gaffney P, Battistutta D, Frost C, Lang C, Russell A
studies.finding_summary: 1,621 adults in Nambour, Australia, were randomized to daily SPF 15+ sunscreen or discretionary use for 4.5 years. The number of squamous-cell carcinomas was 39% lower with daily use (rate ratio 0.61); basal-cell carcinoma was not reduced.

studies.title: Reduced melanoma after regular sunscreen use: randomized trial follow-up
studies.authors: Green AC, Williams GM, Logan V, Strutton GM
studies.finding_summary: Ten years after the Nambour trial ended, the daily-sunscreen group had 11 new melanomas versus 22 in the discretionary group (HR 0.50, borderline significance) and fewer invasive melanomas (3 vs 11).

studies.title: Sunscreen and prevention of skin aging: a randomized trial
studies.authors: Hughes MC, Williams GM, Baker P, Green AC
studies.finding_summary: In 903 Nambour participants under 55, daily broad-spectrum sunscreen users showed no detectable increase in skin aging over 4.5 years, and aging was 24% less than in the discretionary-use group, graded blind from skin casts.

studies.title: Effect of Sunscreen Application on Plasma Concentration of Sunscreen Active Ingredients: A Randomized Clinical Trial
studies.authors: Matta MK, Florian J, Zusterzeel R, Pilli NR, Patel V, Volpe DA, Yang Y, Oh L, Bashaw E, Zineh I, Sanabria C, Kemp S, Godfrey A, Adah S, Coelho S, Wang J, Furlong LA, Ganley C, Michele T, Strauss DG
studies.finding_summary: In 48 healthy adults applying sunscreen at 2 mg/cm² to 75% of the body, avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate all exceeded FDA's 0.5 ng/mL screening threshold after one application. The authors state this does not mean people should stop using sunscreen.

name: Teeth whitening
summary: Peroxide strips and gels do lighten teeth, at the cost of temporary sensitivity. A cosmetic choice with no health benefit.
what:
Teeth darken from surface stains (coffee, tea, wine, tobacco) and from changes inside the tooth with age. **Bleaching** products use hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide (which breaks down into hydrogen peroxide) to lighten the tooth's own color: whitening strips, paint-on gels, tray gels from a dentist, and in-office treatments. **Stain-removal** products such as whitening toothpastes and 'accelerators' polish off surface stain without changing inner color.

Bleaching doesn't lighten crowns, veneers or fillings, so results can look uneven if you have visible dental work. The hydrogen peroxide active page covers strengths and safety.

evidence.summary: A 2018 Cochrane review of 71 trials found home peroxide products whitened teeth versus placebo over 2 weeks to 6 months, but the certainty was low to very low and it could not say which product, strength or schedule is best. Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation were the common side effects, more frequent at higher strengths, and mostly mild and temporary. Most trials were short and many were manufacturer-sponsored.

claims.claim: Peroxide strips and gels whiten teeth
claims.note: Consistent whitening versus placebo in short trials, though evidence certainty is low.

claims.claim: Whitening damages enamel
claims.note: At home-use strengths used as directed, serious enamel damage isn't shown in trials; long-term data are limited and overuse raises risk.

claims.claim: Charcoal and baking soda whiten safely
claims.note: They only scrub surface stain, and charcoal products lack evidence for safety or efficacy.

claims.claim: LED lights speed up home whitening
claims.note: Evidence for added benefit from consumer lights is weak.

claims.claim: Results are permanent
claims.note: Color gradually relapses over months, faster with coffee, tea, wine and smoking.

look_for: Hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide as the listed active if you want an actual shade change.
Lower-strength products used longer if you have sensitive teeth.
A dental check first if you have decay, gum disease, exposed roots, or front crowns and fillings that won't change color.
A potassium-nitrate or stannous-fluoride toothpaste during whitening to limit sensitivity.
skip: Charcoal powders and DIY abrasives.
LED gadgets sold as the key ingredient.
Unbranded high-strength gels bought online, which may exceed legal peroxide limits.
Whitening more often than the label says to chase a brighter shade.
safety: Expect temporary tooth sensitivity and gum irritation; pause or use a lower strength if it's bothersome.

Not advised during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or for children and teenagers, without dental advice; the EU limits over-the-counter products to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide and restricts stronger ones to dental supervision for adults.
Keep gel off the gums and don't use on broken or inflamed gums.
Sudden darkening of a single tooth needs a dentist, not bleach; it can signal a dying nerve.
how_to_use: Follow the label's wear time and course length exactly.
Brush and floss before applying strips so the gel contacts clean enamel.
Avoid staining foods and drinks for a few hours after each session.

studies.title: Home-based chemically-induced whitening (bleaching) of teeth in adults
studies.authors: Eachempati P, Kumbargere Nagraj S, Kiran Kumar Krishanappa S, Gupta P, Yaylali IE
studies.finding_summary: 71 trials: home peroxide gels, strips and other bleaching products whitened teeth versus placebo over 2 weeks to 6 months, with low- to very low-certainty evidence and no reliable way to rank products. Sensitivity and oral irritation were the most common side effects, more common at higher concentrations, and mild and transient.

studies.title: Charcoal and charcoal-based dentifrices: A literature review
studies.authors: Brooks JK, Bashirelahi N, Reynolds MA
studies.journal: Journal of the American Dental Association
studies.finding_summary: 118 articles screened; no clinical trial met inclusion criteria, and some reports described harms such as enamel abrasion. The authors found insufficient evidence for the safety and efficacy claims of charcoal toothpastes and powders.

name: Toner & essence
summary: An optional watery step. Hydrating toners are light moisturizers; acid toners are exfoliants. No toner is needed to 'rebalance' skin.
what:
Toners began as alcohol-heavy astringents to remove soap residue. Today the word covers very different products: **hydrating toners and essences** (glycerin, hyaluronic acid, plant waters) that act as a thin first layer of moisturizer, **exfoliating toners** with glycolic, lactic or salicylic acid, and **soothing toners** built on extracts such as centella.

None of them is a required step. Modern cleansers don't leave skin at a pH that needs correcting, and skin returns to its own pH on its own. Judge a toner by what is in it: an acid toner belongs with exfoliants, a hydrating one with moisturizers.

evidence.summary: There are no good trials showing a toner step improves skin health or outcomes on its own. Any benefit comes from the ingredients: humectants hydrate, and acids exfoliate (covered under exfoliants). Claims about 'rebalancing pH', 'tightening pores' or 'prepping skin to absorb' later products are not supported by independent studies.

claims.claim: Restores skin's pH after cleansing
claims.note: Skin recovers its pH on its own; a gentle cleanser avoids the problem in the first place.

claims.claim: Shrinks pores
claims.note: Pore size is set largely by genetics, oil production and sun damage. Astringents cause brief tightening only.

claims.claim: Helps later products absorb
claims.note: Damp skin can take up some ingredients differently, but there is no evidence this changes results.

claims.claim: Acid toners smooth texture
claims.note: Glycolic and lactic acid have trial evidence for modest improvement in rough, sun-damaged skin; see exfoliants.

look_for: Know which kind you are buying: hydrating (glycerin, hyaluronic acid) or exfoliating (glycolic, lactic, salicylic acid).
Alcohol-free if your skin is dry or sensitive; high denatured alcohol near the top of the list is drying.
Fragrance-free, especially if you plan to use it daily.
For acid toners, a stated percentage and a plan to use them a few times a week, not twice daily.
skip: Buying a toner because a routine says you must. It is optional.
Alcohol-heavy astringent toners for oily or acne-prone skin; stripping oil can make skin feel worse.
'Pore-minimizing' and 'pH-balancing' claims.
Using an acid toner on top of a retinoid and other acids, which stacks irritation.
safety: Acid toners make skin more sun-sensitive while you use them and for about a week after; wear sunscreen.
Stinging, redness or tightness means you are over-exfoliating; stop the acid and let the barrier recover.
Essential oils and witch hazel preparations can irritate or trigger allergy in sensitive skin.
how_to_use: Apply after cleansing with hands or a cotton pad; press in rather than scrub.
Use acid toners 2 to 3 times a week at first, on nights you don't use a retinoid.

name: Toothpaste
summary: Fluoride is the ingredient that matters: decades of trials show fluoride toothpaste prevents decay. Most other claims are secondary.
what:
Toothpaste combines a mild abrasive (hydrated silica, calcium carbonate) that helps the brush remove plaque and surface stain, a detergent, flavor, and in most products **fluoride** as sodium fluoride, stannous fluoride or sodium monofluorophosphate. Fluoride helps enamel resist acid from mouth bacteria and repair early damage.

Specialty pastes add a second job: **potassium nitrate** or **stannous fluoride** for sensitive teeth, stannous fluoride or zinc for gum health and breath, extra abrasives or low-strength peroxide for whitening, and **nano-hydroxyapatite** as a fluoride alternative. The actives pages cover fluoride, stannous fluoride, potassium nitrate and the abrasives.

evidence.summary: A Cochrane review of 70 trials in 42,300 children found fluoride toothpaste prevented about 24% of decayed, missing or filled tooth surfaces versus non-fluoride paste, with bigger effects at higher concentration and more frequent brushing. A later review found 1,450 to 1,500 ppm slightly outperforms 1,000 to 1,250 ppm, and 1,000 to 1,100 ppm reduces decay in adults. Evidence for sensitivity pastes is weaker, and fluoride-free alternatives such as hydroxyapatite have far fewer trials.

claims.claim: Fluoride toothpaste prevents cavities
claims.note: One of the best-established findings in dentistry, across children, adolescents and adults.

claims.claim: Sensitivity toothpaste relieves sensitive teeth
claims.note: Potassium-nitrate pastes reduced measured sensitivity at 6 to 8 weeks in small trials, but self-rated relief was not clearly better. Stannous fluoride pastes are another option.

claims.claim: Whitening toothpaste whitens teeth
claims.note: Abrasives and polishing agents remove surface stain; they don't change the tooth's inner color like peroxide bleaching.

claims.claim: Charcoal toothpaste whitens and detoxifies
claims.note: A review found no good evidence for its claims, and some charcoal pastes are abrasive and lack fluoride.

claims.claim: Fluoride-free is safer
claims.note: At toothpaste doses used as directed, fluoride's benefit is clear. The real risk is young children swallowing too much, which is why dose guidance differs by age.

claims.claim: Hydroxyapatite works as well as fluoride
claims.note: A few promising trials, several industry-funded; far less evidence than fluoride.

look_for: Fluoride at 1,350 to 1,500 ppm for adults (the UK standard); 1,000 ppm and up still protects.
Stannous fluoride if you have bleeding gums, sensitivity or enamel erosion.
Potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride for sensitive teeth; give it 2 to 4 weeks of twice-daily use.
Low-abrasive pastes if you have exposed roots, receding gums or enamel wear.
Age-appropriate amounts for children rather than fluoride-free paste.
skip: Charcoal pastes and powders, especially fluoride-free ones.
Fluoride-free 'natural' pastes as your only paste unless a dentist advises otherwise.
Paying extra for 'whitening' if your aim is a real shade change; peroxide products do that.
Triclosan pastes; most brands have dropped it and plain fluoride pastes work.
safety: Children: a smear or rice-grain amount under age 3, a pea-sized amount from 3 to 6, and supervise brushing so they spit rather than swallow.
Swallowing large amounts of fluoride toothpaste can upset a child's stomach; contact poison control if a young child eats a lot of it.
High-fluoride prescription pastes (2,800 to 5,000 ppm) are for adults at high decay risk, under a dentist's advice.
See a dentist for sensitivity lasting more than a few weeks, which can signal decay, a cracked tooth or gum recession, and for any mouth ulcer, patch or lump lasting 3 weeks.
how_to_use: Brush twice a day for about two minutes, including last thing at night.
Spit, don't rinse, so fluoride stays on your teeth.
Use a soft brush; a powered brush helps most people remove more plaque.
Replace the brush or head every 3 to 4 months, or sooner if bristles splay.

studies.title: Fluoride toothpastes for preventing dental caries in children and adolescents
studies.authors: Marinho VC, Higgins JP, Sheiham A, Logan S
studies.finding_summary: 70 trials (42,300 children): fluoride toothpaste prevented 24% of decayed, missing or filled tooth surfaces versus non-fluoride paste. The effect grew with higher fluoride concentration, more frequent brushing and supervised brushing.

studies.title: Fluoride toothpastes of different concentrations for preventing dental caries
studies.authors: Walsh T, Worthington HV, Glenny AM, Marinho VC, Jeroncic A
studies.finding_summary: 96 trials: 1,000 to 1,250 ppm and 1,450 to 1,500 ppm fluoride pastes reduced decay versus non-fluoride paste, 1,450 to 1,500 ppm slightly more than 1,000 to 1,250 ppm, and 1,000 to 1,100 ppm reduced decay in adults. Higher strengths in young children should be weighed against fluorosis risk.

studies.title: Powered versus manual toothbrushing for oral health
studies.authors: Yaacob M, Worthington HV, Deacon SA, Deery C, Walmsley AD, Robinson PG, Glenny AM
studies.finding_summary: 56 trials: powered brushes reduced plaque by 11% at 1 to 3 months and 21% beyond 3 months, and gingivitis by 6% and 11%, compared with manual brushing (moderate-quality evidence). Clinical importance was uncertain.

studies.title: Potassium containing toothpastes for dentine hypersensitivity
studies.authors: Poulsen S, Errboe M, Lescay Mevil Y, Glenny AM
studies.finding_summary: Six trials: potassium nitrate toothpaste reduced sensitivity to air blasts and touch at 6 to 8 weeks, but participants' own ratings did not improve significantly. The authors found no clear evidence overall, based on few participants.
